evidence.snippet: Obesity, age and the SAA1 polymorphism are susceptibility factors for idiopathic AA amyloidosis.
evidence.explanation: Directly states obesity as a susceptibility factor for idiopathic AA amyloidosis in a 146-patient study with two control groups.

evidence.snippet: Here we describe a family with primary amyloid A amyloidosis due to a chr11:18287683 T>C (human genome version19) mutation in the SAA1 promoter linked to the amyloidogenic SAA1.1 haplotype.
evidence.explanation: Identifies a segregating promoter variant in a rare hereditary form, distinct from common coding susceptibility alleles.

steps/3.description: A rare SAA1 promoter chr11:18287683T>C variant (hg19), linked to SAA1.1, segregated with sustained SAA elevation and hereditary AA amyloidosis in one family.

evidence.snippet: This condition leads to a doubling of the basal SAA1 promoter activity
evidence.explanation: The reported assay supports increased basal promoter activity; the available abstract does not specify the cell system.

steps/4.description: The hereditary promoter variant approximately doubled basal promoter activity in the reported assay. This regulatory mechanism can elevate SAA without the usual systemic inflammatory driver.

evidence.snippet: HS causes the remodeling of HDL-SAA at mildly acidic pH, producing SAA-rich aggregates.
evidence.explanation: Biochemical and culture experiments demonstrate pH-dependent HDL-SAA remodeling, without locating or proving this step in patients.

steps/5.description: At mildly acidic pH, heparan sulfate remodels HDL-associated SAA into SAA-rich aggregates in vitro. This provides a candidate route from lipid-associated precursor toward aggregation; its timing and anatomical site in human disease remain uncertain.

evidence.snippet: We found that SAA1.5 is more resistant to degradation by MMP-1 than SAA1.1. This difference is caused by the capacity of MMP-1 to cleave at the site of the polymorphism at position 57.
evidence.explanation: Immunoblotting and mass spectrometry demonstrate isoform-dependent MMP-1 cleavage in vitro; this does not establish the rate-limiting protease or cleavage sequence in patients.

evidence.snippet: The MS analyses showed that SAA is C-terminally trimmed in the amyloid fibrils. Whether precleavage is necessary for recruitment of SAA to the fibril template or it occurs after its association to the amyloid is not known.
evidence.explanation: Mass spectrometry of extracted mouse AA deposits supports truncation, while the authors explicitly leave the timing of cleavage unresolved. It does not identify MMP-1 as the tissue protease.

steps/6.description: AA deposits contain truncated SAA species, and MMP-1 cleaves SAA isoforms differently in vitro. These observations do not establish that MMP-1 is the relevant human enzyme or that cleavage must precede fibril assembly.

evidence.snippet: Circular dichroism (CD) measurements demonstrated that the C-terminal truncation induces a reduced α-helical structure of the SAA molecule.
evidence.explanation: Compares truncated SAA(1–76) with full-length protein; the experiment tests a defined fragment rather than proving when proteolysis occurs in vivo.

steps/7.description: Synthetic C-terminal truncation reduces alpha-helical structure in SAA(1–76). This experimentally observed conformational effect is distinct from the unresolved timing of proteolysis in tissue deposits.

evidence.snippet: the binding affinity increases upon formation of soluble amyloid oligomers.
evidence.explanation: Recombinant lipid-free SAA assays show stronger glycosaminoglycan binding after oligomer formation. Native human SAA2 did not show detectable binding in these assays.

steps/8.description: Heparan sulfate and heparin interact with SAA and its aggregates. Binding strengthens during oligomerization, and heparin also binds preformed fibrils. Acidic heparin-induced beta-sheet is pH-reversible and distinct from amyloid. Apparent droplets are a proposed intermediate rather than a demonstrated requirement.

evidence.snippet: A-SAA mRNA levels and A-SAA secretion from adipose tissue were significantly correlated with body mass index (r = 0.47; p = 0.028 and r = 0.80; p = 0.0002, respectively).
evidence.explanation: Human tissue expression and secretion measurements support adipose precursor production; the participants were not an AA amyloidosis cohort.

steps/9.description: Human adipocytes express SAA1/SAA2 and adipose SAA secretion correlates with adiposity. This offers a plausible additional precursor source in obesity-associated idiopathic AA amyloidosis; the adipocyte study did not test amyloid deposition or establish adipose dominance during severe systemic inflammation.

evidence.snippet: Therefore, AA amyloidosis can be thought of as a consequence of long-standing inflammatory disease.
evidence.explanation: Frames chronic inflammatory disease as the upstream trigger of the whole chain.

evidence.snippet: The amyloidogenic disease was a chronic infection (40.8%), a chronic inflammation (38%), a tumor (9.9%), a hereditary disease (9.9%), or was undetermined in 1.4% of cases.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the heterogeneous trigger diseases in a renal AA amyloidosis series, supporting the trigger node as an aetiology-agnostic entry point.

steps/10.description: Persistent inflammation from infections, inflammatory arthritis or monogenic autoinflammatory disease can sustain SAA production. These are heterogeneous causes of the common acquired pathway; overt inflammation is not required in every idiopathic or hereditary case.

evidence.snippet: In AA amyloidosis, the expression of cytokines, particularly interleukin 6, leads to overproduction of serum amyloid A (SAA) by the liver.
evidence.explanation: Review synthesis of the inflammatory hepatic precursor-production pathway.

steps/11.description: IL-6, with other inflammatory cytokines, increases hepatic acute-phase SAA expression and secretion. This node describes the inflammatory liver pathway.

evidence.snippet: Mortality, amyloid burden, and renal prognosis all significantly correlated with the SAA concentration during follow-up.
evidence.explanation: Serial measurements in 374 patients associate precursor concentration with burden and outcome; other determinants of conversion remain unresolved.

steps/12.description: Persistent precursor availability contributes to amyloid formation. Serial SAA concentrations correlate with clinical outcomes, but no single concentration or exposure duration determines deposition in every individual.

evidence.snippet: Generation of amyloid fibrils is nucleation dependent, and once formed, fibrils recruit and catalyze the conversion of native molecules.
evidence.explanation: Synthesis of templated fibril assembly.

evidence.snippet: After incubation, amyloid fibrils were observed by TEM in all samples with and without GAGs
evidence.explanation: Glycosaminoglycans modify assembly kinetics but are not required for fibril formation under all tested conditions.

steps/13.description: SAA species assemble into cross-beta amyloid fibrils through nucleation and elongation. Truncation and extracellular cofactors can alter kinetics, while preformed fibrils provide seeds. Neither obligatory prior truncation nor indispensable GAG binding is assumed.

evidence.snippet: Amyloid deposits regressed in 60% of patients who had a median SAA concentration of less than 10 mg per liter, and survival among these patients was superior to survival among those in whom amyloid deposits did not regress (P=0.04).
evidence.explanation: Longitudinal scintigraphy documents regression in a subset; the association does not guarantee reversibility of established organ damage.

evidence.snippet: AA amyloidosis shows vascular deposits in addition to the glomerular deposits
evidence.explanation: Review synthesis of the renal deposition pattern.

steps/14.description: Extracellular fibrils accumulate in renal, hepatic, splenic and other tissues. The burden can regress after sustained precursor suppression, although regression is not universal and organ injury may remain.

evidence.snippet: The clinical presentation of glomerular and vascular forms was distinct with a clear predominance of proteinuria in glomerular form.
evidence.explanation: The 68-case renal biopsy series links deposition pattern to proteinuria; a mechanistic filtration-barrier interpretation is indirect.

steps/15.description: Glomerular amyloid is associated with heavier proteinuria than vascular-predominant disease. Filtration-barrier injury is the clinical interpretation of this anatomical association; nonselectivity and a specific podocyte lesion were not measured in the cited abstract.

evidence.snippet: Amyloid deposition in the myenteric plexus can potentially result in intestinal pseudo-obstruction
evidence.explanation: The review links enteric neural deposition to dysmotility; other gastrointestinal symptoms can have several contributing lesions.

steps/16.description: Enteric amyloid deposition may impair absorption and motility, causing diarrhea, malabsorption or pseudo-obstruction. The clinical review does not establish one lesion that explains all gastrointestinal manifestations.

evidence.snippet: Tubular atrophy, abundance, and distribution pattern of glomerular amyloid deposits at the time of biopsy were independent predictors of renal outcome.
evidence.explanation: Histological predictors support an association with kidney damage, without proving one obligatory clinical sequence.

steps/17.description: Renal involvement can lead to loss of filtration and end-stage kidney disease. The tempo varies with deposition pattern, baseline injury and control of SAA production; vascular or tubular disease need not pass through nephrotic syndrome.

evidence.snippet: The clinical presentation of glomerular and vascular forms was distinct with a clear predominance of proteinuria in glomerular form.
evidence.explanation: Proteinuria predominates in glomerular disease. The 80.9% figure counts the histological form, not the proportion with proteinuria.

evidence.snippet: the prevailing symptoms frequently involve the emergence of proteinuria and gradual reduction in kidney function, apparent in over 90% of patients upon their initial presentation
evidence.explanation: The review reports a combined renal presentation; it does not give a separate proteinuria denominator.

steps/18.description: Proteinuria is a major renal presentation, especially with glomerular deposition. The review groups proteinuria with declining kidney function in its >90% estimate, so that percentage is not assigned to proteinuria alone.

evidence.snippet: Nephrotic syndrome and renal insufficiency were noted in 63.1% and 75% of patients, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Directly quantifies renal insufficiency at 75%, mapping to the FREQUENT band (30-79%).

steps/19.description: Renal insufficiency occurred in 75% of the 68-case renal biopsy series; renal selection limits generalization.

evidence.snippet: At the end of follow-up, 26 patients (38.2%) showed end-stage renal disease.
evidence.explanation: Directly quantifies progression to end-stage renal disease at 38.2%, mapping to the FREQUENT band (30-79%).

steps/20.description: At the end of follow-up, 26/68 patients in the selected renal series had end-stage kidney disease. This cumulative follow-up observation is not an initial-presentation prevalence.

evidence.snippet: Hepato- and splenomegaly commonly manifests during disease progression, whereas splenic rupture is exceptionally rare
evidence.explanation: Directly documents hepatomegaly as a common manifestation of human AA amyloidosis during disease progression.

evidence.snippet: While splenic and hepatic amyloid deposition is commonly detected in serum amyloid P (SAP) scintigraphy, its clinical relevance is limited
evidence.explanation: Records the important caveat that hepatic deposition is frequently imaged but usually not clinically consequential, so this phenotype should not be read as hepatic failure. The limitation is that it qualifies rather than strengthens the association.

steps/21.description: Hepatomegaly can develop with hepatic deposition. Imaging evidence of deposition does not necessarily imply functional liver disease.

evidence.explanation: Directly documents splenomegaly as a common manifestation of human AA amyloidosis, replacing the model-organism-only support this phenotype previously carried.

steps/22.description: Splenomegaly can occur during progression. Splenic deposits can be imaged even when clinically silent; rupture is exceptionally rare.

evidence.snippet: Approximately 30% of cases have gastrointestinal involvement. The predominant symptom is diarrhea that is frequently unresponsive to standard treatment
evidence.explanation: The review describes diarrhea, while the 30% estimate counts any gastrointestinal involvement and is not used as a diarrhea frequency.

steps/23.description: Diarrhea is the predominant symptom of gastrointestinal involvement and can be refractory to usual symptomatic treatment. The reported approximately 30% frequency applies to gastrointestinal involvement overall, not specifically to diarrhea.

evidence.snippet: the presence of the SAAalpha/alpha genotype (OR 2.99, 95% CI 1.47-6.09)
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the independent association of the amyloidogenic SAA1 alpha/alpha genotype with renal amyloidosis in a 277-patient FMF cohort.

evidence.snippet: Finally, the SAA1 polymorphism was confirmed as a susceptibility factor for AA amyloidosis irrespective of the type of the disease.
evidence.explanation: Confirms SAA1 polymorphism as a susceptibility factor across trigger diseases, supporting the SUSCEPTIBILITY relationship type.

evidence.snippet: These results may explain the higher risk of amyloidosis in patients with a SAA1.1/1.1 genotype vs SAA1.5/1.5 or SAA1.1/1.5 genotype.
evidence.explanation: The authors propose isoform-dependent MMP-1 cleavage as one explanation for the clinical association; the assay does not establish mediation of human risk.

evidence.snippet: no association was found between the MICA gene exon 5 polymorphism and the development of renal amyloidosis in FMF patients, whereas the alpha allele and the alpha/alpha genotype of the SAA1 gene were associated with this severe phenotype
evidence.explanation: This independent FMF study supports the SAA1 association and reports a cohort-specific MICA null. It does not prove a universal absence of MICA effects.

A separate rare promoter variant is causal in hereditary AA amyloidosis and is recorded independently below.

evidence.explanation: The cited 277-patient FMF cohort reports an independent association between M694V homozygosity and renal amyloidosis, with OR 4.27 (95% CI 2.01–9.07).

evidence.snippet: Overall, disease severity and the development of amyloidosis in FMF are differentially affected by genetic variations within and outside the MEFV gene.
evidence.explanation: The authors distinguish effects of MEFV and other genetic factors on FMF severity and amyloidosis risk.

evidence.snippet: If FMF is untreated, chronic inflammation may lead to AA amyloidosis, the most severe complication of the disease.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews describes AA as a complication of untreated FMF.

genes/1.notes: MEFV causes familial Mediterranean fever, an upstream inflammatory cause of AA amyloidosis. M694V homozygosity was associated with renal amyloidosis in the cited FMF cohort (OR 4.27, 95% CI 2.01–9.07); treatment and other genetic and environmental factors influence risk.

evidence.snippet: Here we describe a family with primary amyloid A amyloidosis due to a chr11:18287683 T>C (human genome version19) mutation in the SAA1 promoter linked to the amyloidogenic SAA1.1 haplotype.
evidence.explanation: Identifies a segregating promoter variant in a rare hereditary form, distinct from common coding susceptibility alleles.

genes/2.notes: The chr11:18287683T>C promoter variant (hg19) linked to SAA1.1 was reported in a family with autosomal dominant sustained SAA elevation and AA deposition. This rare regulatory cause does not imply Mendelian inheritance for common inflammation-associated AA.

evidence.snippet: Deterioration was related to initial serum creatinine values > or = 1.5 mg/dl (P < 0.01) and to mean colchicine dosage < or = 1.5 mg/day (P < 0.001).
evidence.explanation: Associations in a retrospective 1974–1992 cohort of 68 patients with baseline creatinine ≤2.5 mg/dL; this does not establish an absolute response boundary or a dose appropriate for every patient.

evidence.snippet: At the end of the study period, kidney disease had worsened in 31 patients and remained stable in 22. Proteinuria had regressed in 15 patients.
evidence.explanation: Documents stabilization or regression of proteinuria in a substantial share of colchicine-treated patients. The limitation is that this is an uncontrolled retrospective series without a comparator arm, and disease still worsened in the largest single group.

evidence.snippet: In a study examining 960 patients with FMF without evidence of amyloidosis at baseline, the cumulative rate of proteinuria after 11 years was reported as 1.7% in colchicine-compliant patients while 48.9% in the non-compliants
evidence.explanation: The review summarizes an observational association between colchicine adherence and less subsequent proteinuria; adherence groups were not randomized.

evidence.snippet: However, evidence for its efficacy in AA amyloidosis due to causes other than FMF is still quite limited
evidence.explanation: Records the scope limit deliberately encoded in this treatment's name: colchicine's evidence base is FMF-specific and should not be generalized to AA amyloidosis from other triggers.

treatments/0.description: Colchicine controls FMF inflammation and reduces the risk of AA amyloidosis. In established FMF-associated renal AA, observational studies report stabilization or proteinuria regression in some patients, with worse outcomes when renal injury is advanced. The historical dose and creatinine associations are not universal modern prescribing thresholds; dosing requires individual assessment of renal function, tolerance and interactions.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Suppressing FMF inflammatory attacks removes the cytokine drive at the trigger node, preventing the downstream acute-phase SAA surge.

evidence.snippet: In a retrospective series including 15 patients treated with anti-TNF, amyloidosis progressed in seven patients (46.7%), stabilized in five (33.3%), and regression of proteinuria occurred in three (20%) in 10 months
evidence.explanation: Quantifies outcomes on anti-TNF therapy. The limitation is that amyloidosis still progressed in the largest single group, so this series does not establish efficacy.

evidence.snippet: in a multicenter study in which 36 patients with AA amyloidosis treated with anti-TNF therapy were followed prospectively for 5 years, > 50% decrease in proteinuria was observed in more than half of the patients
evidence.explanation: The stronger of the two datasets - prospective, multicentre, 5-year follow-up - showing a substantial proteinuria response in the majority.

evidence.snippet: a retrospective analysis including 42 patients with AA amyloidosis demonstrated that tocilizumab was superior to anti-TNFs in terms of obtaining a decrease in SAA, improvement in kidney function, and suppression of the disease activity
evidence.explanation: The review reports a 42-patient nonrandomized comparison. Differences in underlying disease and treatment selection limit causal superiority claims.

treatments/1.description: TNF blockade can control an appropriate underlying inflammatory disease, especially inflammatory arthritis, and may improve AA renal markers. Small observational series show variable outcomes. The retrospective tocilizumab comparison does not establish a universal ranking across AA etiologies. Infliximab and adalimumab are antibodies; etanercept is a soluble receptor fusion protein.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Neutralizing TNF-alpha suppresses the inflammatory arthropathy at the trigger node, reducing the cytokine drive to hepatic SAA production.

evidence.snippet: Whole-cohort median pre-treatment SAA fell from 70 to 4 mg/L within 10 days of the first dose; this response has been maintained over an on-treatment follow-up period of 23 months (p<0.0001). AA amyloid deposits either regressed or remained stable.
evidence.explanation: The whole-cohort SAA change covers 20 patients, 14 with AA; amyloid findings apply to the affected subset. This is an uncontrolled series.

evidence.snippet: This small series shows that in patients with treatment-refractory chronic inflammatory conditions TCZ can be effective in suppressing inflammation, and in those with AA amyloidosis, can lead to regression of amyloid deposits.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own conclusion, recorded with its stated limitation. The limitation is that this is an uncontrolled 20-patient case series, of whom 70% had AA amyloidosis, and the authors call for longer follow-up.

evidence.snippet: Steroid pulse therapy, followed by tocilizumab, a IL-6 receptor inhibitor, in combination with oral glucocorticoids dramatically improved kidney and cardiac manifestations with reduction in systemic inflammation.
evidence.explanation: Corroborates organ-level benefit of IL-6 blockade in biopsy-proven AA amyloidosis. The limitation is that it is a single case report with concomitant glucocorticoid therapy.

treatments/2.description: Tocilizumab can suppress SAA in selected refractory inflammatory disorders with AA amyloidosis. A 20-patient uncontrolled series included 14 AA cases and reported rapid SAA reduction with stable or regressing deposits; infections were the predominant adverse effect. A Still disease report also used glucocorticoids, preventing attribution to tocilizumab alone. Choice depends on the cause and clinical context.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: IL-6 receptor blockade removes the principal signal inducing hepatocyte SAA transcription, collapsing precursor supply at the amplifier node.

evidence.snippet: In this trial, canakinumab was effective in controlling and preventing flares in patients with colchicine-resistant familial Mediterranean fever, mevalonate kinase deficiency, and TRAPS.
evidence.explanation: Randomized trial evidence that canakinumab controls the autoinflammatory trigger diseases. The limitation is that the trial endpoint was control of the trigger disease, not amyloid burden or renal outcome in AA amyloidosis.

evidence.snippet: IL-1 inhibitors and the TNF inhibitor etanercept control the severity of disease flares and are effective in preventing AA amyloidosis.
evidence.explanation: TRAPS-specific GeneReviews guidance supports control of this upstream cause, not universal efficacy across AA etiologies.

treatments/3.description: Canakinumab (an IL-1beta antibody) and anakinra (an IL-1 receptor antagonist) can control selected autoinflammatory causes of AA. The cited randomized trial demonstrated fewer flares in colchicine-resistant FMF, mevalonate kinase deficiency and TRAPS, not improved AA renal outcomes. Broader GeneReviews guidance supports IL-1 treatment and amyloidosis prevention in the relevant trigger disorders.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: IL-1 pathway inhibition reduces activity of a responsive underlying autoinflammatory disease; canakinumab neutralizes IL-1beta, whereas anakinra blocks its receptor.

evidence.snippet: Patient survival rates were 94.0% (95% CI, 89.1-99.2) at 1 year and 85.5% (77.8-94.0) at 5 years after transplantation.
evidence.explanation: Provides contemporary patient-survival outcomes after kidney transplantation in 86 patients across 26 French centres.

evidence.snippet: Kidney transplantation is preferred in patients with kidney failure, and the recurrence of amyloidosis in the allograft has become rare as transplant recipients have started to benefit from the new agents.
evidence.explanation: States the preference for transplantation and the modern rarity of allograft recurrence.

evidence.snippet: Histologically proven AA amyloidosis recurrence occurred in 5 transplants (5.8%). An infection requiring hospitalization developed in 55.8% of cases

treatments/2.description: ABL tyrosine-kinase inhibition is directed at the BCR::ABL1 dependency of Ph-positive B-ALL. Ponatinib retains activity against many kinase-domain resistance variants, but vascular and other toxicities require specialist selection and monitoring. Results from a single-centre phase 2 study of ponatinib plus blinatumomab are encouraging rather than proof that one combination should replace every established regimen.

evidence.snippet: Ponatinib, a third-generation TKI with the ability to inhibit most BCR-ABL1 kinase domain mutations, has recently gained approval for resistant Ph-positive ALL.
evidence.explanation: The review directly supports ponatinib-mediated inhibition across many BCR::ABL1 kinase-domain variants in resistant Ph-positive ALL.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: ABL kinase inhibition suppresses BCR::ABL1-dependent signaling in Ph-positive B-ALL.

evidence.snippet: The addition of blinatumomab to consolidation chemotherapy in adult patients in MRD-negative remission from BCP-ALL significantly improved overall survival.

treatments/3.description: Blinatumomab brings CD3-positive T cells into proximity with CD19-positive B-lineage blasts. Its established contexts include relapsed/refractory and MRD-directed use; E1910 additionally supports incorporation into consolidation for adults in MRD-negative remission from B-cell precursor ALL.

evidence.snippet: Blinatumomab is a bispecific T-cell engager molecule composed of an anti-CD19 variable region linked to an anti-CD3 variable region that brings T cells in proximity to leukemic blasts to form cytolytic synapses, leading to apoptosis and lysis of the blasts.
evidence.explanation: The trial report directly states the CD19-CD3 cytolytic mechanism.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: CD19-CD3 engagement creates cytolytic synapses that kill CD19-positive B-lineage blasts.

evidence.snippet: The rate of complete remission was significantly higher in the inotuzumab ozogamicin group than in the standard-therapy group
evidence.explanation: Randomized phase 3 evidence supports superior remission rates in adults with relapsed or refractory ALL; the population and endpoint remain explicit.

treatments/4.description: Inotuzumab ozogamicin binds CD22 and delivers calicheamicin intracellularly, causing DNA double-strand breaks and apoptosis. Its relapsed/refractory benefit must be balanced against serious toxicities, including hepatic veno-occlusive disease reported in trials.

evidence.snippet: Inotuzumab ozogamicin (InO) is a monoclonal antibody against CD22 that is conjugated to calicheamicin, a potent cytotoxic compound that induces double-strand DNA breaks.
evidence.explanation: The review directly supports CD22 targeting and the conjugated cytotoxic mechanism.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: CD22-mediated internalization delivers calicheamicin to B-lineage blasts and induces apoptotic DNA damage.

evidence.snippet: In this global study of CAR T-cell therapy, a single infusion of tisagenlecleucel provided durable remission with long-term persistence in pediatric and young adult patients with relapsed or refractory B-cell ALL, with transient high-grade toxic effects.
evidence.explanation: This supports tisagenlecleucel efficacy and also preserves the reported high-grade-toxicity qualification.

treatments/5.description: Autologous T cells engineered with a CD19-directed chimeric antigen receptor can expand and persist after infusion and produce durable remissions in relapsed or refractory B-cell ALL. evidence.snippet: Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS) (sometimes known as acute radiation sickness) is an acute illness caused by radiation exposure (or irradiation) of the entire body (or most of the body) by a high dose of penetrating radiation in a very short period of time (usually a matter of minutes).
evidence.explanation: Clinical guidance defines the systemic exposure pattern.

evidence.snippet: Hereditary atransferrinemia is a rare but instructive disorder that has previously been reported in only 8 patients in 6 families. It is characterized by microcytic anemia and by iron loading, and can be treated effectively by plasma infusions. We now report the first case known in the United States. We determined the sequences flanking the exons of the human transferrin gene and sequenced all of the exons and some of the flanking regions of the patient's DNA and that of her parents. The patient's DNA revealed a 10-base pair (bp) deletion, followed by a 9-bp insertion of a duplicated sequence. There was also a G-->C transversion at complementary DNA (cDNA) nt 1429, predicting that a proline was substituted for the alanine in amino acid position 477 (Ala 477 Pro). The latter mutation occurs at an evolutionarily highly conserved site; 704 control alleles were screened and this point mutation was not found. Each of the patient's transferrin genes contains one mutation, ie, the patient is a compound heterozygote for these mutations, because one was found in each of her parents. In addition to these mutations, which we regard to be causative in the patient's atransferrinemia, a silent polymorphism at cDNA 1572 G-->C was found in exon 13 as well as 2 previously unreported polymorphisms at IVS8 + 62 c-->t and IVS14-4 c-->a. The mutation in nt 1572 and that in intron 8 were common in the general population; the intron 14 mutation is rare.
evidence.explanation: Molecular characterization and familial segregation support two distinct TF alleles; benign polymorphisms described in the same abstract are not causal variants.

evidence.snippet: DNA analysis of the serum transferrin gene in the patient revealed a previously undescribed mutation in exon 4, a G-->A transition at cDNA 410(Cys137Tyr).

evidence.snippet: A 13-year-old girl born of second-degree consanguinity presented with heart failure, severe anemia, and diabetes mellitus. Her clinical course included heart failure at six months, diabetes at age seven, and progressive LV systolic dysfunction. Iron studies revealed low TIBC, elevated ferritin, low transferrin saturation, and undetectable transferrin levels (<75 mg/dL). Echocardiography showed severe biventricular systolic dysfunction. There was an incidentally detected 4 mm PDA (Fig. 4). As the age advanced, heart failure worsened disproportionately. Cardiac MRI confirmed myocardial iron overload, and genetic testing identified a novel mutation, confirming the diagnosis. This highlights the importance of early recognition and genetic analysis in hereditary atransferrinemia.
evidence.explanation: Primary clinical case embedded in a review. Its intronic TF variant is later classified as a VUS, so the phenotype is clinically consistent but the allele is not functionally confirmed.

evidence.snippet: Hereditary atransferrinemia is a rare but instructive disorder that has previously been reported in only 8 patients in 6 families. It is characterized by microcytic anemia and by iron loading, and can be treated effectively by plasma infusions. We now report the first case known in the United States. We determined the sequences flanking the exons of the human transferrin gene and sequenced all of the exons and some of the flanking regions of the patient's DNA and that of her parents. The patient's DNA revealed a 10-base pair (bp) deletion, followed by a 9-bp insertion of a duplicated sequence. There was also a G-->C transversion at complementary DNA (cDNA) nt 1429, predicting that a proline was substituted for the alanine in amino acid position 477 (Ala 477 Pro). The latter mutation occurs at an evolutionarily highly conserved site; 704 control alleles were screened and this point mutation was not found. Each of the patient's transferrin genes contains one mutation, ie, the patient is a compound heterozygote for these mutations, because one was found in each of her parents. In addition to these mutations, which we regard to be causative in the patient's atransferrinemia, a silent polymorphism at cDNA 1572 G-->C was found in exon 13 as well as 2 previously unreported polymorphisms at IVS8 + 62 c-->t and IVS14-4 c-->a. The mutation in nt 1572 and that in intron 8 were common in the general population; the intron 14 mutation is rare.

genes/0.notes: TF encodes the major plasma iron carrier. Recessive defects can markedly lower circulating protein, but individual missense alleles should not all be assigned the same folding, secretion or iron-binding mechanism without functional evidence. The US compound-heterozygous p.Ala477Pro and deletion-insertion case and Turkish p.Cys137Tyr case are reported primary examples. The adult p.Glu370Lys family broadens the clinical spectrum. A newly reported intronic deletion remains a VUS despite a compatible phenotype. A broader hereditary hypotransferrinemia series also described HFE/HAMP or acquired cofactors; those selected cases do not establish that every carrier develops overload.

evidence.snippet: A 13-year-old girl born of second-degree consanguinity presented with heart failure, severe anemia, and diabetes mellitus. Her clinical course included heart failure at six months, diabetes at age seven, and progressive LV systolic dysfunction. Iron studies revealed low TIBC, elevated ferritin, low transferrin saturation, and undetectable transferrin levels (<75 mg/dL). Echocardiography showed severe biventricular systolic dysfunction. There was an incidentally detected 4 mm PDA (Fig. 4). As the age advanced, heart failure worsened disproportionately. Cardiac MRI confirmed myocardial iron overload, and genetic testing identified a novel mutation, confirming the diagnosis. This highlights the importance of early recognition and genetic analysis in hereditary atransferrinemia.
evidence.explanation: Primary clinical case embedded in a review. Its intronic TF variant is later classified as a VUS, so the phenotype is clinically consistent but the allele is not functionally confirmed.

evidence.snippet: Although ARNIs and SGLT2 inhibitors have not been specifically studied in iron overload cardiomyopathies or atransferrinemia, they have shown efficacy in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) in adults. The treatment should be tailored according to the clinical presentation of the patient [25].
evidence.explanation: The review explicitly distinguishes adult HFrEF evidence from disease-specific evidence.

treatments/5.description: Cardiac failure and diabetes require specialist management alongside iron-directed treatment. The review discusses conventional heart-failure therapy but explicitly lacks atransferrinemia-specific evidence for newer adult HFrEF agents; their adult efficacy is not a pediatric disease-specific recommendation.

evidence.snippet: Our patients need to be in long-term follow-up to monitor the effectiveness of therapy and manage iron overload.
evidence.explanation: Authors recommend ongoing monitoring; only one of their two patients remained in follow-up.

evidence.snippet: Cardiac MRI T2* remains a unique and reliable modality for diagnosing and quantifying cardiac iron overload and monitoring therapy in iron overload cardiomyopathies, including atransferrinemia.
evidence.explanation: Review supports the imaging role, without a controlled mortality benefit.

evidence.snippet: Iron status should be monitored in patients with hypotransferrinemia due to a TF defect in order to detect toxic iron loading early.
evidence.explanation: Published disease-specific monitoring recommendation, not an outcome comparison.

treatments/6.description: Follow hemoglobin, transferrin, ferritin and symptoms, with tissue-iron imaging and organ assessment where indicated. Serum ferritin alone does not identify the distribution of cardiac versus hepatic iron. Growth and treatment requirements may change over time.

None of these clinical observations proves a specific compensatory transporter or a universal safe transferrin threshold.

evidence.snippet: Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) deficiency impairs dopamine synthesis in the basal ganglia, leading to childhood-onset dystonia with excellent response to levodopa.

steps/4.description: Reduced GTPCH1 activity lowers tetrahydrobiopterin availability. BH4 is an obligate cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase, so its deficiency limits catecholamine and dopamine synthesis. Hyperphenylalaninemia is not modeled in this dominant subtype because the systematic DRD review found it in PTS and QDPR disease and only rarely in autosomal recessive GCH1 disease.

evidence.snippet: We show that the defect results in degradation of the gene product, causing IMPDH2 deficiency in patient cells.

Dose changes should be gradual, chronic adverse motor fluctuations are uncommon, and abrupt discontinuation should be avoided. Evidence for the rare branches is much thinner: NR4A2 cases were reported as dopa responsive, whereas response was only hypothesized for the published IMPDH2 family.

evidence.snippet: Virtual absence of the carbonic anhydrase II peak on high-performance liquid chromatography, of the esterase and carbon dioxide hydratase activities of carbonic anhydrase II, and of immunoprecipitable isozyme II was demonstrated on extracts of erythrocyte hemolysates from all patients studied.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates absence of the enzyme by three independent methods across 18 patients from 11 unrelated families.

evidence.snippet: We report here biochemical and immunological evidence for the virtual absence of CA II in erythrocytes of patients affected with this condition, whereas CA I level is not reduced.
evidence.explanation: The founding observation, and establishes that the deficiency is isoenzyme-specific rather than a general carbonic anhydrase failure.

evidence.snippet: The 27-kD truncated enzyme produced when the mutant cDNA was expressed in COS cells was enzymatically inactive, present mainly in insoluble aggregates, and detectable immunologically at only 5% the level of the 29-kD normal carbonic anhydrase II
evidence.explanation: Expression study showing one route to loss of function - truncation with aggregation and accelerated degradation.

evidence.snippet: His-107 appears to have a stabilizing function in the structure of all CA molecules, and its substitution by Tyr apparently disrupts the critical hydrogen bonding of His-107 to two other similarly invariant residues, Glu-117 and Tyr-194, resulting in an unstable CA II molecule.
evidence.explanation: A second route to loss of function - destabilisation of a full-length protein by substitution of an invariant residue.

evidence.snippet: Studies suggest that the mutant proteins undergo local structural perturbations and have compromised native state stability.
evidence.explanation: Purified-protein biophysics confirming reduced native-state stability for two disease-linked missense substitutions.

evidence.snippet: We show that the mutant enzyme expressed in bacteria from the cDNA containing the His-107----Tyr mutation has detectable, though greatly reduced, activity.
evidence.explanation: Direct residual-activity measurement prevents interpreting all CA2 alleles as complete catalytic nulls.

steps/1.description: Biallelic splice, nonsense, frameshift or missense variants reduce CA II abundance or activity. Erythrocyte CA II was virtually absent in the founding biochemical series, with CA I preserved, but this does not establish complete loss of activity in every tissue for every allele. Recombinant His107Tyr retains greatly reduced activity. The exon 7 frameshift produces an inactive, unstable truncated protein that accumulates in insoluble aggregates; p.Trp123Ter is a truncating nonsense allele, not a full-length missense product.

evidence.snippet: Carbonic anhydrase II deficiency (OMIM # 259730), initially called "osteopetrosis with renal tubular acidosis and cerebral calcification syndrome", reveals an important role for the enzyme carbonic anhydrase II (CA II) in osteoclast and renal tubule function.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the one enzyme's loss is what couples the osteoclast and renal tubule phenotypes.

steps/2.description: Reduced CA II activity impairs rapid reversible CO2 hydration to bicarbonate and protons. This limits enzyme-supported substrate supply for osteoclast and renal transport. Other carbonic anhydrase activities can persist: CA II-deficient patients retained an acetazolamide-sensitive renal response. The observed brain phenotype is associated with CA2 deficiency, but its intermediate mechanism is unresolved.

evidence.snippet: provide genetic evidence implicating CA II in osteoclast function and bone resorption
evidence.explanation: Human genetic evidence that CA II is required for osteoclast function - the inference the naturally occurring null makes available.

evidence.snippet: explain previous observations that carbonic anhydrase inhibitors block the normal parathyroid hormone-induced release of calcium from bone
evidence.explanation: Pharmacological corroboration: inhibiting carbonic anhydrase phenocopies the resorption block. Indirect because it argues from inhibitor data rather than from the patients' osteoclasts.

steps/3.description: CA II-dependent proton generation supports acidification of the sealed osteoclast resorption compartment. Deficiency impairs this process despite the presence of osteoclasts. The proximal lesion is in intracellular enzyme activity, distinct from variants directly affecting the ruffled-border transport machinery.

evidence.snippet: Most often, the RTA is of mixed proximal and distal type, but kindreds are reported in which either distal or proximal RTA predominates.
evidence.explanation: The direct statement that the renal defect is usually mixed, with kindred-level variation - the reason this entry does not assert a single RTA tier.

evidence.snippet: These findings indicate that CA II-deficient patients, who lack detectable CA II in their erythrocytes, still expressed an acetazolamide-inhibitable CA activity in their kidneys.
evidence.explanation: Qualifies the node: carbonic anhydrase activity is not wholly absent from the CA II-deficient kidney, so the renal defect is a partial rather than a total loss of tubular carbonic anhydrase function.

steps/4.description: CA II-dependent intracellular CO2 hydration supports proximal bicarbonate reclamation. Deficiency can produce a proximal component of renal tubular acidosis, but the relative proximal and distal contributions vary between patients. Acetazolamide challenge in two affected individuals still increased urinary pH and bicarbonate excretion, indicating residual renal carbonic anhydrase activity rather than complete loss of all isoenzymes.

evidence.explanation: The direct statement that the renal defect is usually mixed, with kindred-level variation - the reason this entry does not assert a single RTA tier.

evidence.explanation: Qualifies the node: carbonic anhydrase activity is not wholly absent from the CA II-deficient kidney, so the renal defect is a partial rather than a total loss of tubular carbonic anhydrase function.

steps/5.description: CA II supports proton secretion by collecting-duct intercalated cells. Its deficiency can impair distal urinary acidification. Car2-null mice additionally show depletion of intercalated-cell markers and reduced bicarbonate-transporter expression; these model findings do not establish an identical cellular population defect in human kidneys.

steps/6.description: Impaired acidification reduces osteoclast-mediated resorption of mineralized bone. The coupling of mineral dissolution and matrix removal explains defective remodeling without requiring an increase in the rate of bone formation.

evidence.snippet: Although CA II deficiency is an "osteoclast-rich" OPT, and therefore transplantation of healthy osteoclasts can improve the skeletal disease, the RTA and central nervous system difficulties persist.
evidence.explanation: Describes an osteoclast-rich disorder in which transplantation can improve bone disease despite persistent renal and central nervous system difficulties.

evidence.snippet: mutations in TCIRG1, CLCN7, OSTM1, SNX10 and PLEKHM1 lead to osteoclast-rich ARO (in which osteoclasts are abundant but have severely impaired resorptive function), whereas mutations in TNFSF11 and TNFRSF11A lead to osteoclast-poor ARO
evidence.explanation: Defines the osteoclast-rich versus osteoclast-poor axis this node is placed on. Indirect because this review enumerates the other recessive loci and does not itself mention CA2.

steps/7.description: Reduced resorption allows dense, poorly remodeled bone to accumulate despite the presence of osteoclasts. Bone density does not imply normal mechanical strength. Resolution of osteopetrosis after hematopoietic transplantation supports an osteoclast-lineage defect; it does not prove that every extra-skeletal outcome is unaffected.

evidence.snippet: The disorder presents late in infancy or early in childhood with fracturing, developmental delay, weakness, short stature, and/or cranial nerve compression and palsy.
evidence.explanation: Lists cranial nerve compression and palsy among the presenting features.

evidence.snippet: All internal auditory canals were normal in size, and no patient had clinically significant hearing loss.
evidence.explanation: Bounds the node: foraminal narrowing in this cohort spared the internal auditory canals, so the claim is not that every cranial foramen narrows.

steps/8.description: Dense skull-base bone can narrow cranial foramina. In the 23-patient cohort, optic nerve involvement affected 23 of 46 eyes and correlated with optic canal narrowing, supporting compression as an important mechanism. This association does not exclude an additional neural contribution. Internal auditory canal size was normal in that cohort.

evidence.snippet: All patients had osteopetrosis, renal tubular acidosis, developmental delay, short stature and craniofacial disproportion with large cranial vault and broad forehead.
evidence.explanation: Craniofacial disproportion with large cranial vault and broad forehead was present in all 23 patients.

steps/9.description: Skeletal overgrowth of the skull produces a large cranial vault and broad forehead, with midfacial and mandibular disproportion. The inference that this geometry narrows the upper airway enough to cause obstructive sleep apnea rests on a case report plus the general osteopetrosis literature, so the node is recorded as provisional.

evidence.snippet: Cerebral calcification uniquely appears in early childhood.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the calcification is an early-childhood feature specific to this osteopetrosis.

evidence.snippet: Intraparenchymal calcifications in CAII-D are common but unrelated to developmental delay and neuropsychiatric symptoms, suggesting complex pathophysiology.
evidence.explanation: Supports an established imaging lesion while the lack of association with developmental measures in this small series leaves its causal relationship to neurological impairment unresolved.

steps/10.description: Intracranial mineral deposition is directly observed on imaging, commonly involving basal ganglia, thalami and the frontal grey-white junction. It can progress during childhood and can be absent at a particular assessment. The lesion is established; the causal intermediates connecting CA II deficiency to deposition and cognitive outcomes remain unresolved. A small clinical series found no significant association between calcium burden and developmental measures.

evidence.snippet: The suspicion of carbonic anhydrase II deficiency was confirmed by arterial blood gases revealing a marked metabolic acidosis fulfilling the diagnostic triad.
evidence.explanation: A worked clinical instance of the systemic acidosis being the measurable expression of this node.

steps/11.description: Renal bicarbonate loss and/or impaired net acid excretion produce metabolic acidosis, commonly hyperchloremic, sometimes with hypokalemia. Oral alkali can improve the acid-base disturbance. The combination with osteopetrosis is a strong diagnostic clue but can also occur with coinherited TCIRG1 and ATP6V1B1 disease.

evidence.snippet: All patients had osteopetrosis, renal tubular acidosis, developmental delay, short stature and craniofacial disproportion with large cranial vault and broad forehead.
evidence.explanation: Osteopetrosis in 23/23 patients from 10 unrelated families.

steps/12.description: Generalized increase in skeletal density due to impaired resorption. All 23 patients in the 2011 founder-allele cohort had osteopetrosis; this cohort observation is not a population-wide penetrance estimate.

evidence.snippet: Most often, the RTA is of mixed proximal and distal type, but kindreds are reported in which either distal or proximal RTA predominates.
evidence.explanation: The basis for binding the parent term rather than a proximal or distal child term.

evidence.snippet: Six subsequent Hispanic patients of Caribbean ancestry, all of whom had osteopetrosis and renal tubular acidosis but who varied widely in clinical severity, were found to be homozygous for the same mutation.
evidence.explanation: Supports the association while the same paper documents absence of detectable RTA in its index patient.

evidence.snippet: Further evaluation showed renal tubular acidosis type 2.
evidence.explanation: A case in which the tubular defect was proximal (type 2), illustrating the segment-level variation the parent-term binding accommodates.

steps/13.description: A proximal, distal or mixed tubular acidification defect can occur; different clinical series report different predominant components. Some molecularly confirmed patients lacked detectable acidosis at assessment.

evidence.snippet: In CA II deficiency, OPT is uniquely accompanied by renal tubular acidosis (RTA) of proximal, distal, or combined type featuring hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, rarely with hypokalemia and paralysis.
evidence.explanation: Names hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis as the acid-base phenotype.

steps/14.description: The systemic, measurable expression of the tubular defect: a normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, occasionally with hypokalemia and consequent paralysis.

evidence.snippet: Optic nerve atrophy was observed in 22.2 %, while brain calcifications were present in 70.0 % of cases.
evidence.explanation: Frequency of brain calcification in a consecutive pediatric series.

evidence.snippet: Brain calcification was generally progressive and followed a distinct distribution, involving predominantly basal ganglia and thalami and grey-white matter junction in frontal regions more than posterior regions.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the anatomical distribution recorded in the preferred_term.

steps/15.description: Intracranial parenchymal calcification, the feature behind the historical name "marble brain disease". Present in 70% of a modern 10-patient series and progressive on serial imaging, but age-dependent: a child without calcification at 9 years has been documented.

evidence.snippet: Other features include developmental delay, short stature, cognitive defects, and a history of multiple fractures by adolescence.
evidence.explanation: Records multiple fractures by adolescence as a recognised feature.

evidence.snippet: The presence of mental retardation and relative infrequency of skeletal fractures distinguish the clinical course of the patients with the Arabic mutation from those of the American and Belgian patients with the His 107-->Tyr mutation.
evidence.explanation: Genotype-dependent fracture frequency - the basis for the qualification in the description.

steps/16.description: Repeated fractures of dense but brittle bone, typically accumulating through childhood. Notably, fractures are reported as relatively infrequent in patients carrying the intron 2 founder allele compared with the His107Tyr families.

evidence.snippet: Optic nerve atrophy was observed in 22.2 %, while brain calcifications were present in 70.0 % of cases.
evidence.explanation: 22.2% in the ten-patient pediatric series falls within OCCASIONAL; the abstract does not state the denominator with evaluable optic-nerve assessment.

evidence.snippet: Globes and retinae were normal, but optic nerve involvement was present in 23/46 eyes and was variable in severity, random in occurrence and statistically correlated with degree of optic canal narrowing.
evidence.explanation: Optic nerve involvement in 23/46 eyes is a broader outcome than optic atrophy and must not be pooled with the patient-level estimate. Canal correlation supports, but does not prove exclusivity of, compression.

steps/17.description: Optic nerve atrophy was reported in 22.2% of the later pediatric series. The earlier cohort reported the broader finding of optic nerve involvement in 23 of 46 eyes, which is a different outcome and denominator. Its association with canal narrowing supports a compressive contribution.

evidence.snippet: The disorder presents late in infancy or early in childhood with fracturing, developmental delay, weakness, short stature, and/or cranial nerve compression and palsy.
evidence.explanation: Names cranial nerve compression and palsy as a presenting feature.

steps/18.description: Compression of cranial nerves in narrowed skull-base foramina, with palsy. The optic nerve is the best documented; the internal auditory canals were of normal calibre in the 23-patient cohort.

evidence.snippet: Herein we report a case of osteopetrosis with RTA associated with severe OSAS successfully treated with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP).
evidence.explanation: The single reported case linking this syndrome to severe OSA.

steps/19.description: Severe obstructive sleep apnea attributable to craniofacial dysmorphism rather than to adenotonsillar hypertrophy alone, reported in one child and successfully managed with CPAP.

evidence.snippet: we postulated a defect in carbonic anhydrase II (CA II), the only one of the three soluble isozymes of carbonic anhydrase that is known to be synthesized in kidney and brain
evidence.explanation: The founding study identifies deficiency of this isoenzyme; it does not establish absence of every compensating activity in all tissues.

edges/1.description: Reduced CA II activity slows the enzyme-catalyzed hydration of CO2; it does not abolish all cellular production of protons or bicarbonate.

evidence.snippet: Although this enzymopathy reveals how CA II is important for the skeleton and kidney tubule, the pathogenesis of the mental subnormality and cerebral calcification is less well understood.
evidence.explanation: Supports the association while explicitly stating that the pathogenesis of the cerebral arm is not understood, which is why the edge is typed as indirect with unknown intermediates.

edges/2.description: Cerebral calcification is an observed component of CA2 deficiency, but the intermediate route from enzyme dysfunction to regional mineral deposition is unresolved.

evidence.snippet: CA II deficiency is the paradigm OPT featuring failure of osteoclasts to resorb bone due to inability to acidify their pericellular milieu.
evidence.explanation: States the causal step from enzyme loss to failed pericellular acidification in the osteoclast.

edges/3.description: Reduced rapid proton generation impairs acidification of the osteoclast resorption compartment.

evidence.snippet: This defect causes a mixed form of RTA due to waste of bicarbonates proximally and an incapacity to acidify the urine distally.
evidence.explanation: The case report discussion explicitly describes the proximal bicarbonate-loss and distal acidification components; this is mechanistic synthesis rather than an original segment-specific transport assay.
