Cholinergic interneurons and cerebellar Purkinje neurons expand too, yet striatal projection neurons are the population lost - so expansion alone does not determine which cells degenerate.

evidence.snippet: CAG expansions in MSNs are associated with higher levels of MSH2 and MSH3 (forming MutSβ), which can inhibit nucleolytic excision of CAG slip-outs by FAN1
evidence.explanation: Provides the cell-type-specific molecular correlate of differential expansion - the MutS beta versus FAN1 balance - linking this node to the MSH3 and FAN1 modifier genes curated in the genetic section.

evidence.snippet: the number of iSPNs decreased with human HD grade progression
evidence.explanation: Single-nucleus counting in human HD caudate and putamen, which is a stronger basis for this node than the marker-gene expression studies it confirms: marker loss is ambiguous between a neuron dying and a neuron losing its identity, whereas nuclei can be counted. The same dataset shows direct- and indirect-pathway neurons becoming transcriptionally less distinct in HD tissue, so identity loss is happening as well as cell loss.

steps/6.description: D2 receptor-expressing medium spiny neurons show earlier huntingtin aggregation and greater sensitivity to CAG somatic instability compared to D1 receptor-expressing neurons.

evidence.snippet: Participants with JHD had substantially reduced intracranial volumes.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the reduced intracranial volume that distinguishes the juvenile-onset structural phenotype.

evidence.snippet: After controlling for the small intracranial volume size, the volumes of subcortical regions (caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, and thalamus) and of cortical white matter were significantly decreased in patients with JHD.
evidence.explanation: Specifies which structures are reduced once intracranial volume is accounted for.

evidence.snippet: However, the cerebellum was proportionately enlarged in the JHD sample.
evidence.explanation: Supports the relative cerebellar enlargement that is specific to the juvenile-onset pattern.

evidence.snippet: Likewise, HD mice had a lower volume of striatum and a higher volume of cerebellum, mirroring the human MRI results.
evidence.explanation: Mouse models carrying very long repeats reproduce the human juvenile-onset morphometric pattern, supporting it as a repeat-length-driven phenotype rather than a cohort artefact.

evidence.snippet: The mean annualized decrease in striatal volume in the JOHD group was -3.99% compared to -0.06% in the GNE
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the annual rate of striatal volume loss in juvenile-onset HD against gene-non-expanded controls.

steps/7.description: Because the juvenile-range allele is expressed throughout brain development, the structural phenotype of juvenile-onset HD is not simply an accelerated version of the adult-onset pattern. Juvenile-onset patients have substantially reduced intracranial volume - a developmental rather than degenerative signature, since intracranial volume is set by brain growth. After correcting for that smaller cranial vault, the caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, thalamus and cortical white matter are all significantly reduced, while the cerebral cortex is largely spared and the cerebellum is proportionately enlarged. The same striatal-down, cerebellum-up pattern is reproduced in R6/2, zQ175 and HdhQ250 mouse models, whose very long repeats make them better models of juvenile than adult-onset disease. This combination - extrastriatal involvement plus relative cerebellar preservation or enlargement - is the leading structural explanation for why juvenile-onset patients present hypokinetic and rigid rather than choreic. Progression is measurable: striatal volume falls about 4% per year in juvenile-onset patients versus essentially no change in gene-non-expanded controls.

evidence.snippet: Paediatric Huntington disease with highly expanded mutations (HE-PHD; >80 CAG repeats) presents atypically, compared to adult-onset Huntington disease (AOHD), with neurodevelopmental delay, epilepsy, abnormal brain glucose metabolism, early striatal damage, and reduced lifespan.
evidence.explanation: Defines the highly expanded pediatric subgroup to which this mechanism is scoped and its atypical clinical profile.

evidence.snippet: In the frontal cortex, this occurred without evidence of extensive neuronal degeneration.
evidence.explanation: Supports treating the transporter reduction as a primary metabolic change rather than a secondary consequence of neuronal loss.

evidence.snippet: Expression JOHD levels were consistently different to those of HE-PHD but similar to those of AOHD.
evidence.explanation: The scope caveat in its own words: juvenile-onset samples resembled adult-onset rather than highly expanded pediatric HD, so this mechanism must not be generalized to juvenile-onset HD as a whole. Recorded as PARTIAL because it constrains rather than supports the node's applicability.

evidence.snippet: Our data suggest a dysfunctional hypometabolic state occurring specifically in paediatric Huntington disease brains.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own hedged interpretation, matching the PROVISIONAL mechanism confidence recorded here.

steps/8.description: A candidate mechanism specific to the most extreme end of the juvenile spectrum. In post-mortem frontal cortex from pediatric HD with highly expanded mutations (HE-PHD, above 80 CAG repeats), the glucose transporters GLUT-1 and GLUT-3 are reduced, as are mitochondrial complexes II-III and hexokinase-II, and the same transporter reduction is seen in patient fibroblasts. Critically, the reduction occurs in cortex WITHOUT evidence of extensive neuronal degeneration, so it is not simply a readout of tissue loss, and the resemblance to GLUT-1 deficiency syndrome offers a mechanistic account of the neurodevelopmental delay and epilepsy seen at these repeat lengths. SCOPE CAVEAT, which curators must preserve: this is NOT a general juvenile-onset HD finding. Juvenile-onset (JOHD) samples in the same study had expression levels consistently different from HE-PHD and similar to adult-onset HD, so the hypometabolic signature segregates with the >80-CAG pediatric subgroup rather than with juvenile onset as such. The study is also very small (brain n=2 HE-PHD, n=3 JOHD, n=6 AOHD), which is why this node is marked PROVISIONAL and is hypothesis-generating rather than a validated juvenile biomarker.

evidence.snippet: Huntington's Disease (HD) became the first disease mapped to a single chromosome and associated with mutations in the huntingtin (HTT) gene, specifically expansions in the trinucleotide cytosine-adenine-guanine (CAG) within exon 1.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the causative CAG repeat expansion in HTT exon 1.

evidence.snippet: Huntington disease is a fatal, inherited, neurodegenerative disease caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the huntingtin gene (HTT), resulting in a toxic polyglutamine tract in the huntingtin protein.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the toxic polyglutamine tract from CAG expansion as the primary molecular cause.

steps/9.description: Huntington disease is caused by expansion of a CAG trinucleotide repeat in exon 1 of the HTT gene beyond 36 repeats. The expanded repeat produces a mutant huntingtin protein with an elongated polyglutamine tract that confers a toxic gain of function. Repeat length inversely correlates with age of onset. Normal alleles have 6-26 repeats; intermediate alleles (27-35) can expand in offspring; 36-39 repeats show reduced penetrance; 40+ repeats are fully penetrant.

evidence.snippet: Variable, glutamine-encoding, CAA interruptions indicate that a property of the uninterrupted HTT CAG repeat sequence, distinct from the length of huntingtin's polyglutamine segment, dictates the rate at which Huntington's disease (HD) develops.
evidence.explanation: The defining statement that onset is set by the uninterrupted CAG repeat at the DNA level rather than by polyglutamine length in the protein.

evidence.snippet: suggesting that the special onset-determining property of the uninterrupted CAG repeat is a propensity for length instability that leads to its somatic expansion
evidence.explanation: Identifies the mechanism connecting this node to the next: the onset-determining property of the uninterrupted tract is its instability, acting through somatic expansion.

evidence.snippet: this LOI variant is associated with dramatically earlier AOO (average of 25 years) despite the same polyglutamine length as in individuals with the interrupting penultimate CAA codon
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the effect and provides the controlled comparison - matched polyglutamine length, differing uninterrupted CAG length, 25-year difference in age of onset.

evidence.snippet: we show that the LOI variant is associated with increased somatic repeat instability, highlighting this as a significant driver of this effect
evidence.explanation: Establishes increased somatic instability as the mediator of the loss-of-interruption effect, supporting the downstream edge.

evidence.snippet: Notably, four internal CAA interruptions completely abolish CAG instability, reversing HD phenotypes such as altered striatal fate acquisition and nuclear disorganization.
evidence.explanation: Turns an association into a manipulation. The other evidence on this node is human genetic association between repeat structure and onset age; here CRISPR-engineered CAA interruptions are placed into the tract in human stem cells and both abolish somatic instability and reverse cellular HD phenotypes in the derived neurons, which is the causal direction the association predicts. The same platform localizes the effect to loss or duplication of the penultimate CAA of canonical alleles.

steps/10.description: The glutamine-encoding repeat in HTT is normally (CAG)n-CAA-CAG: a penultimate CAA codon interrupts the pure CAG tract while encoding the same glutamine. Because CAA and CAG are synonymous, two alleles can encode an identical polyglutamine length while differing in the length of *uninterrupted* CAG at the DNA level. A loss-of-interruption (LOI) variant that removes the interrupting adenines yields a pure CAG tract and is associated with onset roughly 25 years earlier at matched polyglutamine length, and with increased somatic repeat instability. Conversely, patients retaining or duplicating the CAA interruption have later onset than their polyglutamine length predicts. The determinant of onset is therefore a property of the DNA sequence - its propensity for length instability, and hence its somatic expansion rate - rather than the length of the polyglutamine tract in the protein product. This node is why the KB models CAG tract structure separately from polyglutamine proteotoxicity, and it sits upstream of somatic expansion rather than of protein aggregation.

evidence.snippet: The site-specific increases in CAG tract length are driven by active mismatch repair (MMR), while DSBs occur genome-wide and are driven by mutant huntingtin-mediated suppression of nonhomologous joining of DNA broken ends.
evidence.explanation: States the central claim of this node - that mutant huntingtin suppresses non-homologous end joining - and separates it from the MMR-driven expansion mechanism.

evidence.snippet: The disease-length CAG tract leads to early inhibition of DSBR and accumulating DSBs over time ultimately kill neurons.
evidence.explanation: Places inhibition of double-strand break repair upstream and early, establishing the direction of the causal chain from tract length to repair suppression to break accumulation.

steps/11.description: Mutant huntingtin physically associates with the core non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) machinery and suppresses double-strand break repair (DSBR) activity. In HdhQ(150/150) mice, immunoprecipitation-mass spectrometry recovered the Ku70-Ku80 heterodimer as the principal huntingtin capture products (with DNA-PKcs as a minor product, and minor associations with Rad50 and RPA), whereas base excision repair, nucleotide excision repair/transcription-coupled repair and mismatch repair components showed few interactions. Correspondingly, multiplexed host-cell reactivation assays found BER, NER/TCR and MMR activity unchanged by genotype, while clearance of radiation-induced gamma-H2AX foci was delayed in disease striatal cells and tissue - breaks form normally but are repaired inefficiently. The deficit is genotype-, cell-type- and region-specific (striatum over cerebellum, neurons over glia) and appears before the onset of somatic expansion.

evidence.snippet: genome-wide association studies have identified genetic modifiers, mostly DNA repair genes, that significantly influence disease onset and progression. These findings point to somatic CAG repeat expansions in affected tissues as a key pathological mechanism.
evidence.explanation: GWAS studies identify DNA repair gene modifiers influencing onset via somatic CAG expansion.

evidence.snippet: Validation of leads including the mismatch repair protein MSH3, and interstrand cross-link repair protein FAN1, suggest the mechanism is driven by somatic CAG instability, which is supported by the protective effect of CAA substitutions in the CAG tract.
evidence.explanation: Validates MSH3 and FAN1 as key mediators of somatic CAG instability.

evidence.snippet: Somatic expansion of the CAG repeat length, beyond the inherited length, has been associated with hastening the onset of symptoms compared to that predicted from the germline length.
evidence.explanation: Confirms somatic expansion accelerates onset beyond germline prediction.

evidence.snippet: Striatal pallidal neurons (SPNs) with 150-500 + CAG repeats seem to lose positive and then negative features of neuronal identity, de-repress senescence/apoptosis genes, ultimately leading to cell death.
evidence.explanation: Recent review (2026) provides mechanistic detail on how somatic CAG expansion leads to loss of neuronal identity features and de-repression of senescence/apoptosis pathways, culminating in neuronal death. Represents paradigm shift in understanding of somatic instability pathophysiology.

evidence.snippet: The findings on somatic instability in HD suggest that neurodegeneration in HD is an asynchronous DNA process for >95% of a neuron's life, with majority of neurons in all disease stages having a HTT gene which is not biologically harmful.
evidence.explanation: Characterizes somatic instability-driven neurodegeneration as asynchronous, with most neurons remaining non-harmful throughout disease, having significant implications for therapeutic targeting of expansion-bearing neurons.

evidence.snippet: We found that the HTT CAG repeat expands somatically from 40-45 to 100-500+ CAGs in SPNs.
evidence.explanation: Direct single-cell measurement in human striatal projection neurons of the magnitude of somatic expansion, establishing the scale of this node in human tissue rather than by inference from mouse.

evidence.snippet: individuals with higher blood DNA somatic CAG repeat expansion scores have worse HD outcomes
evidence.explanation: Quantitative human cohort evidence (TRACK-HD and Enroll-HD) linking measured somatic expansion to clinical outcome, independent of the mouse-model literature.

steps/12.description: Somatic expansion of the CAG repeat in post-mitotic striatal neurons, driven by DNA mismatch repair machinery (particularly MSH3 and FAN1), accelerates disease progression beyond what is predicted by the inherited germline repeat length. This mechanism is now recognized as a key determinant of onset timing and a major therapeutic target. GWAS have identified DNA repair gene variants as the principal genetic modifiers of HD age of onset.

evidence.snippet: Cleavage of huntingtin by caspase-6 at amino acid 586 is a crucial event in the pathogenesis of HD. Nuclear localization of huntingtin is also an important marker of HD and preventing or delaying its nuclear accumulation is protective in disease models.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates caspase-6 cleavage generates toxic N-terminal fragments and their nuclear accumulation drives pathogenesis.

evidence.snippet: Although Huntington disease has long been viewed as a consequence of age-dependent toxicity from mutant huntingtin, genome-wide association studies have identified genetic modifiers, mostly DNA repair genes, that significantly influence disease onset and progression.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the established view that mutant huntingtin protein toxicity is central to HD pathogenesis.

steps/13.description: The expanded polyglutamine tract causes mutant huntingtin to misfold and form intracellular aggregates (inclusion bodies) in neurons. These aggregates disrupt proteostasis, sequester essential cellular proteins including transcription factors (CBP, Sp1, TFIID, REST/NRSF), and interfere with transcriptional regulation, axonal transport, and synaptic function. Aberrant proteolytic cleavage by caspase-6 generates toxic N-terminal fragments that accumulate in the nucleus.

evidence.snippet: However, NMDAR whole-cell, and especially extrasynaptic, current is elevated in YAC128 MSNs.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the redistribution and its selectivity: the same cells show similar numbers of glutamatergic synapses and similar synaptic NMDAR currents to wild type, so the elevation is confined to the extrasynaptic compartment.

evidence.snippet: Here, we show increased calpain cleavage of GluN2B at both synaptic and extrasynaptic sites, and elevated extrasynaptic total GluN2B expression in the YAC128 striatum.
evidence.explanation: Identifies calpain cleavage of the GluN2B C-terminus, alongside elevated synaptic STEP activity and reduced GluN2B Y1472 phosphorylation, as the trafficking machinery that relocates the receptor in YAC128 striatum.

evidence.snippet: Here, we demonstrate that dysregulation of DAPK1 occurs early in the YAC128 HD mouse model, and contributes to elevated extrasynaptic GluN2B S1303 phosphorylation.
evidence.explanation: Adds the amplification step and an interventional handle: DAPK1 inhibition normalizes extrasynaptic GluN2B phosphorylation and surface expression and prevents YAC128 striatal spine loss in cortico-striatal co-culture.

steps/14.description: Mutant huntingtin shifts GluN2B-containing NMDA receptors from synaptic to extrasynaptic membrane in striatal medium spiny neurons while leaving synaptic NMDAR content unchanged. Calpain cleavage of the GluN2B C-terminus and elevated STriatal-Enriched protein tyrosine phosphatase activity drive the relocation; DAPK1 phosphorylation of GluN2B at S1303 amplifies the resulting receptor function. Because extrasynaptic NMDAR activation shuts off CREB and engages death signalling while synaptic activation is pro-survival, this redistribution turns ordinary glutamatergic input into a toxic signal without requiring any increase in glutamate. It is the specific lesion behind the excitotoxicity hypothesis, and is cell-autonomous: it appears in medium spiny neurons co-cultured with wild-type cortical cells. All direct measurements are in mouse models (see the discussion mismatch_hd_extrasynaptic_nmdar_is_mouse_only).

evidence.snippet: HP:0001332 | Dystonia | Frequent (79-30%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet's curated HPO annotation classifies dystonia as a frequent Huntington disease phenotype.

steps/15.description: Sustained muscle contractions causing abnormal postures, particularly prominent in juvenile-onset HD and in later stages of adult-onset disease.

evidence.snippet: HP:0001336 | Myoclonus | Frequent (79-30%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet's curated HPO annotation classifies myoclonus as a frequent Huntington disease phenotype.

steps/16.description: Myoclonus is a frequent motor manifestation in the Orphanet Huntington disease phenotype profile.

evidence.snippet: HP:0004408 | Abnormality of the sense of smell | Frequent (79-30%)
evidence.explanation: Orphanet's curated HPO annotation classifies abnormality of the sense of smell as a frequent Huntington disease phenotype.

steps/17.description: Abnormality of the sense of smell is a frequent sensory manifestation in the Orphanet Huntington disease phenotype profile.

evidence.snippet: Compared with the LE subgroup, development delay (0 [0%] in the LE subgroup vs nine [90%] in the HE subgroup; p<0·0001), severe gait impairment (nine [35%] in the LE subgroup vs nine [90%] in the HE subgroup; p=0·0072), and seizures (three [11%] in the LE subgroup vs eight [80%] in the HE subgroup; p<0·0001) prevailed over time in the HE subgroup.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies developmental delay as a high-expansion juvenile feature (90% vs 0%), supporting both the phenotype and its repeat-length dependence.

evidence.snippet: Children with disease-onset between 0–10 years (n = 127) had significantly more gait disturbances/ataxia (p = 0.0001), dysarthria (p = 0.008), seizures (p = 0.0008) and developmental regression/delay (p = 0.0001) compared to those with an onset between 11–20 years (n = 101)
evidence.explanation: Establishes that developmental regression/delay is significantly more frequent in childhood-onset than adolescent-onset juvenile HD.

steps/18.description: Loss of previously acquired skills, or failure to acquire them on schedule, is a presenting feature of childhood-onset HD that has no counterpart in adult-onset disease. It is strongly graded by repeat length - developmental delay was recorded in 9 of 10 (90%) highly expanded juvenile patients and in none of 26 with lower expansions - and it is significantly more frequent in onset before age 10 than in adolescent onset. Speech and language delay may precede other motor signs when onset is in the first decade.

evidence.snippet: The brain has the same repair proteins as other tissues, but normal, canonical repair activity is unequal and is characterized by high base excision repair (BER) and low double strand break repair (DSBR).
evidence.explanation: Establishes the BER-high/DSBR-low imbalance in normal brain that makes neurons vulnerable to SSB-to-DSB conversion.

evidence.snippet: The natural imbalance creates conditions where single strand breaks (SSBs) can convert to double strand breaks (DSBs) and reversibly switch between states in response to oxidation both in vivo and in vitro.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports oxidation-dependent SSB-to-DSB conversion as the route by which oxidative load generates double-strand breaks in brain.

steps/19.description: Post-mitotic neurons have no replication fork, so the dominant source of double-strand breaks is endogenous base damage. Base excision repair of oxidised, alkylated or deaminated bases generates transient single-strand break (SSB) intermediates, and closely spaced SSBs on opposite strands convert to a double-strand break. The normal brain runs high BER against low DSBR, an imbalance that makes this conversion sensitive to oxidative and metabolic load. This node is the point at which mitochondrial reactive oxygen species feed the double-strand break arm, and it is the node the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant XJB-5-131 acts on.

evidence.snippet: The disease leads to progressive motor, cognitive and psychiatric decline, primarily resulting from loss of medium spiny neurons in the striatum.
evidence.explanation: Directly confirms MSN loss in the striatum as the primary cause of HD clinical manifestations.

evidence.snippet: Huntingtin is phosphorylated on serine-421 (S421) by the pro-survival signaling protein kinases Akt and SGK. Phosphorylation of huntingtin at S421 is variable in different regions of the brain with the lowest levels observed in the striatum, which is further reduced by the mutation for Huntington disease (HD).
evidence.explanation: Explains selective striatal vulnerability through naturally low levels of neuroprotective S421 phosphorylation in the striatum.

evidence.snippet: HTT loss or mutation has impacts on neuro-epithelial and striatal neurons maturation, and on basal DNA damage and BDNF axonal transport in post-mitotic neurons
evidence.explanation: iPSC-derived models show HTT mutation impairs striatal neuron maturation and BDNF transport, contributing to selective vulnerability.

steps/20.description: GABAergic medium spiny neurons (MSNs) in the caudate nucleus and putamen are selectively vulnerable in HD. Indirect pathway MSNs expressing enkephalin and D2 dopamine receptors are affected earliest, followed by direct pathway MSNs. This selective vulnerability involves excitotoxicity from corticostriatal glutamatergic inputs, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired BDNF signaling, and naturally low levels of protective S421 phosphorylation in striatal neurons.

evidence.snippet: We have identified transcriptional upregulation of genes encoding N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA), α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) and kainate receptors in medium spiny neurons, the cell type preferentially lost early in HD.
evidence.explanation: The study identifies upregulation of glutamate receptors in medium spiny neurons, supporting the idea of excitotoxicity due to overactivation of these receptors leading to neuronal damage.

evidence.snippet: Excitotoxicity refers to neuronal cell death caused by activation of excitatory amino acid receptors. A substantial body of evidence has implicated excitotoxicity as a mechanism of cell death in both acute and chronic neurologic diseases.
evidence.explanation: This reference explains the concept of excitotoxicity and supports the idea that overactivation of glutamate receptors can lead to neuronal damage.

evidence.snippet: Our results indicated that elevated glutamate concentrations (15 mM, 1.5 mM, and 150 microM glutamate in perfusing solutions) would significantly increased both the concentrations of 2,3 and 2,5 DHBA.
evidence.explanation: The study provides direct evidence that elevated glutamate levels increase the formation of hydroxyl radicals, implying oxidative stress induced by excitotoxicity, which supports the statement.

evidence.snippet: Induction of striatal excitotoxicity in CB(2) receptor-deficient mice by quinolinic acid administration exacerbated brain oedema, microglial activation, proinflammatory-mediator state and medium-sized spiny neuron degeneration.
evidence.explanation: This study shows that excitotoxicity induced in the striatum leads to medium spiny neuron degeneration, supporting the idea of excitotoxicity causing neuronal damage in Huntington's Disease.

evidence.snippet: We found an unexpected reduction in PKD1 protein levels in striatal neurons from HD patients.
evidence.explanation: One of the few excitotoxicity-relevant findings confirmed in human HD tissue. PKD1 normally sustains a pro-survival oxidative-stress detoxification pathway in neurons, so its loss from striatal neurons lowers the threshold at which glutamatergic input becomes lethal. Note the human loss is post-transcriptional - PRKD1 mRNA does not fall in HD striatum - whereas in R6/1 mice it tracks reduced Prkd1 transcript.

evidence.snippet: Functionally, pharmacological PKD inhibition in primary striatal neurons exacerbated excitotoxic damage and apoptosis induced by glutamate N-methyl D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors, whereas expression of constitutively active PKD1 (PKD1-Ca) conferred neuroprotection.
evidence.explanation: Converts the human correlation into a directional claim: removing PKD activity worsens, and restoring it mitigates, NMDA-receptor-mediated excitotoxic death in striatal neurons. This is what makes PKD1 loss a candidate contributor to the selective vulnerability of medium spiny neurons rather than an incidental change.

steps/21.description: Overactivation of glutamate receptors leading to neuronal damage.

evidence.snippet: Nonetheless, it is becoming increasingly clear that alterations in mitochondrial function play key roles in the pathogenic processes in HD. The net result of these events is compromised energy metabolism and increased oxidative damage, which eventually contribute to neuronal dysfunction and death.
evidence.explanation: Supports the pathophysiology entry by directly linking mitochondrial dysfunction in HD to compromised energy metabolism, oxidative damage, and neuronal death.

evidence.snippet: There is strong evidence that mitochondrial dysfunction results in neurodegeneration and may contribute to the pathogenesis of Huntington's disease (HD). Studies over the past few years have implicated an impaired function of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR)-gamma coactivator-1alpha (PGC-1alpha), a transcriptional master coregulator of mitochondrial biogenesis, metabolism, and antioxidant defenses, in causing mitochondrial dysfunction in HD.
evidence.explanation: Supports the mitochondrial dysfunction mechanism by connecting impaired PGC-1alpha activity to defective mitochondrial biogenesis, metabolism, and antioxidant defense in HD.

evidence.snippet: Combined calbindin and mitochondrial marker immunofluorescence showed a significant and progressive grade-dependent reduction in the number of mitochondria in spiny striatal neurons, with marked alteration in size.
evidence.explanation: The primary human observation behind this node, measured in the cell population that is preferentially lost. The same tissue shows reduced COX2 protein, reduced mitochondrial transcription factor A and PGC-1alpha, and a fission/fusion shift (Drp1 up, mitofusin 1 down), so loss of organelles, loss of biogenesis regulators and altered dynamics are all present together. Cohort is moderate-to-severe grade, so this establishes progression with severity rather than precedence over neuronal loss.

evidence.snippet: Using ultra-deep mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequencing, we showed an accumulation of mtDNA mutations affecting oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence.explanation: Substantiates the impaired mitochondrial DNA stability this node asserts, alongside proteomic evidence of impaired mtDNA maintenance and lower complex I and IV activity. Measured in HD skeletal muscle rather than brain, so it is evidence that the defect is systemic in gene carriers, not a striatal measurement.

evidence.snippet: The perturbed biochemical phenotype was detectable in TgHD minipigs prior to the development of ultrastructural changes and locomotor impairment, which become evident at the age of 48 months.
evidence.explanation: Bears on timing, which is the weakest axis of this node. Reduced citrate synthase and respiratory complex I, II and IV activity appear in a large-animal HD model before ultrastructural damage or motor signs, which is what a driver rather than a terminal consequence would look like. Still skeletal muscle, and still a transgenic N-terminal fragment model.

evidence.snippet: The presence of the polyQ tract in mutant HTT affects the formation of these protein complexes and determines the negative consequences of mutant HTT on mitophagy, leading to the accumulation of damaged mitochondria and an increase in oxidative stress.
evidence.explanation: Adds the clearance arm. Wild-type huntingtin participates in several steps of mitophagy, and the polyglutamine tract disrupts the complexes involved, so damaged organelles accumulate. Combined with PGC-1alpha repression this makes the deficit two-sided - less production and less removal. Cellular model only; the relative weight of the two arms is unquantified.

steps/22.description: Reduced efficiency of oxidative phosphorylation complexes, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, and impaired mitochondrial DNA stability leading to bioenergetic failure. Both arms of mitochondrial turnover are affected: biogenesis falls through PGC-1alpha repression, and clearance of damaged organelles falls because the polyglutamine tract disrupts the protein complexes required for mitophagy. The deficit appears to be indirect - mutant huntingtin binds isolated brain mitochondria without impairing their respiration, membrane potential, reactive oxygen species production or calcium uptake.

evidence.snippet: In HD transgenic mice (R6/2) that express N-terminal-mutant huntingtin, Sp1 binds to the soluble form of mutant huntingtin but not to aggregated huntingtin.
evidence.explanation: In vivo evidence from HD transgenic mice showing that Sp1 binds soluble mutant huntingtin, supporting the sequestration mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Mutant huntingtin inhibits the binding of nuclear Sp1 to the promoter of nerve growth factor receptor and suppresses its transcriptional activity in cultured cells.
evidence.explanation: Cell culture experiments demonstrating that mutant huntingtin suppresses Sp1-regulated transcription.

evidence.snippet: We found that CBP was depleted from its normal nuclear location and was present in polyglutamine aggregates in HD cell culture models, HD transgenic mice, and human HD postmortem brain.
evidence.explanation: HD cell culture models showing CBP depletion from its normal nuclear location and sequestration into polyglutamine aggregates.

evidence.snippet: We found that CBP was depleted from its normal nuclear location and was present in polyglutamine aggregates in HD cell culture models, HD transgenic mice, and human HD postmortem brain.
evidence.explanation: HD transgenic mice confirming CBP sequestration into polyglutamine aggregates in vivo.

evidence.snippet: We found that CBP was depleted from its normal nuclear location and was present in polyglutamine aggregates in HD cell culture models, HD transgenic mice, and human HD postmortem brain.
evidence.explanation: Human HD postmortem brain tissue showing CBP depletion and sequestration into polyglutamine aggregates.

evidence.snippet: aberrant accumulation of REST/NRSF in the nucleus is present in Huntington disease. We show that wild-type huntingtin coimmunoprecipitates with REST/NRSF and that less immunoprecipitated material is found in brain tissue with Huntington disease.
evidence.explanation: Human postmortem brain data showing aberrant nuclear REST/NRSF accumulation and reduced huntingtin-REST/NRSF interaction in HD.

evidence.snippet: loss of expression of NRSE-controlled neuronal genes is shown in cells, mice and human brain with Huntington disease.
evidence.explanation: Mouse model data confirming loss of NRSE-controlled gene expression in HD, corroborating the REST/NRSF dysregulation mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Wild-type huntingtin inhibits the silencing activity of NRSE, increasing transcription of BDNF. We show that this effect occurs through cytoplasmic sequestering of repressor element-1 transcription factor/neuron restrictive silencer factor (REST/NRSF), the transcription factor that binds to NRSE.
evidence.explanation: Cell-based experiments showing wild-type huntingtin sequesters REST/NRSF in the cytoplasm to permit BDNF transcription, a function lost with the mutant protein.

evidence.snippet: We demonstrate that both gene-specific activator protein Sp1 and selective components of the core transcription apparatus, including TFIID and TFIIF, are direct targets inhibited by mutant htt in a polyglutamine-dependent manner.
evidence.explanation: Broadens this node beyond sequestration of individual regulators: in a biochemically defined transcription assay, mutant huntingtin inhibits the basal apparatus itself, and does so as a function of polyglutamine length. The mechanism is specified - mutant huntingtin binds the RAP30 subunit of TFIIF and blocks formation of the native RAP30-RAP74 complex.

evidence.snippet: Importantly, overexpression of RAP30 in cultured primary striatal cells protects neurons from mutant htt-induced cellular toxicity and alleviates the transcriptional inhibition of the dopamine D2 receptor gene by mutant htt.
evidence.explanation: The rescue arm, and the reason this belongs in the causal graph rather than in a list of binding partners: restoring one displaced basal factor both protects striatal neurons and relieves repression of the dopamine D2 receptor gene, tying transcriptional repression to the D2 medium spiny neuron population that is preferentially lost.

evidence.snippet: Chronic early treatment prevented long-term memory impairments and normalized specific memory-related gene expression in hippocampus.
evidence.explanation: Shows the transcriptional lesion is manipulable rather than merely observed: a selective HDAC3 inhibitor given early to HdhQ111 knock-in mice normalizes gene expression and prevents the behavioural deficit. Grounds the epigenetic arm of this node in an intervention.

evidence.snippet: RGFP966 prevented corticostriatal-dependent motor learning deficits, significantly suppressed striatal CAG repeat expansions, partially rescued striatal protein marker expression and reduced accumulation of mutant huntingtin oligomeric forms.
evidence.explanation: Complicates the usual ordering, in which somatic expansion sits strictly upstream of transcriptional change. Inhibiting a histone deacetylase also suppresses striatal CAG expansion, so the chromatin state feeds back on the repeat instability normally treated as its cause. Consistent with the prior observation that HDAC3 fuels CAG expansion in human cells, so this was a predicted rather than incidental result.

evidence.snippet: Dysregulation of HD-related pathways in striatum was exacerbated by JQ1 in R6/2 mice, but not in NTs, and JQ1 caused a corresponding increase in the formation of a mutant huntingtin protein-dependent high molecular weight species associated with pathogenesis.
evidence.explanation: A negative interventional result that constrains this node rather than supporting a therapy built on it. The same BET bromodomain inhibitor improved motor performance in non-transgenic littermates while worsening striatal transcriptional pathology, weight loss and pole-test performance in R6/2, so an epigenetic modulator's direction of effect cannot be predicted from its mode of action in the absence of mutant huntingtin.

steps/23.description: Mutant huntingtin disrupts transcriptional regulation by interfering with transcription factors and co-activators including Sp1/TAFII130, CBP, TBP and REST/NRSF, leading to widespread downregulation of neuronal genes including BDNF. The interference runs through soluble and oligomeric mutant huntingtin that structurally destabilizes its targets, rather than through physical trapping of those factors inside visible inclusions, and it extends to the basal transcription apparatus itself. Epigenetic silencing driven by H3K9me3 deposition and histone deacetylase activity converges on the same output by a separate route.

evidence.snippet: we report that DSBs drive neuropathology in male HdhQ(150/150) mice, regardless of somatic expansion of the inherited disease allele
evidence.explanation: Supports accumulated double-strand breaks as a driver of neuropathology in this model independently of somatic expansion.

evidence.snippet: We propose that CAG expansion and DSBs promote downstream neuronal pathology as separable drivers.
evidence.explanation: States the separability claim that distinguishes this node from the Somatic CAG Repeat Expansion node.

steps/24.description: Unrepaired double-strand breaks accumulate genome-wide in striatal neurons, detected concordantly by gamma-H2AX, 53BP1 and pKAP-1 immunofluorescence and confirmed as physical DNA breakage by neutral comet assay. Breaks are detectable at 7-10 weeks in HdhQ(150/150) mice - before the onset of somatic expansion (~11-12 weeks), motor abnormalities (~20 weeks) and striatal neuron loss (~60 weeks) - and rise with age in the vulnerable striatum while remaining modest in the resistant cerebellum. Because the expanded CAG tract represents less than 1e-7 of the genome, the great majority of these breaks lie outside the repeat; and inside the repeat, Ku70/Ku80 constrains end-joining length changes to a few nucleotides. Break burden therefore does not translate into tract length, which is the structural basis for treating double-strand breaks and somatic expansion as separable drivers.

evidence.snippet: Compared with the LE subgroup, development delay (0 [0%] in the LE subgroup vs nine [90%] in the HE subgroup; p<0·0001), severe gait impairment (nine [35%] in the LE subgroup vs nine [90%] in the HE subgroup; p=0·0072), and seizures (three [11%] in the LE subgroup vs eight [80%] in the HE subgroup; p<0·0001) prevailed over time in the HE subgroup.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the repeat-length gradient in seizure occurrence within juvenile-onset HD (80% in the highly expanded subgroup vs 11% in the low expansion subgroup).

evidence.snippet: Juvenile HD is far less common and presents with parkinsonism, dystonia and seizures.

steps/55.description: Epilepsy is one of the features the European Huntington Disease Network working group regards as specific to juvenile-onset HD, and it is uncommon in adult-onset disease. Within juvenile-onset HD, seizure occurrence is graded by repeat length: in a REGISTRY/Enroll-HD retrospective series seizures prevailed over time in 8 of 10 (80%) highly expanded juvenile patients compared with 3 of 26 (11%) with lower expansions. Seizures are also significantly more frequent in childhood-onset (0-10 years) than adolescent-onset (11-20 years) juvenile disease.

edges/2.description: Expanded CAG repeat produces mutant huntingtin with toxic polyglutamine tract that misfolds and aggregates.

edges/3.description: Germline CAG repeat undergoes further somatic expansion in post-mitotic striatal neurons, accelerating disease onset.

evidence.snippet: The disease-length CAG tract leads to early inhibition of DSBR and accumulating DSBs over time ultimately kill neurons.
evidence.explanation: Directly links the disease-length tract to early inhibition of double-strand break repair.

edges/4.description: The inherited disease-length tract produces mutant huntingtin that associates with the Ku70-Ku80 end-joining machinery and inhibits double-strand break repair early, before somatic expansion begins.

edges/5.description: The inherited expanded allele carries a specific repeat structure, and expanding the tract lengthens the run of uninterrupted CAG in alleles that lack the penultimate CAA interruption. Note the direction of this edge carefully: expansion sets the length of the uninterrupted run, but it does NOT create the loss-of-interruption variant, which is an independently inherited sequence change. This edge connects the allele to its repeat structure; it is not a claim that expansion removes the interruption.

evidence.snippet: the number of uninterrupted CAG repeats, which is lengthened by the LOI, is the most significant contributor to AOO of HD and is more significant than polyglutamine length
evidence.explanation: Directly supports uninterrupted tract length, acting via instability, as the dominant determinant of onset.

edges/6.description: A longer uninterrupted CAG tract is more prone to length instability, so it raises the somatic expansion rate - the step through which repeat structure translates into earlier onset.

evidence.snippet: SPNs with 150-500+ CAGs lost positive and then negative features of neuronal identity, de-repressed senescence/apoptosis genes, and were lost
evidence.explanation: Establishes the threshold character of this edge in human tissue and names the intermediate transcriptional steps between long somatic expansion and neuronal loss.

edges/7.description: Somatic expansion in striatal neurons exacerbates local protein toxicity and accelerates neuronal death. Human single-cell data indicate this is threshold-like rather than graded: expansion from 40 to about 150 CAGs has no apparent cell-autonomous effect, while neurons crossing roughly 150 repeats lose neuronal identity and die quickly and asynchronously.

edges/8.description: Male meiotic expansion of the inherited tract is the mechanism by which a juvenile-range allele is generated in the offspring.

edges/9.description: A longer polyglutamine tract raises the aggregation propensity of mutant huntingtin, so the juvenile-range allele drives the same aggregation mechanism as adult-onset HD but earlier and more severely.

edges/10.description: The juvenile-range allele acts on a brain that is still developing, producing a structural phenotype that differs from the adult-onset pattern rather than simply preceding it.

edges/11.description: Longer inherited tracts are more somatically unstable, so the juvenile-range allele also enters the somatic expansion cycle from a higher starting length.

evidence.snippet: Expression JOHD levels were consistently different to those of HE-PHD but similar to those of AOHD.
evidence.explanation: Recorded as PARTIAL because it is the constraint on this edge rather than support for it: the hypometabolic state tracks the >80-CAG pediatric subgroup, not juvenile-range expansion generally, which is why the edge carries an explicit scope restriction.

edges/12.description: SCOPE-RESTRICTED EDGE. This edge does NOT apply across the juvenile range. It is asserted only at the highly expanded pediatric extreme (above 80 CAG repeats), where reduced GLUT-1/GLUT-3, mitochondrial complex II-III and hexokinase-II expression were measured in frontal cortex. In the same study, juvenile-onset samples below that threshold had expression levels resembling adult-onset HD, so the edge must not be read as "juvenile-range expansion causes cerebral hypometabolism". The intervening steps are not established, and the target node is marked PROVISIONAL on an n=2 brain sample.

edges/13.description: Striatal, pallidal and thalamic volume loss in juvenile-onset HD reflects the same medium spiny neuron degeneration seen in adult-onset disease, reached earlier and extending further beyond the striatum.

evidence.snippet: Since genetic GLUT-1 deficiency syndrome shows a symptom spectrum similar to HE-PHD, we investigated the potential role of the two main glucose transporters, GLUT-1 and GLUT-3, in HE-PHD.
evidence.explanation: PARTIAL because this states the authors' analogy-based rationale for investigating the transporters, not a demonstration that the transporter deficit causes the neurodevelopmental phenotype.

edges/14.description: PROPOSED, NOT ESTABLISHED. The study's motivating rationale is that genetic GLUT-1 deficiency syndrome produces a symptom spectrum resembling highly expanded pediatric HD, which offers a candidate metabolic account of the neurodevelopmental delay seen at these repeat lengths. What is actually measured is the co-occurrence of the transporter deficit and the clinical picture in the same >80-CAG subgroup, not a demonstrated causal sequence; no rescue or intervention experiment has been done. Treat as a hypothesis to test, not a curated causal fact.

evidence.snippet: Paediatric Huntington disease with highly expanded mutations (HE-PHD; >80 CAG repeats) presents atypically, compared to adult-onset Huntington disease (AOHD), with neurodevelopmental delay, epilepsy, abnormal brain glucose metabolism, early striatal damage, and reduced lifespan.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that epilepsy and abnormal brain glucose metabolism co-occur in this subgroup. INDIRECT because co-occurrence in the same subgroup is not evidence of the causal direction this edge proposes.

edges/15.description: PROPOSED, NOT ESTABLISHED. Same standing as the developmental-delay edge: epilepsy is part of the atypical presentation reported for the highly expanded pediatric subgroup alongside abnormal brain glucose metabolism, and the GLUT-1 deficiency syndrome analogy supplies a candidate mechanism, but causation is not shown. Note the target phenotype is scoped to juvenile HD as a whole while this edge is restricted to the >80-CAG subgroup, so the edge explains only part of the juvenile seizure burden.

edges/16.description: Mutant huntingtin aggregates and toxic fragments cause selective death of striatal medium spiny neurons.

edges/17.description: Nuclear mutant huntingtin and N-terminal fragments sequester transcription factors (Sp1, CBP, REST/NRSF), dysregulating neuronal gene expression.

edges/18.description: Mutant huntingtin sensitizes striatal neurons to NMDA-receptor-mediated glutamatergic excitotoxicity.

edges/19.description: Mutant huntingtin acts cell-autonomously within medium spiny neurons to move GluN2B-containing NMDA receptors out of the synapse, which is the specific route by which it sensitizes them to excitotoxicity.

edges/20.description: Mutant huntingtin impairs mitochondrial bioenergetics, contributing to oxidative stress and energy failure.

edges/37.description: Neuroinflammatory activation contributes to progressive striatal neuronal injury in HD.

edges/39.description: Innate immune signalling initiated inside spiny projection neurons feeds the striatal inflammatory response, making part of that response neuron-intrinsic rather than purely microglial or astrocytic.

edges/40.description: Sustained innate immune activation within the neuron is proposed as a contributor to the enhanced sensitivity of spiny projection neurons to mutant huntingtin.

edges/41.description: Sequestration of RNA-binding proteins by the expanded repeat and aberrant small CAG RNA activity perturb splicing and gene silencing, converging on the same transcriptional output that nuclear mutant huntingtin disrupts by a different route.

edges/42.description: Extrasynaptic NMDA receptors are coupled to CREB shut-off and pro-death signalling, so their relative enrichment converts glutamatergic transmission into an excitotoxic input to medium spiny neurons.

edges/43.description: Glutamate-receptor overactivation produces excitotoxic injury and death of striatal medium spiny neurons.

edges/45.description: Bioenergetic failure and oxidative damage contribute to degeneration of energy-demanding striatal medium spiny neurons.

evidence.snippet: It is proposed that impaired energy metabolism results in deterioration of membrane function and loss of the voltage-dependent Mg2+ block of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors, which allows persistent activation of these receptors by glutamate, even if concentrations of glutamate at the receptor are within the normal physiological range.
evidence.explanation: States the slow-excitotoxicity mechanism this edge encodes. Review-level and explicitly framed as a proposal, so it supplies the mechanism rather than a measurement.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, both ouabain (1-10 microM) and strophanthidin (1-10 microM) dramatically increased the membrane depolarization and the inward current produced by subcritical concentrations of glutamate, AMPA and NMDA.

edges/46.description: ATP depletion compromises Na+/K+ ATPase activity and depolarizes the membrane, which lifts the voltage-dependent Mg2+ block on NMDA receptors and lets ordinary glutamate concentrations become excitotoxic. Because the resulting calcium load damages mitochondria further, the two mechanisms form a feedforward loop in medium spiny neurons, which combine high energy demand with massive cortical glutamatergic input.

The gene encodes huntingtin, a 3,144 amino acid scaffolding protein involved in vesicular transport, transcription, autophagy, and cell survival.

evidence.snippet: HD is living in an era of target-specific drug development with emphasis on the mechanisms related to mutant Huntingtin (HTT) protein. Examples include antisense oligonucleotides (ASO), splicing modifiers and microRNA molecules that aim to reduce the levels of mutant HTT protein.

evidence.snippet: Among emerging and novel treatments for central nervous system (CNS) disorders, gene therapy (GT), particularly using adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated gene delivery, holds great promise.

treatments/3.description: Emerging disease-modifying approaches including antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), splice modulators, and microRNA-based gene therapy targeting mutant huntingtin protein reduction. Allele-selective approaches that spare wild-type HTT are preferred after the tominersen trial showed non-selective lowering can cause harm.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: HTT-lowering ASOs, splice modulators, and microRNA-based therapies reduce the expression of mutant huntingtin, directly suppressing the root CAG repeat-expansion-driven toxicity at the mRNA and protein level.

treatments/3/targets/1.description: By lowering mutant HTT protein levels, these therapies reduce the substrate available for mHTT misfolding and nuclear and cytoplasmic aggregate formation.

evidence.snippet: interventions to limit somatic repeat expansion might be effective across multiple repeat expansion diseases and, when combined with disease-specific approaches, such as huntingtin lowering in Huntington disease, might offer more effective and longer-lasting clinical benefits than either strategy in isolation.

treatments/4.description: Novel therapeutic paradigm targeting DNA mismatch repair machinery (particularly MSH3) to slow or halt somatic CAG repeat expansion in striatal neurons. Considered the most promising emerging strategy as it addresses the upstream DNA-level mechanism rather than downstream protein toxicity.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Inhibiting MSH3 and other mismatch repair factors slows or halts the somatic CAG repeat expansion that drives progressive striatal toxicity, targeting the upstream DNA-level mechanism rather than downstream protein aggregation.

evidence.snippet: Disease-modifying activity is suggested by the reduction of aberrant accumulation of mutant HTT protein and expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) in both models.

evidence.snippet: to determine whether an implantation of hNSC-01 is a safe and tolerable study intervention for Huntington's disease
evidence.explanation: The first-in-human REGEN4HD trial is evaluating intrastriatal hNSC-01 implantation for safety and tolerability in early-stage HD.

treatments/5.description: Investigational regenerative cell therapy in which good manufacturing practice (GMP)-grade human embryonic stem cell-derived neural stem cells (hNSC-01) are stereotactically implanted into the striatum. Rather than acting by neuronal replacement alone, the grafted cells are proposed to work through neuroprotection and trophic support (including BDNF), reconstruction of striatal synaptic circuitry, and reduction of mutant huntingtin accumulation. This is the cell-therapy approach being evaluated first-in-human in the UCI Health REGEN4HD trial (NCT07451613).

treatments/5/targets/0.description: Intrastriatal hNSC grafts provide trophic support (notably BDNF) and synaptic/circuit reconstruction intended to protect and functionally compensate for the vulnerable striatal medium spiny neurons whose degeneration drives HD motor and cognitive decline.

treatments/5/targets/1.description: In HD mouse models, hNSC transplantation reduced aberrant accumulation of mutant huntingtin, indicating a disease-modifying effect on mHTT proteostasis beyond simple cell replacement.

evidence.snippet: AAV5-miHTT caused a dose-dependent and sustained HTT protein reduction with subsequent suppression of mutant HTT aggregate formation in the striatum and cortex.

treatments/6.description: One-time HTT-lowering gene therapy delivering an engineered microRNA (miHTT) via an adeno-associated virus serotype 5 (rAAV5) vector by MRI-guided stereotactic infusion into the caudate and putamen. The vector-expressed miHTT drives non-allele-selective (total) lowering of huntingtin mRNA and protein in striatal neurons. In the Phase 1/2 program (NCT04120493 / NCT05243017) the high dose showed slowing of clinical progression and lowered CSF neurofilament light chain, and a BLA submission is planned.

treatments/6/targets/0.description: The AAV5-delivered miHTT microRNA degrades huntingtin mRNA, lowering total (mutant and wild-type) huntingtin expression and thereby suppressing the downstream toxicity of the CAG-repeat-expanded transcript at its source.

treatments/6/targets/1.description: By reducing huntingtin mRNA, AMT-130 lowers mutant huntingtin protein levels, decreasing the substrate available for mHTT misfolding and aggregate formation in striatal neurons.

treatments/13.description: PRECLINICAL ONLY - no human trial has been conducted. XJB-5-131 is a synthetic antioxidant in which a tempol nitroxide radical-scavenging moiety is linked to a mitochondria-targeting carrier peptide derived from gramicidin S, concentrating the antioxidant at the mitochondrial membrane. By suppressing mitochondrial reactive oxygen species it prevents base oxidation and blocks the conversion of base excision repair single-strand break intermediates into double-strand breaks. In HdhQ(150/150) mice dosed at 2 mg/kg intraperitoneally three times weekly from 60 to 90 weeks - that is, started only after double-strand breaks had accumulated and disease was well established - it reduced striatal neuronal gamma-H2AX staining and neutral comet tail moments, restored NeuN staining, and improved motor performance, with no substantial change in somatic CAG tract length. That dissociation is the interventional basis for treating double-strand breaks as a therapeutic target separable from somatic expansion.

evidence.snippet: XJB-5-131 reduces oxidative damage to mitochondrial DNA, maintains mitochondrial DNA copy number, suppresses motor decline and weight loss, enhances neuronal survival, and improves mitochondrial function.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the drug's mechanism as suppression of mitochondrial oxidative DNA damage, the input to the SSB-to-DSB conversion node.

treatments/13/targets/0.description: Mitochondrial localisation of the nitroxide lowers the reactive oxygen species load that drives endogenous base oxidation, reducing the supply of single-strand break intermediates that convert to double-strand breaks. evidence.snippet: The mutational expansion of polyglutamine beyond a critical length produces a toxic gain of function in huntingtin and results in neuronal death. In the course of the disease, expanded huntingtin is proteolyzed, becomes abnormally folded, and accumulates in oligomers, fibrils, and microscopic inclusions.
evidence.explanation: Directly states the toxic gain-of-function framing and details the aggregation cascade from proteolysis through misfolding to inclusion body formation.

evidence.snippet: These findings point to somatic CAG repeat expansions
evidence.explanation: Major review reframes HD pathogenesis: somatic CAG repeat expansion driven by DNA repair (MMR) gene activity is now recognized as a rate-limiting upstream process that determines disease onset and progression — qualifying the simple gain-of-function model with a necessary upstream-amplifier step.

evidence.snippet: MSN-specific deletion of Msh2
evidence.explanation: MSN-specific Msh2 deletion eliminates striatal HTT CAG expansions and dramatically inhibits intranuclear huntingtin inclusions — providing direct genetic evidence that somatic expansion in MSNs is a critical step in the toxic gain-of-function pathway.
