evidence.explanation: Therapeutic proof-of-concept: di-valent siRNA targeting MSH3 blocks somatic CAG expansion in the striatum of HD mouse models without affecting other MMR functions, validating somatic expansion as a tractable therapeutic target downstream of the canonical gain-of-function mutation.

hypotheses/0.description: The expanded polyglutamine tract in mutant huntingtin confers a toxic gain-of-function through protein misfolding, oligomerization, and aggregation into inclusion bodies. This is the widely accepted primary disease mechanism, with polyQ expansion beyond the pathogenic threshold (~36 repeats) driving neurodegeneration predominantly in the striatum.

evidence.snippet: In HD transgenic mice (R6/2) that express N-terminal-mutant huntingtin, Sp1 binds to the soluble form of mutant huntingtin but not to aggregated huntingtin.
evidence.explanation: In vivo evidence from HD transgenic mice showing that Sp1 binds soluble mutant huntingtin, supporting the sequestration mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Mutant huntingtin inhibits the binding of nuclear Sp1 to the promoter of nerve growth factor receptor and suppresses its transcriptional activity in cultured cells.
evidence.explanation: Cell culture experiments demonstrating that mutant huntingtin suppresses Sp1-regulated transcription.

evidence.snippet: We found that CBP was depleted from its normal nuclear location and was present in polyglutamine aggregates in HD cell culture models, HD transgenic mice, and human HD postmortem brain.
evidence.explanation: HD cell culture models showing CBP depletion from its normal nuclear location and sequestration into polyglutamine aggregates.

evidence.snippet: We found that CBP was depleted from its normal nuclear location and was present in polyglutamine aggregates in HD cell culture models, HD transgenic mice, and human HD postmortem brain.
evidence.explanation: HD transgenic mice confirming CBP sequestration into polyglutamine aggregates in vivo.

evidence.snippet: We found that CBP was depleted from its normal nuclear location and was present in polyglutamine aggregates in HD cell culture models, HD transgenic mice, and human HD postmortem brain.
evidence.explanation: Human HD postmortem brain tissue showing CBP depletion and sequestration into polyglutamine aggregates.

evidence.snippet: aberrant accumulation of REST/NRSF in the nucleus is present in Huntington disease. We show that wild-type huntingtin coimmunoprecipitates with REST/NRSF and that less immunoprecipitated material is found in brain tissue with Huntington disease.
evidence.explanation: Human postmortem brain data showing aberrant nuclear REST/NRSF accumulation and reduced huntingtin-REST/NRSF interaction in HD.

evidence.snippet: loss of expression of NRSE-controlled neuronal genes is shown in cells, mice and human brain with Huntington disease.
evidence.explanation: Mouse model data confirming loss of NRSE-controlled gene expression in HD, corroborating the REST/NRSF dysregulation mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Wild-type huntingtin inhibits the silencing activity of NRSE, increasing transcription of BDNF. We show that this effect occurs through cytoplasmic sequestering of repressor element-1 transcription factor/neuron restrictive silencer factor (REST/NRSF), the transcription factor that binds to NRSE.
evidence.explanation: Cell-based experiments showing wild-type huntingtin sequesters REST/NRSF in the cytoplasm to permit BDNF transcription, a function lost with the mutant protein.

evidence.snippet: Western blots showed that these transcription factors were not trapped in huntingtin inclusions.
evidence.explanation: Refutes the physical-sequestration reading of this hypothesis, and is the reason the description now says interference rather than sequestration. TBP, CBP and Sp1 were examined by immunohistochemistry, double labelling, electron microscopy and western blot in HD mouse brain; all three were diffusely nuclear despite abundant inclusions, with no difference from wild type. It does not refute transcriptional dysregulation itself - the same paper proposes that soluble mutant huntingtin interacting with nuclear transcription factors is the alternative route.

evidence.snippet: Interaction of toxic huntingtin with the benign polyQ repeat of TBP structurally destabilizes the transcription factor, independent of the formation of insoluble coaggregates.
evidence.explanation: The mechanism that replaces sequestration, and the one that reconciles the contradiction: soluble monomers and small oligomers of huntingtin exon 1 deactivate TBP by destabilizing it, explicitly without co-aggregation. The claim is interventional as well as observational - Hsp70/Hsp40 chaperones block the conformational rearrangement that generates the toxic species and prevent TBP deactivation.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, soluble mutant huntingtin inhibits Sp1 binding to DNA in postmortem brain tissues of both presymptomatic and affected HD patients.
evidence.explanation: Places the Sp1 lesion before clinical onset in human tissue, which is what makes this arm a candidate initiating step rather than a terminal consequence. Independently reports that the inhibiting species is soluble, converging with PMID:15225551 by a different route.

evidence.snippet: Coexpression of Sp1 and TAFII130 in cultured striatal cells from wild-type and HD transgenic mice reverses the transcriptional inhibition of the dopamine D2 receptor gene caused by mutant huntingtin, as well as protects neurons from huntingtin-induced cellular toxicity.
evidence.explanation: The rescue arm for the Sp1 pathway. Restoring the activator and its coactivator both relieves repression of the dopamine D2 receptor gene and protects striatal neurons, which ties this transcriptional lesion to the D2 medium spiny neuron population that is preferentially lost.

evidence.snippet: We now show that increased binding of the RE1 silencing transcription factor/neuron-restrictive silencer factor (REST/NRSF) repressor occurs at multiple genomic RE1/NRSE loci in HD cells, in animal models, and in postmortem brains, resulting in a decrease of RE1/NRSE-mediated gene transcription.
evidence.explanation: Genome-wide occupancy data in human postmortem HD brain by ChIP-on-chip, which is a stronger claim than single-locus work: the repression is widespread across REST target genes, not confined to BDNF.

evidence.snippet: The same molecular phenotype is produced in cells and brain tissue depleted of endogenous huntingtin, thereby directly validating the loss-of-function hypothesis of HD.
evidence.explanation: Distinguishes this arm from the rest of the hypothesis. Removing wild-type huntingtin reproduces the REST occupancy phenotype, so the REST lesion follows from loss of a normal huntingtin function rather than from a toxic activity of the mutant - which matters for HTT-lowering strategies that reduce both alleles.

hypotheses/1.description: Mutant huntingtin disrupts transcriptional regulation by interfering with key transcription factors and co-activators (Sp1/TAFII130, CBP, TBP, REST/NRSF), leading to widespread downregulation of neuronal survival genes including BDNF. This is a canonical downstream mechanistic layer in HD, linking mutant huntingtin protein interactions to loss of neuronal maintenance programs. The interference is now understood as functional inhibition by soluble and oligomeric mutant huntingtin - which structurally destabilizes its target - rather than physical trapping of transcription factors inside visible inclusions; the REST/NRSF arm is separate again, and turns on loss of the wild-type protein's cytoplasmic retention of the repressor.

evidence.snippet: mutant huntingtin causes disruption of mitochondrial function by inhibiting expression of PGC-1alpha
evidence.explanation: Identifies PGC-1α transcriptional repression as the strongest mechanistic link from mHTT to mitochondrial dysfunction. PGC-1α KO crossbred with HD KI exacerbates striatal neurodegeneration; PGC-1α restoration via lentivirus is neuroprotective in HD mice — direct causal validation of the canonical pathway.

evidence.snippet: Nonetheless, it is becoming increasingly clear that alterations in mitochondrial function play key roles in the pathogenic processes in HD. The net result of these events is compromised energy metabolism and increased oxidative damage, which eventually contribute to neuronal dysfunction and death.
evidence.explanation: Frames mitochondrial dysfunction as a key pathogenic mechanism linking compromised energy metabolism and oxidative damage to neuronal death.

evidence.snippet: There is strong evidence that mitochondrial dysfunction results in neurodegeneration and may contribute to the pathogenesis of Huntington's disease (HD). Studies over the past few years have implicated an impaired function of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR)-gamma coactivator-1alpha (PGC-1alpha), a transcriptional master coregulator of mitochondrial biogenesis, metabolism, and antioxidant defenses, in causing mitochondrial dysfunction in HD.
evidence.explanation: Links PGC-1alpha impairment to mitochondrial dysfunction in HD, connecting transcriptional dysregulation of mitochondrial biogenesis genes to bioenergetic failure.

evidence.snippet: Overall, our results suggest that mHtt does not directly impair mitochondrial functions, arguing against the involvement of this mechanism in HD pathogenesis.
evidence.explanation: The source behind this entry's reframing, and it refutes one specific limb rather than the hypothesis. Mutant huntingtin from YAC128 brain cytosol bound wild-type brain mitochondria - in greater amount than mitochondria isolated from YAC128 mice carry natively - and respiration, membrane potential, reactive oxygen species production and calcium uptake capacity were all unchanged; enriching YAC128 mitochondria further changed nothing either. What survives is the indirect route through PGC-1alpha repression and impaired mitophagy. Marked IN_VITRO because the test is a reconstitution assay on isolated organelles, which cannot exclude compartment-specific interactions in intact neurons.

evidence.snippet: These findings reveal that there are both mitochondrial loss and altered mitochondrial morphogenesis with increased mitochondrial fission and reduced fusion in HD.
evidence.explanation: The human postmortem anchor this hypothesis previously lacked. Everything else supporting it in this entry was review-level or from PGC-1alpha mouse work; this measures the organelles themselves in HD caudate.

hypotheses/2.description: Mutant huntingtin impairs mitochondrial function through reduced oxidative phosphorylation complex activity, disrupted calcium homeostasis, and transcriptional repression of PGC-1alpha. This is a canonical convergent mechanism in HD that links transcriptional dysregulation and mutant huntingtin stress to bioenergetic failure, oxidative damage, and neuronal death, particularly in energy-demanding striatal medium spiny neurons.

evidence.snippet: Many lines of evidence support a role for neuronal damage arising as a result of excessive activation of glutamate receptors by excitatory amino acids in the pathogenesis of Huntington disease. The N-methyl-d-aspartate subclass of ionotropic glutamate receptors (NMDARs) is more selective and effective than the other subclasses in mediating this damage.
evidence.explanation: Comprehensive review establishing NMDAR-mediated excitotoxicity as a key pathogenic mechanism in HD with evidence from human tissue, animal models, and cell-based systems.

evidence.snippet: This is the first direct in vivo evidence of NR2B-NMDAR-mediated excitotoxicity in the context of HD. Our results are consistent with previous suggestions that direct and/or indirect interactions of mutant huntingtin with NMDARs are a proximate cause of neurodegeneration in HD.
evidence.explanation: Provides the first direct in vivo genetic evidence for the excitotoxicity hypothesis by showing exacerbated striatal neurodegeneration when NR2B-NMDAR subunits are overexpressed in an HD mouse model.

evidence.snippet: The data suggest that MSN cell-autonomous increases in extrasynaptic NMDARs are driven by the HD mutation.
evidence.explanation: Localizes the lesion. In YAC128 cortico-striatal co-cultures synaptic NMDAR currents and synaptic subunit composition are indistinguishable from wild type while extrasynaptic current and GluN2B surface expression rise, and the rise occurs whether or not the co-cultured cortical cells carry mutant huntingtin - so the defect is intrinsic to the medium spiny neuron rather than imposed by its cortical input.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, combined calpain inhibition and STEP inactivation reduced extrasynaptic, while increasing synaptic GluN2B expression in the YAC128 striatum.
evidence.explanation: Supplies the trafficking mechanism and shows it is reversible: blocking calpain and STEP together moves GluN2B back from extrasynaptic to synaptic sites in YAC128 striatum, which makes the redistribution a manipulable step rather than a correlate.

evidence.snippet: At both 6 months and 1 yr, QA lesions showed striking sparing of NADPH-diaphorase neurons as compared with both AMPA and KA lesions, neither of which showed preferential sparing of these neurons.
evidence.explanation: The classical pharmacological argument, and the reason the hypothesis names NMDA receptors specifically rather than excitotoxicity in general. Only the NMDAR agonist reproduces the interneuron-sparing pattern of HD striatum; kainate and AMPA lesions do not.

evidence.snippet: A concomitant proliferation of astrocytes with GLT1 transcripts may represent a compensatory mechanism protecting neostriatal neurons from glutamate excitotoxicity.
evidence.explanation: The human postmortem picture, and it constrains the model rather than confirming it. NR1, NR2B and GLT1 mRNA all fall with disease severity, the authors attribute the NMDAR loss to neuronal loss rather than to receptor regulation, and they read the astrocytic GLT1 response as protective. Only the earliest-stage matrix zones show subunit levels above control.

evidence.snippet: For this reason many NMDA receptor antagonists have disappointingly failed advanced clinical trials for a number of diseases including stroke and neurodegenerative disorders such as Huntington's disease.
evidence.explanation: Refutes the strong reading of this hypothesis - that NMDAR-mediated excitotoxicity is a rate-limiting and therapeutically tractable driver of HD progression - while leaving the amplifier reading intact. Marked INDIRECT because trial failure is compatible with several explanations besides the mechanism being unimportant, including wrong disease stage and the loss of physiological NMDAR signalling that pan-receptor blockade causes.

hypotheses/3.description: Historical but still supported superimposed model proposing that mutant huntingtin and corticostriatal circuit dysfunction enhance NMDA receptor-mediated excitotoxicity in striatal medium spiny neurons. This hypothesis is best viewed as a selective-vulnerability amplifier rather than the sole initiating lesion.

evidence.snippet: We propose that CAG expansion and DSBs promote downstream neuronal pathology as separable drivers.
evidence.explanation: States the hypothesis in the authors' own terms.

evidence.snippet: DSBs and transcriptional dysfunction occur in animals that cannot somatically expand their inherited allele.
evidence.explanation: The zQ175/MSH3(-/-) separation-of-function result - double-strand breaks and transcriptional pathology without any somatic expansion.

evidence.snippet: Conversely, suppression of DSBs is sufficient to reverse neuropathology even when somatic expansion is active.
evidence.explanation: The interventional arm - rescue of neuropathology by suppressing breaks while expansion continues.

evidence.snippet: This had no effect on the deposition of huntingtin aggregation in the nuclei of striatal neurons, nor on the dysregulated striatal transcriptional profile.
evidence.explanation: Independent support for the premise that abolishing somatic expansion does not by itself correct striatal molecular pathology in zQ175, which is what motivates looking for a second, expansion-independent driver.

evidence.snippet: The natural imbalance creates conditions where single strand breaks (SSBs) can convert to double strand breaks (DSBs) and reversibly switch between states in response to oxidation both in vivo and in vitro.
evidence.explanation: Supplies the mechanistic basis in normal brain for the oxidation-driven route by which double-strand breaks are generated in this model.

evidence.snippet: Our data support a model in which CAG expansions are necessary but may not be sufficient for cell death
evidence.explanation: The one piece of HUMAN evidence bearing on this hypothesis. Deep molecular profiling of human striatum and cerebellum reaches the same premise the mouse work starts from - somatic expansion is necessary but not sufficient for neuronal death - independently of any mouse model. Marked PARTIAL because it establishes only the insufficiency premise; it says nothing about double-strand breaks or end joining, which remain mouse-only claims (see mismatch_hd_dsbr_absent_from_human_gwas).

hypotheses/4.description: Genome-wide DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are a driver of HD neuropathology that is mechanistically separable from somatic CAG expansion. On this model the two forms of DNA damage coexist but act through distinct routes: site-specific CAG tract lengthening is driven by active mismatch repair, whereas DSBs arise genome-wide from mutant huntingtin-mediated suppression of non-homologous end joining acting on a background where oxidation converts base excision repair single-strand break intermediates into double-strand breaks. Three observations support separability. (1) DSBs accumulate in zQ175/MSH3(-/-) mice, which cannot somatically expand their allele, alongside the same transcriptional dysfunction seen in expansion-competent zQ175. (2) Pharmacological suppression of DSBs with the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant XJB-5-131 rescues striatal neuron loss and motor performance in HdhQ(150/150) mice while leaving somatic tract length substantially unchanged. (3) Geometry - the CAG tract is under 1e-7 of the genome, so most breaks fall outside it, and Ku70/Ku80 limits end-joining length changes inside it to a few nucleotides, so break burden and tract length are largely decoupled. The therapeutic implication is that expansion suppression and DSB suppression are independent targets that may need to be combined.

evidence.snippet: Ablation of Msh3 prevented somatic expansion throughout the brain and periphery, and reduction of Msh3 by 50% decreased the rate of expansion.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the intervention worked as intended on its molecular target, so the absent phenotypic benefit is not an efficacy failure.

evidence.snippet: This had no effect on the deposition of huntingtin aggregation in the nuclei of striatal neurons, nor on the dysregulated striatal transcriptional profile.
evidence.explanation: The negative result at a juvenile-range repeat length that motivates this mismatch discussion.

evidence.snippet: It is striking that highly expanded CAG repeats of a similar size in humans cause disease onset before 2 years of age, indicating that somatic CAG repeat expansion in the brain is not required for pathogenesis.
evidence.explanation: The authors' explicit bridge from the mouse result to human juvenile-onset disease, and the basis for treating this as a translational mismatch rather than a model artefact.

open_questions/0.rationale: In the zQ175 knock-in model, whose approximately 185-CAG allele sits in the juvenile/pediatric rather than adult range, complete Msh3 ablation abolished somatic expansion throughout brain and periphery and 50% reduction slowed it - yet neither striatal nuclear huntingtin aggregation nor the dysregulated striatal transcriptional profile improved. This is the opposite of the result obtained when Msh3 is ablated in knock-in models carrying shorter, adult-range repeats, where the intervention is beneficial. The authors' own translational argument is that human repeats of comparable size cause onset before age 2, so somatic expansion in brain cannot be required for pathogenesis at these lengths. The mismatch is therefore two-sided and specifically juvenile. Model-to-human: the negative result is a mouse result, and no trial of somatic-instability-directed therapy has been run in children with juvenile-onset HD - they are excluded from most HD trials, so the human counterpart of this experiment does not exist. Human-to-model: the repeat length at which the benefit of somatic-expansion suppression disappears is unknown in humans, because the trajectory of somatic expansion in mutation-carrier brain has not been measured. Until that threshold is located, an MSH3- or FAN1-directed agent validated in adult-onset HD must not be assumed to transfer to juvenile-onset patients, and the practical implication the authors draw - treat as early as possible, before the threshold is crossed - is itself untested in this group. This discussion deliberately does not resolve the general somatic-expansion gap recorded in gap_hd_somatic_expansion_threshold_rescue; it is the juvenile-range special case of it, where the sign of the expected effect may differ.

open_questions/1.rationale: Human single-cell data now argue for a long silent phase of somatic repeat growth followed by a high-repeat toxicity threshold. A standardized isogenic striatal-neuron experiment would separate repeat-length threshold, mutant huntingtin proteostasis, and DNA-repair perturbation effects before treating somatic-expansion inhibition as a general disease-modifying strategy.

evidence.snippet: The site-specific increases in CAG tract length are driven by active mismatch repair (MMR), while DSBs occur genome-wide and are driven by mutant huntingtin-mediated suppression of nonhomologous joining of DNA broken ends.
evidence.explanation: The mouse claim whose human counterpart is unconfirmed.

open_questions/2.rationale: This is a translational-validity question rather than an absence of evidence: the mouse evidence is direct (huntingtin-Ku70/Ku80 co-immunoprecipitation, pathway-selective repair deficit, delayed break clearance, four concordant break markers), but the corresponding human genetic signal is missing. The authors offer a reconciliation that is plausible and untested - double-strand breaks form at effectively random genomic positions and so vary between patients, and non-homologous end joining in mutant-huntingtin-expressing cells is inefficient rather than absent, so a partial effect may not reach genome-wide significance in onset association studies. Two further considerations cut against dismissing the mismatch. GWAS onset modifiers detect variance in the timing of onset, which need not be the same quantity as the mechanism driving degeneration once the disease-length allele is inherited; and Ligase IV, an NHEJ component, has surfaced in a mouse CRISPR screen as a repressor of CAG expansion, implying that NHEJ genes may act on both axes and confound a simple modifier readout. Until double-strand break burden and end-joining activity are measured directly in human HD brain, the expansion-independent driver arm should be treated as demonstrated in mouse and unconfirmed in human.

evidence.snippet: DSBs and transcriptional dysfunction occur in animals that cannot somatically expand their inherited allele.
evidence.explanation: Establishes co-occurrence, which is what makes the causal direction an open question rather than a settled edge.

open_questions/3.rationale: The source study is explicit that this was not tested: double-strand break accumulation was shown to coincide with transcriptional dysfunction in both zQ175 and zQ175/MSH3(-/-) mice regardless of somatic expansion, but no experiment established the causal direction. The authors also note a tension in their own model - transcriptional changes in HD are reproducible between studies, which is difficult to derive from breaks distributed at random across the genome. Their proposed resolution is that repair at preferred sites (clustered single-strand breaks at neuronal gene enhancers, where SAR-seq peaks co-localise with PARP and XRCC1) yields recurrent variants while random breaks elsewhere contribute undetectably. The edge from Genome-Wide Double Strand Break Accumulation to Transcriptional Dysregulation is therefore curated with causal_link_type INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES and PARTIAL evidence.

evidence.snippet: a pharmacological inhibitor, XJB-5-131, inhibits the lengthening of the repeat tracks, and correlates with rescue of motor decline in these animals
evidence.explanation: The 2015 claim that XJB-5-131 inhibits repeat lengthening.

evidence.snippet: Conversely, suppression of DSBs is sufficient to reverse neuropathology even when somatic expansion is active.
evidence.explanation: The 2026 position that rescue occurs while somatic expansion continues, which is in tension with XJB-5-131 acting as an expansion suppressor under this regimen.

open_questions/4.rationale: Budworth et al. 2015 reported that XJB-5-131 inhibits lengthening of the repeat tract in HdhQ(150) mice and that this correlated with rescue of motor decline, framing the drug as an expansion suppressor. Polyzos et al. 2026 reports that in congenic HdhQ(150/150) mice the same compound rescues neuropathology with no substantial impact on somatic expansion, and uses that dissociation as a central argument for double-strand breaks being an expansion-independent driver. The two studies differ in zygosity, in the congenic background, and above all in treatment window - early dosing in the 2015 study versus dosing begun at 60 weeks in the 2026 study, by which point most expansion has already occurred. A treatment that slows the rate of expansion would look effective when started early and ineffective when started late, which would reconcile the reports without either being wrong. This matters beyond bookkeeping: if XJB-5-131 does suppress expansion under some regimens, then the late-start experiment is the only one that cleanly separates the two drivers, and the separability argument rests on it alone. Curators should not assert either effect as settled.

evidence.snippet: Using a single-cell based assay, we found that, in HT22 cells or primary neurons transfected with mutant huntingtin, cell toxicity was accompanied by CBP depletion, rather than merely recruitment.
evidence.explanation: The depletion side, at single-cell resolution and with the full chain established in one system: CBP depletion, then histone hypo-acetylation, then toxicity, with CBP overexpression rescuing both the acetylation and the toxicity. The paper opens by acknowledging that the role of CBP has been controversial, so the disagreement is recognized in the primary literature and not an artifact of this review.

evidence.snippet: Although some CBP staining appeared as dots in the selective brain regions (e.g. hypothalamus and amygdala), double labeling showed that most CBP was not co-localized with huntingtin nuclear inclusions.
evidence.explanation: The no-depletion side, in whole mouse brain rather than transfected cells. Note the concession embedded in the sentence: punctate CBP staining does appear in some regions, so the disagreement is about whether that represents sequestration, not about whether any redistribution occurs at all.

evidence.snippet: Hsp70/Hsp40 chaperones interfere with the conformational change in mutant huntingtin and inhibit the deactivation of TBP.
evidence.explanation: The route out of the impasse, demonstrated for TBP rather than CBP: blocking the conformational rearrangement that generates soluble toxic species prevents transcription factor deactivation, which is an intervention rather than an observation and does not require any aggregate. Whether the same holds for CBP is what the proposed experiment would establish.

open_questions/5.rationale: Both sides are experimentally serious and neither is obviously wrong. The depletion side has cross-system concordance (cell culture, transgenic mice, human postmortem brain) plus a single-cell result in which CBP loss, histone hypo-acetylation and toxicity travel together and are all reversed by CBP overexpression. The no-depletion side tested the model four ways in HD mouse brain, found CBP diffusely nuclear despite abundant inclusions, showed most CBP not co-localized with inclusions by double labelling and electron microscopy, and confirmed by western blot that it was not trapped. The likely reconciliation is that the two are measuring different things: transfected single cells with high mutant huntingtin expression versus whole mouse brain, and functional availability versus total protein. That reconciliation is plausible but untested, which is why this is recorded as a controversy rather than resolved in favour of either. The wider mechanism is not in doubt in the same way. TBP deactivation by soluble oligomers is demonstrated with a chaperone rescue, and the entry's description has been written around functional inhibition accordingly; what remains open is specifically whether CBP is additionally lost from the nucleus.

evidence.snippet: HTT is involved in different mitophagy steps, promoting the physical proximity of different protein complexes during the initiation of mitophagy and recruiting mitophagy receptors essential for promoting the interaction between damaged mitochondria and the nascent autophagosome.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the clearance arm and the specific complexes involved, which is what makes a paired flux measurement worth running rather than speculative.

evidence.snippet: Studies over the past few years have implicated an impaired function of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR)-gamma coactivator-1alpha (PGC-1alpha), a transcriptional master coregulator of mitochondrial biogenesis, metabolism, and antioxidant defenses, in causing mitochondrial dysfunction in HD.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the biogenesis arm, the comparator against which the clearance arm would be weighed.

open_questions/6.rationale: The two arms have been studied independently and never in the same preparation, so the question has no answer rather than a contested one. It matters because the therapeutic strategies diverge completely: PGC-1alpha activation for a biogenesis-limited deficit, mitophagy induction for a clearance-limited one, and the failure of untargeted bioenergetic supplementation in HD is a reason to want the distinction before designing the next trial. The measurement is tractable - simultaneous turnover reporters in isogenic human neurons - and does not need new model construction.

evidence.snippet: The data suggest that MSN cell-autonomous increases in extrasynaptic NMDARs are driven by the HD mutation.
evidence.explanation: The model-side claim whose human validity is at issue.

evidence.snippet: In the neostriatum of HD, NR1, NR2B and GLT1mRNA decreased in correlation to disease severity.
evidence.explanation: The human observation that does not follow from the mouse model. Note the technique cannot separate synaptic from extrasynaptic receptors, so it constrains total receptor content only, which is part of why the mismatch is unresolved rather than decided.

evidence.snippet: For this reason many NMDA receptor antagonists have disappointingly failed advanced clinical trials for a number of diseases including stroke and neurodegenerative disorders such as Huntington's disease.
evidence.explanation: The clinical arm of the mismatch. The same review supplies the standing alternative explanation - that blocking all NMDAR activity removes physiological signalling too - so trial failure supports the existence of the mismatch without settling its cause.

open_questions/7.rationale: This is a mismatch rather than a plain evidence gap: the mouse evidence is strong, mechanistic and interventional, and the human evidence exists but does not obviously agree with it. The three human observations are individually weak arguments - subunit mRNA loss is expected from neuronal loss, absence of a genome-wide significant modifier signal is weak evidence of no effect for a mechanism that may act downstream of onset, and pan-NMDAR blockade removes physiological signalling along with pathological signalling - but they point the same way, and none of them is what the mouse work predicts. The measurement that would settle it does not exist: no PET ligand distinguishes synaptic from extrasynaptic NMDA receptors, so the compartment claim cannot be tested in living human brain at all. Until it can, extrasynaptic redistribution should be curated as a mouse mechanism with a plausible but unconfirmed human counterpart, and the excitotoxicity hypothesis should stay ALTERNATIVE.

evidence.snippet: Msh3 and Pms1 drive fast somatic mHtt CAG-expansion
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the expansion-incompetent cross exists and corrects synaptic and locomotor phenotypes, which is what makes the missing compartment-resolved measurement worth doing rather than speculative.

evidence.snippet: Activation of both STEP and calpain is calcium-dependent, and disruption of calcium homeostasis occurs early in the HD striatum.
evidence.explanation: Supplies the readouts the proposed cross would measure, and shows the trafficking machinery is driven by calcium dysregulation rather than by repeat length directly - which is precisely why the ordering cannot be assumed.

open_questions/8.rationale: The two mechanisms are routinely described as sequential - expansion raises the effective polyQ length, which then disrupts receptor trafficking - but the ordering is asserted rather than demonstrated. Msh3 deletion in Q140 mice abolishes somatic expansion and corrects synaptic and locomotor defects, yet the published readouts do not include compartment-resolved NMDAR localization, so the two mechanisms could equally be parallel consequences of the inherited allele. Which it is decides whether somatic-expansion suppression alone should be expected to normalize excitotoxic vulnerability, or whether the two need separate interventions. The experiment is a straightforward addition to an existing cross rather than new model construction.

evidence.snippet: Over 60 mutations producing truncations in the apoB gene ranging from apoB2 to apoB-89 have been identified as causes of FHBL
evidence.explanation: Documents the range of truncating APOB alleles causing FHBL1.

steps/3.description: A nonsense, frameshift, or canonical splice-site variant in APOB truncates the apoB open reading frame, producing a shortened apoB protein (apoB-XX nomenclature, denoting the percentage of full-length apoB translated) instead of full-length apoB-100/apoB-48. Over 60 distinct truncating APOB mutations, ranging from apoB-2 to apoB-89, have been reported as causes of FHBL1.

evidence.snippet: To test whether loss-of-function mutations in PCSK9 have the opposite effect, we sequenced the coding region of PCSK9 in 128 subjects (50% African American) with low plasma levels of LDL and found two nonsense mutations (Y142X and C679X)
evidence.explanation: The discovery study explicitly frames these as loss-of-function variants, the mirror image of the known gain-of-function hypercholesterolemia alleles.

steps/4.description: A PCSK9 nonsense or loss-of-function missense variant reduces or abolishes secreted PCSK9 activity. First identified through sequencing of PCSK9 in subjects with low plasma LDL specifically to test whether loss-of-function variants would have the mirror-image effect of the gain-of-function PCSK9 variants that cause autosomal dominant hypercholesterolemia (kb/disorders/Autosomal_Dominant_Hypercholesterolemia_3.yaml).

evidence.snippet: These two participants were compound heterozygotes for two distinct nonsense mutations in ANGPTL3 (encoding the angiopoietin-like 3 protein).
evidence.explanation: The discovery study identifies the causal ANGPTL3 nonsense mutations by exome sequencing.

steps/5.description: Biallelic ANGPTL3 loss-of-function variants (compound heterozygous or homozygous nonsense/frameshift alleles) abolish secreted ANGPTL3 activity. Discovered by whole-exome sequencing of two siblings with combined hypolipidemia not linked to APOB.

evidence.snippet: The activities of lipoprotein lipase and endothelial lipase, key enzymes in the metabolism of circulating triglycerides and HDL cholesterol, respectively, are elevated in Angptl3-knockout mice
evidence.explanation: Mouse knockout data establish elevated lipase activity as the mechanism for the triglyceride/HDL phenotypes.

evidence.snippet: The mechanism by which deficiency of ANGPTL3 lowers LDL cholesterol remains to be determined.
evidence.explanation: The authors explicitly state that the LPL/EL-inhibition mechanism explains the triglyceride and HDL-cholesterol phenotypes but not the LDL-cholesterol phenotype, hence PROVISIONAL confidence and PARTIAL support for extending this node's mechanism to the LDL branch.

steps/6.description: ANGPTL3 normally inhibits lipoprotein lipase and endothelial lipase, the key enzymes that hydrolyze circulating triglyceride-rich lipoproteins and HDL, respectively. Loss of ANGPTL3 function increases the activity of both enzymes. This is the established mechanism for the triglyceride and HDL-cholesterol reductions; the mechanism by which ANGPTL3 deficiency also lowers LDL cholesterol is less well resolved (see mechanism_confidence below).

evidence.snippet: these lower than expected levels result from a 74% lower secretion rate of VLDL apoB-100 from the liver, decreased production of LDL apoB-100, increased catabolism of VLDL and extremely low secretion of the truncated apoB
evidence.explanation: Kinetic evidence directly establishes the reduced hepatic secretion mechanism.

steps/7.description: Truncated apoB reduces the pool of apoB-lipoprotein particles available for hepatic VLDL and intestinal chylomicron assembly and secretion, a production-limited mechanism distinct from the lipidation defect of abetalipoproteinemia. Kinetic studies attribute the disproportionately low heterozygous apoB levels to markedly reduced VLDL apoB-100 secretion, decreased LDL apoB-100 production, increased VLDL catabolism, and extremely low secretion of the truncated species itself.

evidence.snippet: In 32 subjects with FHBL, average hepatic fat content measured by MR spectroscopy was 14.8% + 12.0% compared to 5.2% + 5.9%, respectively, for 33 normolipidemic controls
evidence.explanation: Directly measures increased hepatic fat content in FHBL subjects compared to matched controls.

steps/8.description: Reduced hepatic VLDL export retains triglyceride within hepatocytes, producing hepatic steatosis that can progress to steatohepatitis, fibrosis, and rarely cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma, even in heterozygous carriers. This hepatic-storage consequence is characteristic of the APOB production-limited route and is not seen with the PCSK9 or ANGPTL3 clearance-enhanced routes.

evidence.snippet: PCSK9 is a secreted serine protease that enhances the degradation of the LDL-receptor. Loss of function mutations in the PCSK9 gene prevent the PCSK9-mediated degradation of the LDL receptor and thus increase uptake of LDL by the liver, a process leading to a 30 to 70% reduction in plasma LDL-C levels
evidence.explanation: States both the normal PCSK9 mechanism and the quantitative effect of its loss on plasma LDL cholesterol.

steps/9.description: PCSK9 normally binds the hepatic LDL receptor and directs it toward lysosomal degradation after endocytosis rather than recycling it to the cell surface. Loss-of-function PCSK9 variants remove this restraint, so more LDL receptor recycles back to the hepatocyte surface. This is the exact mechanistic node that PCSK9-inhibitor biologics (evolocumab, alirocumab) pharmacologically reproduce to lower LDL cholesterol in hypercholesterolemia.

steps/10.description: More LDL receptor is available at the hepatocyte surface for receptor-mediated uptake of circulating LDL, increasing hepatic clearance of apoB-containing lipoproteins from plasma.

evidence.snippet: carriers of ANGPTL3 nonsense mutations had decreased rates of VLDL apolipoprotein B production and increased fractional catabolic rates for LDL apolipoprotein B
evidence.explanation: Physiological kinetic studies in carriers directly support both reduced VLDL production and increased LDL catabolism.

steps/11.description: Unrestrained lipoprotein lipase and endothelial lipase activity accelerates catabolism of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins and HDL, lowering triglycerides and HDL cholesterol together with LDL cholesterol rather than selectively lowering apoB-containing particles as in the APOB and PCSK9 routes. Carriers of ANGPTL3 loss-of-function variants additionally show decreased VLDL apoB production and increased LDL fractional catabolism, indicating ANGPTL3 also acts directly on hepatic lipoprotein secretion and clearance independent of its role inhibiting circulating lipases.

evidence.snippet: These data indicate that moderate lifelong reduction in the plasma level of LDL cholesterol is associated with a substantial reduction in the incidence of coronary events, even in populations with a high prevalence of non-lipid-related cardiovascular risk factors.
evidence.explanation: States the general principle that lifelong LDL reduction from PCSK9 loss of function substantially reduces coronary events.

steps/12.description: A shared downstream consequence of the PCSK9 and ANGPTL3 clearance-enhanced routes: lifelong, moderate reduction of circulating LDL cholesterol (and, for ANGPTL3, triglycerides) from birth is associated with substantially reduced coronary heart disease risk, providing the human-genetics validation for PCSK9-inhibitor and ANGPTL3-inhibitor drug development.

evidence.snippet: Several mutations in the apolipoprotein (apo) B, proprotein convertase subtilisin kexin 9 (PCSK9) and microsomal triglyceride transfer protein genes result in low or absent levels of apoB and LDL cholesterol (LDL-C) in plasma which cause familial hypobetalipoproteinemia (FHBL) and abetalipoproteinemia (ABL).
evidence.explanation: States the shared convergent biochemical phenotype across the causal genes covered in this entry.

steps/13.description: The convergent biochemical phenotype: plasma apoB and LDL cholesterol persistently below the 5th percentile, reached by three mechanistically distinct routes (reduced hepatic/intestinal apoB production, enhanced hepatic LDL-receptor-mediated clearance, or enhanced lipolytic catabolism of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins).

evidence.snippet: The most common clinical findings are hepatomegaly, steatorrhea, and failure to thrive / growth deficiency.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists the characteristic gastrointestinal manifestations of biallelic APOB-FHBL.

steps/14.description: In the severe (homozygous or compound heterozygous FHBL1) form, insufficient intestinal chylomicron secretion impairs absorption and transport of dietary lipid, causing steatorrhea and fat-soluble-vitamin malabsorption. This branch is not seen in heterozygous FHBL1 or in the PCSK9/ANGPTL3 clearance-enhanced routes, which do not affect intestinal chylomicron assembly.

evidence.snippet: In the absence of treatment, affected individuals can develop atypical pigmentation of the retina; progressive loss of deep tendon reflexes, vibratory sense, and proprioception; muscle pain or weakness; dysarthria; ataxia; tremors; and steatohepatitis, fibrosis, and rarely, cirrhosis of the liver.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews describes the untreated natural history driven by fat-soluble-vitamin deficiency.

steps/15.description: Impaired absorption and lipoprotein transport reduce the bioavailability of vitamins A, D, E, and K in severe (biallelic) FHBL1, mirroring the vitamin deficiency of abetalipoproteinemia and driving the same downstream retinal, neurologic, and coagulation complications when untreated.

evidence.snippet: Familial hypobetalipoproteinemia is an inherited disorder of lipid metabolism defined by very low levels (<5th percentile of age- and sex-specific values) of plasma apolipoprotein B and LDL cholesterol.
evidence.explanation: States the defining biochemical threshold for the disease across its genetic causes.

steps/16.description: The defining biochemical phenotype across all subtypes, apoB and LDL cholesterol below the 5th percentile.

evidence.snippet: The lipid profile is one of hypocholesterolemia with low plasma low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, low plasma high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, low plasma triglycerides, and low plasma apolipoprotein (apo) B and apo A-I levels.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews describes the total-cholesterol reduction as part of the combined hypolipidemia profile.

steps/17.description: Total cholesterol is reduced secondary to the reduced apoB-lipoprotein pool.

evidence.snippet: compound heterozygotes had a very low level of HDL cholesterol (mean, 18 mg per deciliter
evidence.explanation: Quantifies decreased HDL cholesterol specific to biallelic ANGPTL3 carriers.

steps/18.description: Characteristic of biallelic ANGPTL3 deficiency, distinguishing combined hypolipidemia from the LDL-selective APOB and PCSK9 routes; segregates as a recessive trait requiring biallelic loss.

evidence.snippet: Individuals with a heterozygous, typically truncating pathogenic variant in APOB are usually asymptomatic with mild liver dysfunction and hepatic steatosis.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews states hepatic steatosis as a characteristic finding in heterozygous FHBL1.

steps/19.description: The main clinical manifestation of heterozygous FHBL1, due to defective hepatic triglyceride export.

evidence.snippet: about 5%-10% of individuals with heterozygous APOB-FHBL develop relatively more severe nonalcoholic steatohepatitis requiring medical attention and occasionally progressing to cirrhosis, albeit very rarely
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews quantifies the minority of heterozygous carriers who progress to clinically significant liver disease.

steps/20.description: Rare but reported progression from hepatic steatosis to steatohepatitis and cirrhosis, occasionally with hepatocellular carcinoma, even in individuals with only one truncating APOB allele.

evidence.snippet: may present from infancy through to adulthood with a range of clinical symptoms including deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins and gastrointestinal and neurologic dysfunction
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews describes gastrointestinal dysfunction and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency broadly rather than naming fat malabsorption specifically, hence PARTIAL; the low-fat dietary management recommendation elsewhere in the chapter is consistent with this but is a treatment recommendation, not a phenotype observation.

steps/21.description: Intestinal lipid absorption is impaired in severe (homozygous/compound heterozygous) FHBL1. Frequency is deliberately omitted: GeneReviews documents the clinical sign (steatorrhea, curated separately below) and the underlying gastrointestinal dysfunction, but does not quantify "fat malabsorption" as a distinct, separately banded finding.

evidence.snippet: deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins and gastrointestinal and neurologic dysfunction
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews links fat-soluble vitamin deficiency (including vitamin E) to the neurologic complications of biallelic disease.

steps/22.description: Fat-soluble vitamin deficiency in severe (biallelic) FHBL1, the deficiency most closely tied to neurologic complications.

evidence.snippet: Although there is one normal allele in heterozygous FHBL, plasma apoB-100 levels are approximately 24% of normal rather than the predicted 50%
evidence.explanation: Stable-isotope kinetic data show heterozygous truncating alleles disproportionately reduce apoB output below the simple gene-dosage expectation.

edges/3.description: Truncated apoB is produced in reduced quantity and is secreted far less efficiently than the predicted 50% gene-dosage share.

edges/4.description: Fewer apoB-lipoprotein particles are secreted into plasma.

evidence.snippet: This decreased secretion of apoB from the liver results in decreased triglyceride export from the liver, which in turn leads to the development of fatty liver
evidence.explanation: States the direct causal step from reduced apoB secretion to hepatic triglyceride retention and fatty liver.

edges/5.description: Reduced hepatic apoB secretion decreases triglyceride export from the liver in VLDL, producing hepatic steatosis even as less apoB-lipoprotein reaches plasma.

evidence.snippet: Individuals with a heterozygous, typically truncating pathogenic variant in APOB are usually asymptomatic with mild liver dysfunction and hepatic steatosis.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews states hepatic steatosis as the characteristic manifestation of heterozygous FHBL1.

edges/6.description: Hepatocyte triglyceride retention is observed as hepatic steatosis.

evidence.snippet: Steatohepatitis, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma have all been described in subjects with truncated apoBs
evidence.explanation: Documents progression to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma in truncated-apoB carriers.

edges/7.description: Chronic hepatic triglyceride accumulation can progress to steatohepatitis and, rarely, cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma, even in individuals with only a heterozygous truncating allele.

evidence.snippet: Loss of function mutations in the PCSK9 gene prevent the PCSK9-mediated degradation of the LDL receptor and thus increase uptake of LDL by the liver
evidence.explanation: States the direct causal mechanism linking PCSK9 loss of function to reduced LDL receptor degradation.

edges/8.description: Loss of PCSK9 function removes the normal restraint on hepatic LDL receptor turnover.

edges/9.description: Reduced receptor degradation increases steady-state hepatic LDL receptor abundance available for uptake.

evidence.snippet: these mutations were associated with a 28 percent reduction in mean LDL cholesterol and an 88 percent reduction in the risk of CHD
evidence.explanation: Population data directly link PCSK9 loss-of-function variants to reduced LDL cholesterol.

edges/10.description: Enhanced hepatic LDL-receptor-mediated uptake increases clearance of circulating LDL, unlike the production-limited APOB route.

edges/11.description: Loss of ANGPTL3 removes its normal inhibitory restraint on lipoprotein lipase and endothelial lipase.

edges/12.description: Increased lipase activity accelerates lipolytic catabolism of VLDL and HDL; the LDL branch is less mechanistically resolved.

edges/13.description: Accelerated catabolism of VLDL and LDL, together with reduced VLDL apoB production, reduces circulating apoB-lipoprotein concentration.

evidence.snippet: compound heterozygotes had a very low level of HDL cholesterol (mean, 18 mg per deciliter
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the HDL-cholesterol reduction specific to biallelic (compound heterozygous) carriers.

edges/14.description: Endothelial lipase activation also accelerates HDL catabolism, distinguishing this route from the LDL-selective APOB and PCSK9 routes. Unlike the LDL/triglyceride traits, this HDL effect segregates as a strictly recessive trait requiring biallelic ANGPTL3 loss.

evidence.snippet: The 3 individuals with complete ANGPTL3 deficiency showed no evidence of coronary atherosclerotic plaque.
evidence.explanation: Direct imaging evidence of absent coronary atherosclerosis in complete ANGPTL3 deficiency.

evidence.snippet: Carrier status was associated with a 34% reduction in odds of CAD (odds ratio: 0.66; 95% confidence interval: 0.44 to 0.98; p = 0.04).
evidence.explanation: Population-level genetic association between heterozygous ANGPTL3 loss-of-function carrier status and reduced CAD odds.

edges/15.description: Lifelong reduction of all three major apoB/lipid fractions by ANGPTL3 deficiency is associated with reduced coronary atherosclerotic burden and lower odds of coronary artery disease.

edges/16.description: Reduced apoB-lipoprotein particle number is measured as decreased LDL cholesterol.

edges/17.description: Reduced apoB-lipoprotein particle number lowers total cholesterol.

evidence.snippet: Persons with hypobetalipoproteinemia may also have fat malabsorption due to impaired incorporation of dietary fats into chylomicrons in the absorptive cells of the intestine.
evidence.explanation: States the intestinal fat-malabsorption branch specific to the apoB production-limited route.

edges/18.description: When severe (homozygous/compound heterozygous FHBL1), reduced intestinal chylomicron secretion impairs dietary fat absorption. This branch does not occur in heterozygous FHBL1 or in the PCSK9/ANGPTL3 clearance-enhanced routes.

edges/19.description: Defective chylomicron export produces impaired dietary fat absorption.

evidence.snippet: Individuals with biallelic APOB-related familial hypobetalipoproteinemia (APOB-FHBL) may present from infancy through to adulthood with a range of clinical symptoms including deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins and gastrointestinal and neurologic dysfunction.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews links intestinal dysfunction to fat-soluble-vitamin deficiency and downstream neurologic disease.

edges/20.description: Chylomicron failure impairs absorption and transport of vitamins A, D, E, and K.

edges/21.description: Reduced vitamin E absorption and transport lowers circulating vitamin E, the deficiency most closely tied to neurologic complications.

evidence.snippet: The diagnosis of biallelic APOB-related familial hypobetalipoproteinemia (APOB-FHBL) or heterozygous APOB-FHBL is established in a proband with either biallelic or a heterozygous pathogenic variant(s), respectively, in APOB identified by molecular genetic testing
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews states the molecular diagnostic criterion for both allelic states.

evidence.snippet: PNPLA3 and TM6SF2 have been extensively validated as risk factors for MASLD,89,90 and the TM6SF2 E167K and PNPLA3 I148M variants can promote the profibrotic phenotype of hepatic stellate cells.91,92 Cases have been reported with combined APOB and PNPLA3 variants leading to fibrosis or cirrhosis,93
evidence.explanation: Reports PNPLA3 I148M as a validated modifier that can promote fibrosis progression when co-occurring with a causal APOB variant.

genes/1.notes: PNPLA3 I148M is a common MASLD risk variant, independent of the APOB truncating/missense alleles that cause FHBL1 itself. Co-occurrence of a PNPLA3 risk variant with a causal APOB variant has been reported to promote progression to fibrosis or cirrhosis, offering a candidate explanation for the variable hepatic severity among carriers of the same APOB allele. Curated as a liver-disease modifier, not as a second causal gene for the hypobetalipoproteinemia biochemical phenotype.

evidence.snippet: sequence variants in the proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 serine protease gene (PCSK9) that are associated with reduced plasma levels of LDL cholesterol
evidence.explanation: Establishes the PCSK9-LDL cholesterol association at population scale.

evidence.snippet: The molecular diagnosis of familial combined hypolipidemia is established in a proband with suggestive laboratory findings and biallelic pathogenic variants in ANGPTL3 identified by molecular genetic testing.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews states the molecular diagnostic criterion for the biallelic disease.

evidence.snippet: Individuals with heterozygous APOB-FHBL: no treatment typically required.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews states that heterozygous FHBL1 generally requires no treatment, in contrast to the biallelic form.

evidence.snippet: reduce their vitamin A supplement dose by 50%
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews specifies the pregnancy-specific vitamin A dose adjustment for biallelic FHBL1.

treatments/0.description: For biallelic (severe) FHBL1, a low-fat diet (<30% of total calories) with adequate caloric intake plus high-dose oral vitamin A, D, E, and K supplementation, mirroring management of abetalipoproteinemia. No treatment is typically required for heterozygous FHBL1, PCSK9 loss-of-function, or ANGPTL3 deficiency.

evidence.snippet: low-fat diet (<30% of total calories) while ensuring adequate caloric intake; high-dose oral fat-soluble vitamin supplementation (vitamin E: 100-300 IU/kg/day; vitamin A: 100-400 IU/kg/day; vitamin D: 800-1200 IU/day; vitamin K: 5-35 mg/week)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews specifies the dietary and vitamin management regimen for biallelic APOB-FHBL.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: A low-fat diet reduces the dietary lipid burden on the impaired intestinal chylomicron-export pathway in biallelic FHBL1.

evidence.snippet: high-dose oral fat-soluble vitamin supplementation may ameliorate or prevent clinical features of APOB-FHBL
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports vitamin replacement as ameliorating or preventing clinical features.

treatments/0/targets/1.description: High-dose oral fat-soluble vitamin supplementation increases vitamin availability despite persistent intestinal malabsorption.

evidence.snippet: liver transplantation may be considered for those with end-stage liver disease
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists liver transplantation as a management option for end-stage liver disease in biallelic APOB-FHBL.

treatments/1.description: Considered for biallelic (severe) FHBL1 patients who progress to end-stage liver disease from chronic hepatic triglyceride retention and steatohepatitis.

evidence.snippet: liver transplantation may be considered for those with end-stage liver disease
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists liver transplantation as a management option for end-stage liver disease in biallelic APOB-FHBL.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Transplantation replaces the failing liver rather than correcting the underlying APOB-lipoprotein secretion defect, which persists in extrahepatic tissue.

evidence.snippet: laboratory studies to include lipid profile, liver function tests, vitamin levels, INR, calcium, phosphorus, uric acid, CBC, vitamin B12, folate and TSH every 1-2 years
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews specifies the biochemical surveillance schedule for biallelic APOB-FHBL.

evidence.snippet: ophthalmology evaluation and neurologic examination every 6-12 months after age 10 years; hepatic ultrasound and bone mineral densitometry studies every 3-5 years after age 10 years
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews specifies the periodic specialist and imaging surveillance schedule for biallelic APOB-FHBL.

treatments/2.description: Longitudinal follow-up in biallelic (severe) FHBL1 assesses growth, gastrointestinal symptoms, lipid profile, liver function, fat-soluble vitamins, coagulation, and other chemistries, alongside periodic ophthalmologic, neurologic, hepatic imaging, and bone-density evaluation, mirroring the surveillance schedule used for abetalipoproteinemia.

evidence.snippet: The recent reports of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma associated with FHBL suggest that liver enzymes should be monitored in subjects with FHBL and if elevated, hepatic imaging be considered
evidence.explanation: The review recommends liver-enzyme monitoring and imaging surveillance for FHBL carriers.

treatments/3.description: Periodic liver function testing and hepatic ultrasound because heterozygous FHBL1 carries a real, if usually mild, risk of hepatic steatosis progressing to steatohepatitis, fibrosis, or rarely cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.

evidence.snippet: At conception, each sib of an affected individual has a 25% chance of being affected, a 50% chance of being heterozygous for APOB-FHBL and having laboratory findings and (rarely) clinical features, and a 25% chance of being unaffected and not a heterozygote.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews provides the autosomal-recessive recurrence-risk framework for biallelic APOB-FHBL.

treatments/4.description: Counseling addresses the autosomal recessive recurrence risk for the severe biallelic FHBL1 and ANGPTL3-deficiency forms, carrier testing, and evaluation of at-risk relatives when a familial variant is known.

evidence.snippet: moderate lifelong reduction in the plasma level of LDL cholesterol is associated with a substantial reduction in the incidence of coronary events
evidence.explanation: This entry's own human-genetics finding is the rationale cited for developing PCSK9-inhibitor therapy.

treatments/5.description: Fully human monoclonal antibody against PCSK9. Not a treatment for hypobetalipoproteinemia itself - PCSK9 loss-of-function hypobetalipoproteinemia is clinically benign and requires no treatment - but a pharmacological reproduction of the exact PCSK9-loss-of-function mechanism curated in this entry, developed and used to lower LDL cholesterol in hypercholesterolemic patients (see kb/disorders/Autosomal_Dominant_Hypercholesterolemia_3.yaml). Included here as the therapeutic validation of this entry's human-genetics rationale.

evidence.snippet: Evolocumab is a monoclonal antibody that inhibits proprotein convertase subtilisin-kexin type 9 (PCSK9) and lowers low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol levels by approximately 60%.
evidence.explanation: States the drug's molecular target and quantitative effect on LDL cholesterol.

treatments/5/targets/0.description: Evolocumab neutralizes circulating PCSK9, pharmacologically reproducing the reduced-LDL-receptor-degradation state that PCSK9 loss-of-function variants produce genetically, increasing hepatic LDL clearance.

evidence.snippet: At week 24, patients in the evinacumab group had a relative reduction from baseline in the LDL cholesterol level of 47.1%, as compared with an increase of 1.9% in the placebo group
evidence.explanation: Quantifies evinacumab's LDL-lowering effect in a randomized trial, the clinical validation of the mechanism curated in this entry.

treatments/6.description: Monoclonal antibody against ANGPTL3. Not a treatment for hypobetalipoproteinemia itself - ANGPTL3 deficiency is clinically silent and requires no treatment - but a pharmacological reproduction of this entry's ANGPTL3-loss-of-function mechanism, developed and approved to lower LDL cholesterol in homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, where it lowers LDL cholesterol by an LDL-receptor-independent route. Included here as the therapeutic validation of this entry's human-genetics rationale.

evidence.snippet: Loss-of-function variants in the gene encoding angiopoietin-like 3 (ANGPTL3) are associated with hypolipidemia and protection against atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Evinacumab, a monoclonal antibody against ANGPTL3, has shown potential benefit in patients with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia.
evidence.explanation: The pivotal trial's own background statement explicitly frames evinacumab as reproducing the ANGPTL3 loss-of-function state curated in this entry.

treatments/6/targets/0.description: Evinacumab neutralizes circulating ANGPTL3, pharmacologically reproducing the loss-of-ANGPTL3-inhibition state that biallelic ANGPTL3 loss-of-function variants produce genetically, de-repressing lipoprotein and endothelial lipase and lowering LDL, HDL, and triglycerides.

evidence.snippet: Three genetic forms exist: (i) premature stop codon specifying mutations of APOB; (ii) FHBL linked to a susceptibility locus on the chromosome 3p21; and (iii) FHBL linked neither to APOB nor to the chromosome 3p21.
evidence.explanation: States that molecularly uncharacterized non-APOB FHBL loci exist independent of the genes curated in this entry.

evidence.snippet: Liver fat in the chromosome 3p21-linked FHBL is normal.
evidence.explanation: Shows the 3p21-linked form does not share the hepatic steatosis mechanism curated for the APOB route, arguing it is mechanistically distinct rather than a minor variant.

evidence.snippet: Significant lod scores were not found for regions on chromosomes 3 and 10 previously reported to be associated with familial hypobetalipoproteinemia,6,7 nor for any other regions in the genome.
evidence.explanation: Independently corroborates that FHBL families exist that map to loci other than APOB, PCSK9, or ANGPTL3.

open_questions/0.rationale: This entry curates three molecularly resolved causal genes, but the literature independently documents at least one additional linked locus (chromosome 3p21) and further families with hypobetalipoproteinemia linked to neither APOB nor that locus, whose causal gene(s) remain unidentified. Unlike heterozygous APOB-FHBL1, the chromosome 3p21-linked form does not have increased liver fat, so it is not simply a phenocopy of the production-limited APOB route and may represent a fourth distinct mechanism.

evidence.snippet: The FGFR3 gene encodes fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 protein, a negative regulator of chondrogenesis. Gain-of-function mutations result in constitutively activated FGFR3, leading to aberrant signal transduction, and accounting for inhibition of chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation.
evidence.explanation: Comprehensive review of FGFR3 molecular pathology establishing that gain-of-function mutations cause constitutive activation leading to impaired chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation.

evidence.snippet: Hypochondroplasia (HCH) is a mild dwarfism caused by missense mutations in fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3), with the majority of cases resulting from a heterozygous p.Asn540Lys gain-of-function mutation.
evidence.explanation: The first HCH mouse model confirms that the Asn540Lys gain-of-function mutation is sufficient to cause progressive dwarfism via FGFR3 activation.

steps/2.description: The FGFR3 N540K mutation causes constitutive activation of the receptor tyrosine kinase, resulting in ligand-independent FGFR3 signaling in growth plate chondrocytes, osteoblasts, and other skeletal cells.

evidence.snippet: Gain-of-function mutations result in constitutively activated FGFR3, leading to aberrant signal transduction, and accounting for inhibition of chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation.
evidence.explanation: The FGFR3 therapeutic review establishes that aberrant MAPK/ERK signal transduction downstream of activated FGFR3 inhibits chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation.

evidence.snippet: FGF2 treatment of primary chondrocyte cultures from Fgfr3Asn534Lys/+ mice resulted in increased and sustained Erk1/2 phosphorylation compared with control cells (P < 0.05), thus indicating that the p.Asn534Lys mutation overactivated FGFR3 and its downstream MAPK pathway
evidence.explanation: Primary chondrocyte cultures from the HCH knock-in mouse show increased and sustained ERK1/2 phosphorylation upon FGF2 stimulation, providing direct experimental evidence that the N540K/N534K gain-of-function mutation hyperactivates the downstream MAPK cascade.

steps/3.description: Constitutively activated FGFR3 drives hyperactivation of the Ras-MAPK/ERK signaling cascade in growth plate chondrocytes, suppressing chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation.

evidence.snippet: Fgfr3Asn534Lys/+ mice exhibited progressive dwarfism and impairment of the synchondroses of the cranial base, resulting in defective formation of the foramen magnum.
evidence.explanation: The HCH mouse model demonstrates that FGFR3 gain-of-function causes progressive dwarfism through impaired endochondral ossification.

evidence.snippet: progressive disorganization of the growth plate in Fgfr3Asn534Lys/+ mice compared with Fgfr3+/+ from P14 that was characterized by reduced hypertrophic zone width and delayed secondary ossification center (SOC) formation
evidence.explanation: Growth-plate histology in the HCH mouse shows progressive disorganization with a reduced hypertrophic zone and delayed secondary ossification center formation, the cartilage-level mechanism by which FGFR3 activation impairs endochondral ossification.

steps/4.description: Suppressed chondrocyte proliferation and altered hypertrophic differentiation downstream of MAPK/ERK hyperactivation impair endochondral ossification, reducing longitudinal bone growth and causing short stature.

evidence.snippet: Trabecular bone mineral density (BMD) of long bones and vertebral bodies was decreased, but cortical BMD increased with age in both tibiae and femurs. These results demonstrate that bones in Fgfr3Asn534Lys/+ mice, due to FGFR3 activation, exhibit some characteristics of osteoporosis.
evidence.explanation: The HCH mouse model reveals a complex bone mineralization phenotype with decreased trabecular BMD and paradoxically increased cortical BMD with reduced mechanical toughness, suggesting osteoporosis risk in aging HCH patients.

evidence.snippet: transcriptional profiling of the femoral cortical bone demonstrated a downregulation of markers of the osteoblast lineage
evidence.explanation: Transcriptional profiling of cortical bone in the HCH mouse shows downregulation of osteoblast-lineage markers, providing a molecular basis for the aberrant osteoblast and osteocyte function underlying the bone mineralization defect.

evidence.snippet: long bones were brittle with reduced toughness
evidence.explanation: Despite the paradoxical increase in cortical BMD, mechanical testing shows the long bones are brittle with reduced toughness, directly supporting the reduced-toughness characterization and an increased fracture risk in HCH.

steps/5.description: FGFR3 activation alters osteoblast and osteocyte function, leading to decreased trabecular bone mineral density in long bones and vertebrae, with a paradoxical age-related increase in cortical BMD accompanied by reduced toughness. These changes produce bone with osteoporosis-like characteristics.

evidence.snippet: Fgfr3Asn534Lys/+ mice exhibited progressive dwarfism and impairment of the synchondroses of the cranial base, resulting in defective formation of the foramen magnum.
evidence.explanation: Mouse model demonstrates that FGFR3 gain-of-function directly disrupts cranial base synchondrosis development and foramen magnum formation, explaining the craniofacial features of HCH.

steps/6.description: FGFR3 activation impairs the synchondroses of the cranial base, leading to premature closure and defective formation of the foramen magnum. This contributes to relative macrocephaly and potential foramen magnum stenosis.

evidence.snippet: Hypochondroplasia is a skeletal dysplasia characterized by short stature; stocky build; disproportionately short arms and legs; broad, short hands and feet; mild joint laxity; and relative macrocephaly.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews identifies short stature as part of the core clinical phenotype of hypochondroplasia.

evidence.snippet: The patients presented with a short stature and/or short limbs.
evidence.explanation: In this Korean FGFR3 N540K cohort, short stature and/or short limbs were the presenting growth abnormality.

evidence.snippet: Hypochondroplasia (HCH) is a disproportionate short-statured skeletal dysplasia condition caused by gain-of-function pathogenic variants in the fibroblast growth receptor 3 gene (FGFR3).
evidence.explanation: Expert consensus likewise frames HCH as a disproportionate short-stature disorder.

steps/7.description: Disproportionate short stature is the defining growth phenotype of hypochondroplasia. In many children it becomes more obvious in toddlerhood or early school age as growth velocity falls relative to peers.

evidence.snippet: Hypochondroplasia is an autosomal dominant skeletal dysplasia expressing postnatal onset of short stature with mild rhizomelic shortening of the limbs.
evidence.explanation: A molecularly confirmed neonatal case report documents mild rhizomelic limb shortening as an early manifestation.

evidence.snippet: Between ages 2-3 years, a characteristic growth pattern including limb shortening and body disproportion may become evident.
evidence.explanation: Expert consensus states that limb shortening and body disproportion typically become clinically apparent between ages 2 and 3 years.

steps/8.description: Mild proximal limb shortening and body disproportion may emerge after infancy and can be subtle in the neonatal period.

evidence.snippet: Hypochondroplasia is a skeletal dysplasia characterized by short stature; stocky build; disproportionately short arms and legs; broad, short hands and feet; mild joint laxity; and relative macrocephaly.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews includes broad, short hands among the characteristic clinical features of hypochondroplasia.

steps/9.description: Hands are often short as part of the appendicular skeletal phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Hypochondroplasia is a skeletal dysplasia characterized by short stature; stocky build; disproportionately short arms and legs; broad, short hands and feet; mild joint laxity; and relative macrocephaly.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews includes broad, short feet among the characteristic clinical features of hypochondroplasia.

steps/10.description: Short feet accompany the short-limbed skeletal phenotype.

evidence.snippet: short and broad phalange (particularly the proximal and middle phalanges), and prominent ulnar styloid processes.
evidence.explanation: Human hand radiographs in this FGFR3 N540K hypochondroplasia study show relative shortening and broadening of the middle phalanges.

steps/11.description: Hand radiographs can show short, broad middle phalanges in affected children.

evidence.snippet: short and broad phalange (particularly the proximal and middle phalanges), and prominent ulnar styloid processes.
evidence.explanation: Human hand radiographs in this FGFR3 N540K hypochondroplasia study show relative shortening and broadening of the proximal phalanges.

steps/12.description: Hand radiographs can show short, broad proximal phalanges in affected children.

evidence.snippet: carpal bone age was also determined using the standard Greulich and Pyle atlas and was delayed
evidence.explanation: The study reports delayed carpal bone age in all three imaged human hypochondroplasia patients, supporting delayed skeletal maturation as an associated radiographic feature.

steps/13.description: Delayed carpal bone age has been documented on hand radiographs in children with FGFR3 N540K hypochondroplasia.

evidence.snippet: The mean (SD) HCH-I was -3.0 (1.2) in the HCH cohort, compared to -0.2 (0.9) in the CIGS cohort. An HCH-I below -2 correctly identified 78% of children with HCH, while only 2.4% of CIGS children fell below the cut-off.
evidence.explanation: This large 2026 cohort study shows marked head-height disproportion in HCH, directly supporting relative macrocephaly as a characteristic phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Genu varum, macrocephaly, and developmental delay were observed in 11 (55.0%), 9 (45.0%), and 5 (25.0%) patients, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Macrocephaly was observed in 9/20 patients (45%), which falls in the FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: features suggestive of HCH include a sustained fall in length/height centiles over the first 2 years of life, relative macrocephaly, neonatal seizures, and specific radiographic and neuroimaging findings.
evidence.explanation: Expert consensus identifies relative macrocephaly as a key feature suggestive of HCH.

steps/14.description: Head circumference is often relatively large for height, with measurable head-height disproportion even when absolute macrocephaly is not striking.

evidence.snippet: Hypochondroplasia is a skeletal dysplasia characterized by short stature; stocky build; disproportionately short arms and legs; broad, short hands and feet; mild joint laxity; and relative macrocephaly.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists mild joint laxity among the characteristic clinical features of hypochondroplasia.

steps/15.description: Mild ligamentous laxity can accompany the skeletal phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Genu varum, macrocephaly, and developmental delay were observed in 11 (55.0%), 9 (45.0%), and 5 (25.0%) patients, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Genu varum was observed in 11/20 patients (55%), which falls in the FREQUENT band.

steps/16.description: Bowing of the legs is one of the most frequently observed skeletal features, reported in over half of patients with confirmed N540K mutations.

evidence.snippet: Medical complications common to achondroplasia (e.g., foramen magnum stenosis, spinal stenosis, tibial bowing, obstructive apnea) occur less frequently in hypochondroplasia, but intellectual disability and epilepsy may be more prevalent.
