evidence.snippet: Three-year-old female showing slight tibial bending with elongation of the distal fibula.
evidence.explanation: The FGFR3 N540K hypochondroplasia imaging series documents tibial bending in an affected child.

steps/17.description: Tibial bowing or bending is a recognized lower-limb manifestation, overlapping clinically with the broader genu varum/leg-bowing phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Six patients had peritrigonal white matter reduction, and 4 had abnormally shaped lateral ventricles.
evidence.explanation: Abnormally shaped lateral ventricles were observed on MRI in four neurologically evaluated patients with FGFR3 N540K-related HCH.

steps/18.description: Abnormally shaped lateral ventricles have been observed in HCH patients on neuroimaging.

evidence.snippet: Of the 12 patients who underwent neuroimaging, five (41.7%) showed abnormal findings (one required operation for obstructive hydrocephalus).
evidence.explanation: One child in this 20-patient Korean cohort required surgery for obstructive hydrocephalus, showing that hydrocephalus can occur as a clinically important complication.

steps/19.description: Obstructive hydrocephalus requiring neurosurgical treatment has been reported in a small subset of affected children.

evidence.snippet: Medical complications common to achondroplasia (e.g., foramen magnum stenosis, spinal stenosis, tibial bowing, obstructive apnea) occur less frequently in hypochondroplasia, but intellectual disability and epilepsy may be more prevalent.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists foramen magnum stenosis as a recognized complication of hypochondroplasia, while noting it is less frequent than in achondroplasia.

evidence.snippet: Fgfr3Asn534Lys/+ mice exhibited progressive dwarfism and impairment of the synchondroses of the cranial base, resulting in defective formation of the foramen magnum.
evidence.explanation: The hypochondroplasia mouse model provides mechanistic support that FGFR3 gain-of-function impairs cranial-base synchondroses and foramen magnum formation.

steps/20.description: Foramen magnum narrowing can occur in hypochondroplasia, though it is reported less often than in achondroplasia.

evidence.snippet: Medical complications common to achondroplasia (e.g., foramen magnum stenosis, spinal stenosis, tibial bowing, obstructive apnea) occur less frequently in hypochondroplasia, but intellectual disability and epilepsy may be more prevalent.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews explicitly lists spinal stenosis among recognized but less frequent hypochondroplasia complications.

steps/21.description: Spinal canal stenosis occurs less often than in achondroplasia but remains a clinically important complication in hypochondroplasia.

evidence.snippet: Foramen magnum stenosis, thoracolumbar kyphosis, genu varum, and spinal stenosis are management by orthopedists and neurosurgeons using similar strategies employed in achondroplasia.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews identifies thoracolumbar kyphosis as a hypochondroplasia manifestation requiring orthopedic or neurosurgical management.

steps/22.description: Thoracolumbar kyphosis may require orthopedic or neurosurgical monitoring in the same general management framework used for achondroplasia.

evidence.snippet: Radiologic features include shortening of long bones with mild metaphyseal flare; a lack of widening or a narrowing of the lumbar interpedicular distances with shortening of the pedicle length and posterior scalloping of the vertebral bodies; short, broad femoral neck; and squared, shortened ilia.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews identifies lack of widening or narrowing of the lumbar interpedicular distances as a characteristic radiographic feature.

evidence.snippet: Hypochondroplasia is a genetic skeletal dysplasia characterized by disproportionate short stature, stocky appearance and several clinical and radiological features very similar, but much milder, than those of classical achondroplasia, including shortened and stubby long bones, decreased lumbo-sacral interpediculate distances, posterior scalloping of the lumbar vertebrae, metaphyseal flaring, and moderate macrocephaly.
evidence.explanation: This radiology-focused review independently confirms decreased lumbosacral interpediculate distance as a salient hypochondroplasia sign.

steps/23.description: Lack of the normal caudal widening or frank narrowing of the lumbar/lumbosacral interpedicular distance is a classic radiographic clue to hypochondroplasia.

evidence.snippet: Radiologic features include shortening of long bones with mild metaphyseal flare; a lack of widening or a narrowing of the lumbar interpedicular distances with shortening of the pedicle length and posterior scalloping of the vertebral bodies; short, broad femoral neck; and squared, shortened ilia.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists posterior scalloping of the vertebral bodies among the core radiographic features.

evidence.explanation: A radiology review likewise identifies posterior scalloping of the lumbar vertebrae as part of the classic pattern.

steps/24.description: Posterior vertebral body scalloping is a recurrent spinal radiographic finding in hypochondroplasia.

evidence.snippet: Radiologic features include shortening of long bones with mild metaphyseal flare; a lack of widening or a narrowing of the lumbar interpedicular distances with shortening of the pedicle length and posterior scalloping of the vertebral bodies; short, broad femoral neck; and squared, shortened ilia.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews describes mild metaphyseal flare as a characteristic long-bone radiographic feature.

evidence.snippet: Hypochondroplasia is a genetic skeletal dysplasia characterized by disproportionate short stature, stocky appearance and several clinical and radiological features very similar, but much milder, than those of classical achondroplasia, including shortened and stubby long bones, decreased lumbo-sacral interpediculate distances, posterior scalloping of the lumbar vertebrae, metaphyseal flaring, and moderate macrocephaly.

evidence.snippet: Trabecular bone mineral density (BMD) of long bones and vertebral bodies was decreased, but cortical BMD increased with age in both tibiae and femurs. These results demonstrate that bones in Fgfr3Asn534Lys/+ mice, due to FGFR3 activation, exhibit some characteristics of osteoporosis.

The second sentence carries the attribution to FGFR3 activation that this causal edge asserts, which the measurement alone does not. Note the deficit is compartment-specific rather than uniform hypomineralization: trabecular BMD falls while cortical BMD rises with age. Marked MODEL_ORGANISM: this arm has not been demonstrated in human hypochondroplasia bone.

edges/3.description: Beyond the growth plate, the same allele alters osteoblast and osteocyte function, producing the mineralization defect that gives the entry its bone-quality arm.

evidence.snippet: Fgfr3Asn534Lys/+ mice exhibited progressive dwarfism and impairment of the synchondroses of the cranial base, resulting in defective formation of the foramen magnum.

evidence.explanation: Demonstrates sustained downstream signalling in chondrocytes carrying the HCH allele, the cellular step between receptor activation and growth-plate failure.

edges/5.description: Sustained MAPK/ERK signalling suppresses chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation in the growth plate, which is what impairs endochondral bone formation and shortens the long bones.

evidence.snippet: We now report a single FGFR3 mutation found in 8 out of 14 unrelated patients with hypochondroplasia. This mutation causes a C to A transversion at nucleotide 1620, resulting in an Asn540Lys substitution in the proximal tyrosine kinase domain.
evidence.explanation: Landmark Nature Genetics paper identifying the recurrent FGFR3 N540K mutation as the cause of hypochondroplasia in the majority of genetically confirmed cases.

evidence.snippet: The N540K variant accounts for 60-70% of reported cases and is associated with severe manifestations.
evidence.explanation: Korean clinical series confirms the high frequency of the N540K variant among genetically confirmed HCH cases.

evidence.snippet: Overall, 85.5% of ACH cases and 57.2% of HCH cases were related to de novo genetic variants
evidence.explanation: French nationwide data confirms that the majority of HCH cases arise from de novo FGFR3 variants.

genes/0.notes: The c.1620C>A or c.1620C>G (p.Asn540Lys) mutation in the tyrosine kinase domain of FGFR3 is the most common causative variant, found in 50-70% of clinically diagnosed hypochondroplasia cases. This recurrent mutation was identified in 8 of 14 unrelated patients in the landmark 1995 study. Other FGFR3 mutations account for additional cases, but a significant proportion of clinically diagnosed patients have no identifiable FGFR3 mutation, suggesting genetic heterogeneity or phenotypic overlap with other conditions.

evidence.snippet: FGFR3 | HGNC:3690 | hypochondroplasia | MONDO:0007793 | AD | Definitive
evidence.explanation: ClinGen classifies the FGFR3-hypochondroplasia gene-disease relationship as definitive with autosomal dominant inheritance.

evidence.snippet: Vosoritide was well tolerated with no treatment-related serious adverse events. Injection site reactions occurred in 83.3% of participants. No participants discontinued therapy due to an adverse event. Annualized growth velocity increased by 2.26 standard deviations (SD) and height SDS increased by 0.36 SD during the treatment period versus the observation period.
evidence.explanation: Phase 2 trial in 24 children with HCH demonstrated that vosoritide significantly increased growth velocity with a favorable safety profile.

treatments/0.description: Vosoritide is a C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP) analog that counteracts FGFR3 overactivation by stimulating the NPR2/cGMP pathway, which antagonizes MAPK/ERK signaling in growth plate chondrocytes. A phase 2 trial demonstrated a 1.81 cm/year increase in annualized growth velocity with acceptable safety.

evidence.snippet: Among 16 growth-hormone-treated patients (two were growth-hormone deficient), the increase in height standard deviation scores was significant after a mean 5.4±0.7 years of treatment (+0.6 and+1.8 using growth references for healthy controls and achondroplasia children, respectively).
evidence.explanation: Korean cohort data shows statistically significant height gains with GH therapy in HCH, though the magnitude of improvement is modest.

treatments/1.description: Recombinant human growth hormone has been used with variable response. In one Korean cohort, 16 patients treated for a mean of 5.4 years showed a significant increase in height standard deviation scores.

evidence.snippet: Four patients underwent surgical limb lengthening at a mean age of 8.8±3.3 years.
evidence.explanation: Surgical limb lengthening was performed in 4 of 20 Korean HCH patients, typically in mid-childhood.

treatments/2.description: Surgical correction of leg bowing or other skeletal deformities may be considered if functionally significant. Surgical limb lengthening has been performed in some patients.

evidence.snippet: Ursachi et al. evaluated in vitro potency of infigratinib against N540K variant by expressing C-terminally V5-tagged FGFR3 in rat L6 cells (non-disease relevant cell) and concluded that FGFR3-N540K is weakly inhibited by infigratinib (IC50
evidence.explanation: States the opposing finding and the methodological objection to it, in the original authors' own words.

evidence.snippet: In these condition-relevant models, our findings markedly differ from those reported by Ursachi et al. The poor sensitivity of infigratinib to the N540K variant of FGFR3 observed in these other studies is likely due to the specific cell system and receptor construct employed.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the dispute is unresolved and turns on model choice.

evidence.snippet: Currently, infigratinib is being evaluated in a phase 2/3 clinical trial in children with HCH.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the question is expected to be settled clinically, which is why no mechanism claim should be curated ahead of it.

open_questions/0.rationale: This is a live, unresolved disagreement in the 2026 literature with direct consequences for a drug already in phase 2/3 trials in hypochondroplasia, so it must not be curated as settled in either direction. Ursachi et al. (J Bone Miner Res 2026) reported that infigratinib inhibits FGFR3-N540K only weakly (IC50 ~514 nM) relative to wild type and to the achondroplasia p.Gly380Arg allele, consistent with earlier oncology-derived evidence that N540K is a gatekeeper-adjacent resistance substitution. The original authors replied that the discrepancy is methodological — that the weak-inhibition result was obtained with C-terminally V5-tagged FGFR3 in rat L6 myoblasts, a non-cartilage system, whereas their own work used untagged full-length FGFR3 in ATDC5 chondrogenic cells and the Fgfr3-N534K mouse, and that C-terminal tagging is known to perturb FGFR3 signaling, particularly for N540K. Both positions are internally coherent, and the disagreement is about which in vitro system is the valid proxy for a chondrocyte, not about the data. Crucially, the achondroplasia result cannot be transferred: the phase 3 infigratinib evidence (PMID:42370681) is entirely in p.Gly380Arg achondroplasia, a different allele in a different position in the receptor. Until the hypochondroplasia trial reads out, dismech should not curate infigratinib as an effective hypochondroplasia treatment, and should not curate it as ineffective either. Note also that TYRA-300, an FGFR3-selective inhibitor, has separate preclinical activity in the same Fgfr3-N534K hypochondroplasia mouse model, so a negative result for infigratinib against N540K would not close the receptor-directed strategy.

evidence.snippet: In vivo, CT-CM-NPs effectively delivered the Hedgehog pathway agonist Purmorphamine to the growth plate cartilage in an HCH mouse model, resulting in upregulated Hedgehog signaling, restored impaired ciliogenesis, improved chondrocyte phenotypes, and ultimately increased bone and body length.
evidence.explanation: The mouse result whose human relevance is unestablished.

evidence.snippet: Pharmacological therapy remains the primary treatment but provides only partial symptomatic relief, as the avascular and alymphatic nature of growth plate cartilage severely limits drug delivery and accumulation.
evidence.explanation: States the delivery barrier that motivates the approach.

open_questions/1.rationale: Every systemic therapy for FGFR3 chondrodysplasia has to reach a tissue with no blood supply and no lymphatic drainage, which caps achievable growth-plate drug concentration and is a plausible contributor to the modest effect sizes seen with CNP analogues. A 2026 study addressed this with chondrocyte-membrane-coated nanoparticles bearing a collagen-II-binding peptide, using them to deliver the Hedgehog agonist purmorphamine to the growth plate of a hypochondroplasia mouse and reporting restored ciliogenesis and increased bone and body length. This is a mouse result with an engineered delivery vehicle and a Hedgehog-pathway payload that bypasses FGFR3 altogether, so its translational validity is the open question, not its internal validity: nanoparticle biodistribution, immunogenicity on repeat dosing, and growth-plate penetration all differ substantially between mouse and child, and no human data exist.

evidence.snippet: However, immunoblot analyses on protein extracts from fibroblasts of the two affected individuals sharing the p.Pro1115Arg variant showed reduced EPRS amounts.
evidence.explanation: Direct measurement of reduced EPRS1 protein in patient fibroblasts.

evidence.snippet: EPRS activity was reduced in one affected individual's lymphoblasts and in a purified recombinant protein model.
evidence.explanation: Reduced enzymatic activity, measured in patient cells and in recombinant protein, complements the reduced protein amount.

steps/1.description: Biallelic variants in EPRS1. The variants are not equivalent: they act through different proximate routes, which is why this node branches rather than asserting a single consequence. No blanket functional_impact_category is set here — PMID:33805425 explicitly leaves open whether R339X acts by loss of function or by toxic gain of function, so the category is recorded per variant on the nodes below.

evidence.snippet: Patient lymphoblastoid cell lines express markedly reduced EPRS1 protein due to dual defects in nuclear export and cytoplasmic translation of variant EPRS1 mRNA.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the export and translation defect in patient-derived cells.

evidence.snippet: The defect was rescued by antisense morpholinos predicted to expose m6A sites on target EPRS1 mRNA, or by m6A modification of the mRNA by METTL3-dCas13b, a targeted RNA methylation editor.
evidence.explanation: Rescue in both directions supports the causal role of m6A site accessibility, and identifies a therapeutic handle.

steps/2.description: The p.Pro1482Thr variant reduces METTL3-mediated m6A writing and reading by YTHDC1 and YTHDF1/3, producing dual defects in nuclear export and cytoplasmic translation of the EPRS1 transcript. This is a rescuable lesion: antisense morpholinos exposing the m6A sites, or targeted RNA methylation with METTL3-dCas13b, restored expression in patient cells.

evidence.snippet: Patient lymphoblastoid cell lines express markedly reduced EPRS1 protein due to dual defects in nuclear export and cytoplasmic translation of variant EPRS1 mRNA.
evidence.explanation: States both the reduction and its cause, in that order.

evidence.snippet: For nearly all EPRS1 and RARS1 variants, the relevant aminoacyl charging activity in patient fibroblasts is reduced by about 30–50% compared to healthy controls
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the functional deficit across the EPRS1 and RARS1 variant sets — roughly a 30-50% reduction in charging activity in patient fibroblasts, which is the magnitude this node asserts.

steps/3.description: Reduced amount and reduced specific activity of the EPRS1 enzyme, measured in patient fibroblasts, lymphoblasts and recombinant protein. This is the convergence point of the loss-of-protein routes; the aggregation branch reaches myelination without passing through it.

evidence.snippet: Whereas cells expressing the wild-type proteins exhibited phenotypes with myelin web-like structures bearing processes following the induction of differentiation, cells expressing the R339X mutant proteins did not.
evidence.explanation: Links the aggregation phenotype to failed morphological differentiation, the cellular step that precedes myelination.

steps/4.description: R339X mutant EPRS1 forms polymeric aggregates in Rab7-positive late endosomal vesicles and upregulates Rab7 regulatory signalling, blocking the morphological differentiation that oligodendroglial cells require to form myelin sheets.

evidence.snippet: We therefore hypothesized that leukodystrophies caused by mutations in genes encoding cytoplasmic aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases share a common underlying mechanism, such as reduced protein availability, abnormal assembly of the multisynthetase complex, and/or abnormal aminoacylation, all resulting in reduced translation capacity and insufficient myelin deposition in the developing brain.
evidence.explanation: Graded PARTIAL because the sentence is explicitly framed as a hypothesis the authors advance, not as a result they demonstrate.

steps/5.description: Lowered aminoacylation capacity is proposed to limit the high protein synthesis demand of active myelination. This node is the hypothesized convergence point of the aaRS leukodystrophies and has not been measured directly in HLD15 brain tissue.

evidence.snippet: In brain imaging, HLD15 appears as a hypomyelinating leukodystrophy with thin corpus callosum.
evidence.explanation: Describes the imaging signature. Graded OTHER because this is the review framing of the paper rather than its own experimental result.

steps/6.description: The defining tissue-level lesion: hypomyelination of central white matter with a thin corpus callosum on MRI.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report on four unrelated affected individuals with hypomyelination and bi-allelic pathogenic variants in EPRS, the gene encoding cytoplasmic glutamyl-prolyl-aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase.
evidence.explanation: Hypomyelination in all four originally reported individuals.

steps/7.description: Diffuse hypomyelination of cerebral white matter on MRI.

evidence.snippet: In brain imaging, HLD15 appears as a hypomyelinating leukodystrophy with thin corpus callosum.
evidence.explanation: States the thin corpus callosum as part of the HLD15 imaging signature.

steps/8.description: Thinning of the corpus callosum accompanying the hypomyelination.

evidence.snippet: Exome sequencing of two siblings with severe cognitive and motor impairment and progressive hypomyelination characteristic of HLD revealed homozygosity for a missense single-nucleotide variant (SNV) in EPRS1 (c.4444 C > A; p.Pro1482Thr), encoding glutamyl-prolyl-tRNA synthetase, consistent with HLD15.
evidence.explanation: Documents severe cognitive and motor impairment in the two reported siblings.

evidence.snippet: We describe a 40-year-old woman with mild intellectual disability, ataxia, dystonia, and MRI showing hypomyelination.
evidence.explanation: A counterpoint rather than a confirmation: this patient's cognitive impairment was mild and adult-presenting. Graded PARTIAL because it supports developmental impairment as a feature while contradicting "severe" as a universal descriptor.

steps/9.description: Severe cognitive and motor impairment with childhood onset.

edges/2.description: For p.Pro1482Thr, the variant masks m6A site accessibility — the proximate lesion is at the RNA level and is upstream of, not downstream of, the fall in protein.

edges/3.description: For R339X, residual mutant protein mislocalizes and aggregates — a separate branch from the loss-of-protein route, not a consequence of it.

edges/4.description: Defective export and translation of the transcript is why the protein is reduced — the causal direction PMID:38769304 reports.

edges/5.description: Less EPRS1 protein lowers aminoacylation capacity.

edges/6.description: Oligodendroglial cells that fail to differentiate cannot deposit myelin.

edges/7.description: Reduced translational output during the myelination window yields insufficient myelin deposition.

edges/8.description: Constrained translational capacity during brain development contributes to the global developmental impairment, beyond the myelin deficit alone.

edges/9.description: The tissue-level myelin deficit is what MRI reports as hypomyelination.

edges/10.description: Reduced myelinated commissural volume thins the corpus callosum.

evidence.snippet: EPRS is a bifunctional aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase that catalyzes the aminoacylation of glutamic acid and proline tRNA species.
evidence.explanation: Describes the gene product and its two catalytic activities.

evidence.snippet: Hypomyelinating leukodystrophy 15 (HLD15) results from biallelic pathogenic variants in EPRS1, but exonic deletions have not been reported.
evidence.explanation: Extends the mutational spectrum beyond point variants: the first reported EPRS1 exonic deletion, which matters diagnostically because a single detected candidate variant may hide a structural second allele.

evidence.snippet: RT-PCR from lymphoblastoid cells demonstrated exon-15 skipping leading to a frameshift (p.Asn582Serfs*10) and nonsense-mediated decay, leaving predominant expression of the paternally inherited missense allele.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates the deletion allele is degraded by nonsense-mediated decay, so the phenotype is driven by whatever residual function the surviving missense allele retains — a concrete instance of the reduced-EPRS1 mechanism above.

genes/0.notes: Biallelic EPRS1 variants cause HLD15. EPRS1 is bifunctional, carrying both glutamyl- and prolyl-tRNA synthetase domains, and is a subunit of the multi-tRNA synthetase complex.

evidence.snippet: To date, no therapeutic strategy has been established, and symptomatic treatment, such as anticonvulsant medications for patients with spasticity, is the typical response
evidence.explanation: States both the absence of disease-modifying therapy and the symptomatic measures used instead.

treatments/0.description: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Management is symptomatic — for example anticonvulsant medication for patients with spasticity — alongside serial imaging and supportive care.

evidence.snippet: We therefore hypothesized that leukodystrophies caused by mutations in genes encoding cytoplasmic aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases share a common underlying mechanism, such as reduced protein availability, abnormal assembly of the multisynthetase complex, and/or abnormal aminoacylation, all resulting in reduced translation capacity and insufficient myelin deposition in the developing brain.
evidence.explanation: The authors state this explicitly as a hypothesis, not a demonstrated result, which is why the status here is EMERGING.

evidence.snippet: The p.Pro1115Arg variation did not affect the assembly of the multisynthetase complex (MSC) as monitored by affinity purification-mass spectrometry.
evidence.explanation: A negative result against one of the three limbs this hypothesis proposes. For at least one variant, MSC assembly is intact, so "abnormal assembly of the multisynthetase complex" is not a general mechanism — which is why the hypothesis is curated as a three-part proposal rather than a settled pathway.

hypotheses/0.description: The unifying proposal that cytoplasmic aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase leukodystrophies, HLD15 among them, share a final common path of reduced translation capacity in the developing brain, whatever the proximate defect in the individual enzyme.

evidence.snippet: In contrast to current models, the variant does not alter the sequence of m6A target sites, but instead reduces their accessibility for modification.
evidence.explanation: States the distinguishing feature of this mechanism against the conventional sequence-altering model.

hypotheses/1.description: For the p.Pro1482Thr variant, reduced EPRS1 protein arises not from altered catalysis but from an RNA-level defect: the variant masks the accessibility of variant-distal m6A sites, impairing METTL3-mediated methylation and therefore nuclear export and translation of the EPRS1 mRNA.

evidence.snippet: Here, we show that the HLD15-associated nonsense mutation of Arg339-to-Ter (R339X) localizes EPRS1 proteins as polymeric aggregates into Rab7-positive vesicle structures in mouse oligodendroglial FBD-102b cells.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the aggregation phenotype in an oligodendroglial cell model.

hypotheses/2.description: For the R339X nonsense variant, residual mutant protein forms polymeric aggregates in Rab7-positive vesicles, dysregulates Rab7 signalling and blocks the morphological differentiation of oligodendroglial cells — a gain-of-toxic-function route rather than simple loss of charging activity.

evidence.snippet: ProRS-domain variants often show the typical HLD15 imaging pattern, whereas GluRS-domain variants may be associated with seizures, deafness, and less obvious hypomyelination, though the number of reported cases is limited.
evidence.explanation: Graded PARTIAL and OTHER: the authors hedge explicitly ("may be associated", "though the number of reported cases is limited") and are summarizing eight published patients rather than testing the association. It is a pattern worth recording, not an established genotype-phenotype rule.

hypotheses/3.description: EPRS1 is bifunctional, carrying separate glutamyl-tRNA synthetase (GluRS) and prolyl-tRNA synthetase (ProRS) domains. The published series suggests the two are not clinically equivalent: ProRS-domain variants track with the typical hypomyelinating imaging pattern, while GluRS-domain variants track with seizures, deafness and less obvious hypomyelination. This is an axis of variant non-interchangeability independent of the molecular routes above — those distinguish how a variant lowers EPRS1 function, this distinguishes which of the enzyme's two functions is lost.

open_questions/0.rationale: The R339X aggregation work describes mutant protein actively dysregulating Rab7 signalling and blocking oligodendroglial differentiation — a gain-of-toxic-function that a pure loss-of-capacity model does not predict. If that is right, variants may not be interchangeable, which matters directly for whether a translation-directed therapy would help every patient. Curated as three separate hypothesis groups rather than one so the distinction is not lost.

open_questions/1.rationale: PMID:38769304 rescued EPRS1 expression with morpholinos and with METTL3-dCas13b, but in lymphoblastoid cell lines — not in oligodendrocytes, and not in vivo. Myelination is a developmental window that may have closed by the time a patient is diagnosed, so a rescue of expression is not yet a rescue of disease. This is a model-fidelity question rather than an absence of evidence.

open_questions/2.rationale: No treatments are curated. Management reported in the sources is symptomatic. The m6A-directed rescue above is a cell-culture result, not a therapy, and curating it as a treatment would misrepresent its stage.

evidence.snippet: overexpression of wild-type POLR3A protein significantly enhanced Pol III transcription of 5S rRNA and tRNA Leu-CAA.
evidence.explanation: Establishes POLR3A as a determinant of Pol III transcription, the activity impaired by HLD7 variants.

evidence.snippet: Recessive mutations in the POLR3A gene cause POLR3-HLD (the second-most-common form of childhood-onset hypomyelinating leukodystrophy), a neurodegenerative disorder featuring deficient cerebral myelin formation.
evidence.explanation: Supports recessive POLR3A variants as the cause of POLR3-HLD with deficient myelin formation.

steps/1.description: Biallelic pathogenic variants in POLR3A (the largest, catalytic subunit of RNA polymerase III) impair Pol III, the enzyme that transcribes many small non-coding RNAs including tRNAs and 5S rRNA. This is the proximal molecular lesion of HLD7.

evidence.snippet: Pol III transcription function was frustrated (POLR3A, BC200, and tRNA Leu-CAA expression decreased), and MBP and 18S rRNA expressions were decreased.
evidence.explanation: Directly links the POLR3A p.Cys767Phe variant to reduced Pol III transcripts and decreased myelin basic protein expression.

evidence.snippet: Pol III transcription was also shown to be aberrant, with a significant decrease in 7SK RNA and several distinct tRNA genes
evidence.explanation: Supports reduced Pol III tRNA output as a shared mechanism across POLR3-related leukodystrophies.

steps/2.description: The mutant POLR3A protein fails to support normal Pol III activity, reducing Pol III transcript outputs (e.g., tRNA Leu-CAA, BC200) and downstream readouts of myelin biology, linking transcriptional dysfunction to reduced myelin basic protein expression.

evidence.snippet: a neurodegenerative disorder featuring deficient cerebral myelin formation.
evidence.explanation: Supports deficient cerebral myelin formation as the cellular/tissue-level consequence in POLR3-HLD.

evidence.snippet: An increasing number of studies have reported genetic mutations that cause protein misfolding, protein dysfunction, and/or mislocalization associated with HLD.
evidence.explanation: Supports protein dysfunction as the mechanistic theme underlying hypomyelinating leukodystrophies including POLR3-related disease.

steps/3.description: Reduced Pol III transcript supply is hypothesized to impair oligodendrocyte differentiation and the high translational demand of myelin protein synthesis, yielding deficient central nervous system myelination.

evidence.snippet: the combination of hypomyelination with relative T2 hypointensity of the ventrolateral thalamus, optic radiation, globus pallidus, and dentate nucleus, cerebellar atrophy, and thinning of the corpus callosum suggests the diagnosis.
evidence.explanation: Describes the diffuse hypomyelination pattern that defines the disease at the tissue/imaging level.

evidence.snippet: Her MRI was notable for diffuse hypomyelination with myelin preservation of early myelinating structures, characteristic of POLR3-related leukodystrophy.
evidence.explanation: Supports diffuse hypomyelination with preservation of early-myelinating structures as characteristic of POLR3-related leukodystrophy.

steps/4.description: Diffuse hypomyelination of central nervous system white matter, with relative preservation of early-myelinating structures, is the defining tissue-level output and produces the characteristic brain MRI pattern of POLR3-related leukodystrophy.

edges/1.description: Defective Pol III lowers production of its small non-coding RNA transcripts (tRNAs, 5S rRNA).

edges/2.description: Reduced Pol III transcript supply perturbs oligodendrocyte translation and myelin production.

edges/3.description: Oligodendrocyte and myelin dysfunction manifests as diffuse CNS hypomyelination.

evidence.snippet: The proband and her two living brothers (IV2 and IV4) were detected to carry a homozygous mutation of the POLR3A (NM_007055.4) gene c. 2300G > T (p.Cys767Phe), and her consanguineous married parents (III1 and III2) were p.Cys767Phe heterozygous carriers.
evidence.explanation: Documents a homozygous POLR3A variant segregating recessively in an HLD7 family with consanguineous parents.

evidence.snippet: splice variant POLR3A c.1770 + 5 G > C was proved to disrupt the normal splicing of intron 13 and led to a premature stop codon at position 618 (p.(P591Vfs*28)).
evidence.explanation: Functionally confirms a POLR3A splice variant identified by trio-based whole-exome sequencing.

evidence.snippet: Individualized care by a multidisciplinary team including a pediatric neurologist, clinical geneticist, physiotherapist, occupational therapist, speech and language pathologist, neuropsychologist, rehabilitation physician, dentist, endocrinologist, ophthalmologist, ear-nose-and-throat specialist, and primary care physician is recommended.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews specifies multidisciplinary supportive management.

evidence.snippet: Special caution needs to be taken when managing dysphagia in this disorder as it is known to vary widely, even in a single day.
evidence.explanation: Captures the GeneReviews dysphagia management caution.

treatments/0.description: Management is supportive and symptom-directed via a multidisciplinary team (neurology, genetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech-language pathology, neuropsychology, rehabilitation, dentistry, endocrinology, ophthalmology, ENT). Particular caution is needed managing dysphagia, which can vary widely even within a single day, and dystonia should be monitored and treated to prevent complications.

evidence.snippet: Carrier testing for at-risk relatives and prenatal diagnosis for pregnancies at increased risk are possible if both pathogenic variants in the family are known.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports carrier testing and prenatal diagnosis within genetic counseling.

treatments/1.description: Genetic counseling is appropriate given autosomal recessive inheritance; each sib of an affected individual has a 25% risk. Carrier testing for at-risk relatives and prenatal diagnosis are possible when both familial variants are known.

evidence.snippet: The deletion size ranges from approximately 7 to 20 Mb, with the proximal breakpoint within or telomeric to subband 11q23.3 and the deletion extending usually to the telomere.
evidence.explanation: Defines the location and size range of the causal 11q terminal deletion.

steps/0.description: A partial deletion of the long arm of chromosome 11, from a proximal breakpoint within or telomeric to 11q23.3 extending usually to the telomere; deletion size ranges from ~7 to 20 Mb. Most are de novo.

evidence.snippet: Jacobsen syndrome is a MCA/MR contiguous gene syndrome caused by partial deletion of the long arm of chromosome 11.
evidence.explanation: Establishes Jacobsen syndrome as a contiguous-gene (haploinsufficiency) syndrome.

steps/1.description: Reduced dosage of the contiguous distal 11q genes drives the multisystem phenotype. The congenital platelet disorder (Paris-Trousseau thrombocytopenia) is attributed to haploinsufficiency of FLI1 (11q24), a transcription factor required for megakaryopoiesis; other genes in the interval contribute to the cardiac, craniofacial, and neurodevelopmental features.

evidence.snippet: Abnormal platelet function, thrombocytopenia or pancytopenia are usually present at birth.
evidence.explanation: Documents the hallmark congenital platelet disorder of Jacobsen syndrome.

evidence.snippet: is highly penetrant in JS, affecting at least 88.5% of cases
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the near-complete penetrance of the Paris-Trousseau platelet abnormality, supporting the VERY_FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: In peripheral blood there are two different types of abnormal platelets: giant platelets and platelets with giant alpha granules.
evidence.explanation: Describes the characteristic Paris-Trousseau platelet morphology behind the persistent platelet dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: The most common clinical features include pre- and postnatal physical growth retardation, psychomotor retardation, and characteristic facial dysmorphism
evidence.explanation: Psychomotor retardation is among the most common features.

evidence.snippet: Mental development is normal or borderline in less than 3% of cases, mild to severe mental retardation is observed in 97% of cases.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the near-universal cognitive involvement, supporting the VERY_FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: The degree of neurocognitive deficiency is strongly associated with the size of the deletion
evidence.explanation: Supports the deletion-size genotype-phenotype correlation noted here.

evidence.snippet: Patients commonly have malformations of the heart, kidney, gastrointestinal tract, genitalia, central nervous system and skeleton.
evidence.explanation: Cardiac malformations are among the common malformations.

evidence.snippet: Congenital heart malformations occur in 56% of cases.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the cardiac-malformation rate, supporting the FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: Cardiac malformations were reported in 95% of deceased children
evidence.explanation: Supports congenital heart disease as the leading driver of early mortality.

evidence.snippet: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a rare and severe condition that occurs in about 1/5000 infants, is observed in 5% of JS children.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the marked enrichment of hypoplastic left heart syndrome in Jacobsen syndrome.

edges/0.description: The deletion removes one copy of the contiguous distal 11q genes.

evidence.snippet: The deletion is de novo in 85% of reported cases, and in 15% of cases it results from an unbalanced segregation of a familial balanced translocation or from other chromosome rearrangements.
evidence.explanation: Gives the de novo vs familial-translocation origins of the deletion.

genes/0.notes: Partial deletion of distal 11q (copy-number loss), ~7-20 Mb, from a breakpoint at or telomeric to 11q23.3 to the telomere. De novo in ~85% of cases; ~15% arise from unbalanced segregation of a familial balanced translocation or other rearrangement, and a minority from breakage at the FRA11B fragile site. No coordinate slot exists in the schema; the deletion is recorded here in prose.

evidence.snippet: There is in vivo and in vitro evidence that FLI1 plays a fundamental role in megakaryocytes differentiation and that heterozygous loss of the FLI-1 gene is associated with dysmegakaryocytopoiesis and the Paris-Tousseau trombocytopenia in JS
evidence.explanation: Directly attributes the Paris-Trousseau platelet phenotype to heterozygous FLI1 loss within the deletion (source spelling preserved).

genes/1.notes: FLI1 (11q24) encodes an ETS transcription factor essential for megakaryopoiesis; its haploinsufficiency within the deletion is the recognized cause of the Paris-Trousseau thrombocytopenia and abnormal platelet function — a component phenotype of the contiguous-gene deletion, not the whole syndrome. In vitro over-expression of FLI1 in haploinsufficient patient CD34+ cells restores normal megakaryopoiesis, though the source notes other distal 11q genes may also contribute.

evidence.snippet: Management is multi-disciplinary and requires evaluation by general pediatrician, pediatric cardiologist, neurologist, ophthalmologist.
evidence.explanation: Establishes multidisciplinary supportive care as the management approach.

treatments/0.description: No curative therapy exists. Management is multidisciplinary — cardiac care (heart surgery may be needed in the neonatal period), hematologic monitoring and bleeding precautions for the platelet disorder, feeding support, and ophthalmologic, auditory, endocrine, and immunologic follow-up.

evidence.snippet: Thrombocytopenia and other hematological problems must be taken into account preoperatively. Prophylactic transfusion with platelets can be lifesaving.
evidence.explanation: Supports perioperative prophylactic platelet transfusion for the bleeding diathesis.

treatments/1.description: Because of thrombocytopenia and persistent platelet dysfunction, bleeding risk is highest in infancy and around procedures; prophylactic platelet or whole-blood transfusion is used before, during, or after surgery.

evidence.snippet: There is a high recurrence risk when a parent has a balanced translocation, or deletion 11q in the mosaic form.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the family configurations with high recurrence risk.

evidence.snippet: Prenatal diagnosis of 11q deletion is possible by amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling and cytogenetic analysis.
evidence.explanation: Documents the available prenatal diagnostic route.

treatments/2.description: Recurrence risk after a de novo deletion is generally considered negligible, but recurrence has been documented, is 50% when a parent is affected, and is high with a parental balanced translocation or 11q mosaicism; prenatal cytogenetic diagnosis by amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling is possible.

evidence.snippet: which weakens the splice acceptor of GAA exon 2 and induces partial and complete exon 2 skipping. It also allows a low level of leaky wild-type splicing, leading to a childhood/adult phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the leaky-splicing mechanism by which c.-32-13T>G yields residual enzyme and a late-onset phenotype.

evidence.snippet: The presence of at least one splice site variant (c.546 G > C/p.T182 = , c.1076-22 T > G, c.2646 + 2 T > A, and the classic c.-32-13T > G variant) was associated with LOPD, while the presence of non-splice site variants on both alleles was associated with IOPD.
evidence.explanation: Human genotype-phenotype data tying retention of a leaky splice allele to the late-onset phenotype.

steps/1.description: The LOPD-defining lesion is partial rather than complete loss of acid alpha-glucosidase. The commonest LOPD allele, c.-32-13T>G (IVS1), sits in intron 1 and weakens the splice acceptor of GAA exon 2. Most transcripts from that allele are aberrantly spliced (partial or complete exon 2 skipping), but a low level of correctly spliced, fully functional transcript escapes. That residual activity - conventionally quoted as roughly 1-30% of normal, though see the caveat in the biochemical section and in notes - is what shifts the phenotype from infantile to late onset. In the great majority of LOPD patients the leaky allele is carried in trans with a second, more deleterious pathogenic variant, so the leaky allele is the one setting how much enzyme the patient makes.

evidence.snippet: Late-onset Pompe disease (LOPD) is a rare autosomal recessive glycogen storage disease that results in accumulation of glycogen in muscle cells causing muscular weakness.
evidence.explanation: Anchors muscle-cell glycogen accumulation as the storage lesion that produces LOPD weakness.

steps/2.description: Partial GAA activity permits slow lysosomal glycogen accumulation that is concentrated in skeletal muscle, including the respiratory muscles, rather than the generalized multisystem storage of infantile disease. The tissue selectivity reflects the very high glycogen flux of muscle relative to its residual degradative capacity, so muscle is the first compartment in which the reduced enzyme reserve is exhausted.

evidence.snippet: Confocal microscopy of live single muscle fibers exposed to fluorescently labeled rhGAA indicates that a significant portion of the endocytosed enzyme in the KO was trapped as a partially processed form in the autophagic areas instead of reaching its target--the lysosomes.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates autophagic mistargeting of therapeutic enzyme in skeletal muscle fibers.

evidence.snippet: The therapy, which relies on receptor-mediated endocytosis of recombinant human GAA (rhGAA), appears to be effective in cardiac muscle, but less so in skeletal muscle.
evidence.explanation: States the cardiac-versus-skeletal-muscle discrepancy in ERT response that this node explains.

evidence.snippet: numerous lysosomes and autolysosomes loaded with lipofuscin appear to be a hallmark of LOPD skeletal muscle
evidence.explanation: Human LOPD muscle biopsies confirm an autophagic-lysosomal lesion in the late-onset form itself, not only in the knockout mouse.

evidence.snippet: As in mouse models, autophagic buildup, filled with potentially toxic ubiquitinated protein aggregates, glycogen particles, autophagy substrate p62/SQSTM1, and lipofuscin (an indicator of oxidative damage and mitochondrial dysfunction), is a prominent feature in muscle from patients with the disease; in some fibers, particularly from biopsies of adult patients, the enlarged lysosomes in the surrounding buildup-free areas look like innocent bystanders compared to the autophagic pathology
evidence.explanation: States that the autophagic buildup, not the enlarged lysosome, is the dominant lesion in patient muscle, and specifically in biopsies from adult patients - which is the late-onset population this entry covers. It also names the p62/SQSTM1 and lipofuscin content of the buildup.

evidence.snippet: However, a major mechanism underlying autophagic buildup is an impairment of autophagosomal–lysosomal fusion, a condition known as autophagic block.
evidence.explanation: Supplies the mechanism by which the buildup forms and therefore why endocytosed enzyme delivered into that compartment does not reach a functional lysosome.

evidence.snippet: All of the generated GAA-KO cells lacked GAA activity and presented an increased autophagy and increased glycogen content by means of myotube differentiation as well as the downregulation of mannose 6-phosphate receptors (CI-MPRs)
evidence.explanation: Isogenic GAA-null myotubes reproduce both the increased autophagy of this node and downregulation of the CI-MPR receptor that recombinant enzyme depends on for uptake, a second route by which delivered enzyme fails to reach the lysosome.

steps/3.description: Skeletal myofibers in Pompe disease develop large autophagic areas alongside glycogen-filled lysosomes. These areas trap endocytosed recombinant human GAA in a partially processed form so that it never reaches the lysosome, which is a mechanistic explanation for why enzyme replacement therapy is far more effective in cardiac than in skeletal muscle and why it slows rather than arrests the LOPD myopathy. Because LOPD is a decades-long disease treated for decades, this therapeutic ceiling is a defining clinical problem of the late-onset form.

evidence.snippet: The expression of the genes involved in glycolysis was reduced, whereas the expression of the genes involved in the metabolism of lipids and amino acids was increased in non-vacuolated fibres, indicating early metabolic abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates metabolic reprogramming in histologically unaffected LOPD myofibers, before vacuolation.

evidence.snippet: Upregulation of genes associated with inflammation, apoptosis and muscle regeneration was observed only in vacuolated fibres.
evidence.explanation: Separates the later inflammatory/degenerative programme from the earlier metabolic one, which is the staging claim of this node.

evidence.snippet: Notably, enzyme replacement therapy (the only available therapy for the disease) showed a tendency to restore dysregulated metabolism, particularly within slow fibres.
evidence.explanation: Bounds the reversibility claim - the authors report a tendency, not a demonstrated restoration, which is why this node is PROVISIONAL.

evidence.snippet: Defects in oxidative metabolism, muscle contractile protein regulation, cytoskeletal rearrangement, and membrane reorganization persisted.
evidence.explanation: Independent corroboration by a different modality - muscle proteomics rather than single-nucleus transcriptomics - that the oxidative-metabolism defect of this node is real and survives a year of enzyme replacement therapy.

evidence.snippet: Metabolic changes, ER stress and UPR (unfolded protein response) contribute to muscle proteostasis dysregulation with active membrane remodeling (high levels of LC3BII/LC3BI) and accumulation of p62, suggesting imbalance in the autophagic process.
evidence.explanation: Supplies the p62 and LC3 protein-level readout of the autophagic imbalance that the transcriptomic study infers from autophagy gene upregulation.

steps/4.description: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing combined with spatial transcriptomics of LOPD muscle biopsies shows that myofibers are transcriptionally abnormal before they are histologically abnormal. Fibers that are not yet vacuolated already show reduced glycolytic gene expression with increased lipid and amino-acid metabolism, upregulated autophagy genes, and downregulated ribosomal and mitochondrial programmes producing defective oxidative phosphorylation. Inflammation, apoptosis, and regeneration signatures appear only once vacuolation is established. This staging matters for LOPD specifically, because it identifies an early, possibly still-tractable metabolic derangement that precedes the structural damage enzyme replacement therapy cannot undo. The study reports only a "tendency" for therapy to restore the dysregulated metabolism, so reversibility is a hypothesis this node raises rather than a result it records.

evidence.snippet: Transmission electron microscopy disclosed lysosomal glycogen accumulation within skeletal, cardiac, and vascular smooth muscle cells
evidence.explanation: Direct human ultrastructural demonstration that lysosomal glycogen accumulates in vascular smooth muscle cells in late-onset Pompe disease, which is what makes this a curated node rather than a proposed one.

evidence.snippet: Organs containing smooth muscle cells (the bladder, intestine, and esophagus) were also affected
evidence.explanation: Extends the same storage lesion from vascular to visceral smooth muscle, supporting the visceral half of this node.

evidence.snippet: Increased levels of glycogen were present in smooth muscle cells of the aorta, trachea, esophagus, stomach, and bladder of Gaa-/- mice, compared to wild type mice.
evidence.explanation: Independent quantitative confirmation in a GAA-deficient mouse that the storage lesion is present across vascular, airway, gastrointestinal and genitourinary smooth muscle.

steps/5.description: Residual GAA activity is exhausted in smooth muscle as well as in skeletal muscle. Autopsy of a woman with LOPD demonstrated lysosomal glycogen inside vascular smooth muscle cells by transmission electron microscopy, alongside involvement of the bladder, intestine, and esophagus. This is a distinct cellular compartment from the skeletal and respiratory myofiber storage that dominates the LOPD clinical picture, and it is the substrate for the disease's two extra-muscular arms: the dilative arteriopathy of large arteries, and the gastrointestinal and genitourinary symptoms that patients report independently of limb weakness. Smooth-muscle storage is the reason LOPD is a systemic lysosomal disease rather than a pure myopathy.

evidence.snippet: A significant increase in the MR-derived fat fraction of the psoas muscle was found between baseline and follow-up 1 (P = 0.016), as was a significant decrease in the performance on the 6-minute walk test (P = 0.006) and 4-step stair climb test (P = 0.034)
evidence.explanation: Shows progressive fatty replacement of proximal/axial muscle with concurrent functional decline during ERT.

steps/6.description: Chronic storage and autophagic injury destroy myofibers, which are replaced by fat. The distribution is characteristically limb-girdle and axial, with early involvement of the psoas and paraspinal muscles; quantitative fat fraction on lumbar MRI correlates with strength, walking distance, stair climbing and supine spirometry, and continues to rise during enzyme replacement therapy.

evidence.snippet: Diaphragm needle EMG revealed both myopathic and neurogenic changes in 3 (60%) and myopathic potentials in 1 patient.
evidence.explanation: Provides the electrophysiological observation of combined neurogenic and myopathic diaphragm involvement.

evidence.snippet: Our study provide new insights regarding respiratory mechanisms in LOPD, suggesting a contribution of spinal phrenic motor neuron dysfunction for diaphragm weakness.
evidence.explanation: The authors themselves frame the phrenic motor neuron contribution as a suggestion requiring confirmation, which is why this node is PROVISIONAL.

evidence.snippet: limited penetration across the blood-brain barrier (BBB), resulting in persistent central nervous system involvement, and immune responses against the infused enzyme
evidence.explanation: Supports the pharmacological half of this node's argument - intravenous recombinant enzyme does not reach the central nervous system, so a phrenic motor neuron contribution would not be corrected by enzyme replacement therapy.

steps/7.description: Diaphragm weakness in LOPD is disproportionate to limb weakness and is the proximate cause of nocturnal hypoventilation and ultimately of ventilatory failure. Neurophysiological study of treated LOPD patients found that those with respiratory failure had absent or severely reduced phrenic nerve compound muscle action potentials and diaphragm EMG showing neurogenic as well as myopathic changes, implicating spinal phrenic motor neuron dysfunction alongside myofiber disease. Because intravenous recombinant enzyme does not cross the blood-brain barrier, a motor neuron contribution would explain residual respiratory decline on enzyme replacement therapy. The motor neuron arm is curated as PROVISIONAL: the supporting series is small (eight patients) and calls for confirmation.

evidence.snippet: We report evidence of dilated arteriopathy involving primarily the ascending thoracic aorta in 5 females with late-onset Pompe disease.
evidence.explanation: The case series that established thoracic aortic dilatation as an LOPD complication rather than an incidental finding.

evidence.snippet: Intracranial vasculopathy involving both large arteries and small vessels is an important organ damage in LOPD patients.
evidence.explanation: A 30-patient imaging cohort establishing intracranial arteriopathy as a systematic organ manifestation of LOPD.

evidence.snippet: the histological work-up of resected aortic tissue revealed changes mimicking those observed in patients with classic connective tissue diseases
evidence.explanation: Supports the arteriopathy while complicating the mechanism - the resected wall looked like a connective-tissue disease rather than a storage lesion, which is part of why this node is PROVISIONAL.

evidence.snippet: Microbleeds, predominantly located in the cerebellum and brainstem, were detected in 7 patients (7/22) via susceptibility-weighted imaging.
evidence.explanation: Supports the small-vessel half of this node. Recorded here rather than as a phenotype because HPO has no cerebral microbleed term.

steps/8.description: Progressive dilatation, ectasia and aneurysm formation affecting the ascending thoracic aorta and the intracranial arteries, with the vertebrobasilar system most often involved, together with a small-vessel component that shows up as white matter hyperintensity and cerebellar and brainstem microbleeds. It is the second organ system LOPD damages after muscle, and it is largely uncoupled from myopathy severity: patients are identified on surveillance imaging rather than by limb weakness, and enzyme replacement therapy did not change vessel calibre over a year of follow-up in the one series that looked. The node is recorded as PROVISIONAL rather than ESTABLISHED because the causal step from smooth-muscle glycogen to wall weakness is inferred rather than demonstrated - one aortic specimen showed connective-tissue changes resembling a fibrillinopathy rather than a storage lesion, and the Gaa-/- mouse accumulates little aortic glycogen, which led that study's authors to decline to attribute aortic wall weakness to glycogen accumulation (see animal_models).

evidence.snippet: late-onset Pompe disease (LOPD) (i.e., individuals with onset before age 12 months without cardiomyopathy, and all individuals with onset after age 12 months)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews makes absence of cardiomyopathy definitional for LOPD.

steps/9.description: Absence of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a defining feature of LOPD and part of its formal case definition, not merely a statistical tendency. Residual GAA activity is sufficient to keep cardiomyocyte glycogen storage subclinical, so the cardiorespiratory collapse that kills untreated infants does not occur; the respiratory system, not the heart, becomes the life-limiting organ. This node is curated as a mechanistic contrast rather than as a claim that the myocardium is entirely normal - adult arteriopathy and rare conduction findings are described in the umbrella Pompe disease entry.

evidence.snippet: Late-onset Pompe disease (LOPD) patients may still need ventilation support at some point of their disease course, despite regular recombinant human alglucosidase alfa treatment.
evidence.explanation: Documents residual progression to ventilatory support despite ongoing enzyme replacement therapy.

evidence.snippet: Whilst disease-modifying enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) delays progression of locomotor dysfunction and prolongs life, its effect on respiratory function and SDB remains unclear.
evidence.explanation: States that the respiratory benefit of ERT in LOPD is not established, bounding the claim of therapeutic benefit.

evidence.snippet: 178 proteins were changed in abundance in LOPD patients, 47 of them recovered normal level after ERT. Defects in oxidative metabolism, muscle contractile protein regulation, cytoskeletal rearrangement, and membrane reorganization persisted.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the molecular residue of disease in LOPD muscle after a year of enzyme replacement therapy - roughly a quarter of the altered proteome normalizes.

steps/10.description: Enzyme replacement therapy changes the trajectory of LOPD but does not normalize it. Walking distance and forced vital capacity improve modestly relative to placebo in the short term, yet muscle fat fraction continues to increase, some patients still progress to ventilatory support, and the effect on sleep-disordered breathing is undocumented. This residual disease burden is a mechanistic consequence of the autophagic mistargeting node and, possibly, of the motor neuron arm of diaphragm weakness, which intravenous enzyme cannot reach.

evidence.snippet: LOPD can manifest from the first decade to as late as the seventh decade of life with progressive proximal muscle weakness primarily affecting the lower limbs, which may require use of a wheelchair.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews identifies progressive lower-limb-predominant proximal weakness as the defining LOPD motor phenotype.

evidence.snippet: It causes a progressive proximal myopathy, accompanied by respiratory muscle weakness, which can lead to ventilatory failure.
evidence.explanation: Confirms progressive proximal myopathy as the core LOPD phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Most patients will present with a lower limb girdle and truncal muscle weakness pattern
evidence.explanation: Frequency evidence - "most patients" maps to the VERY_FREQUENT band (80-100%).

steps/11.description: Slowly progressive limb-girdle weakness with lower-limb predominance is the cardinal motor manifestation of LOPD, and may progress to wheelchair use.

evidence.snippet: It causes a progressive proximal myopathy, accompanied by respiratory muscle weakness, which can lead to ventilatory failure. In untreated LOPD, the most common cause of death is respiratory failure.
evidence.explanation: Establishes respiratory muscle weakness progressing to ventilatory failure as the dominant cause of death in untreated LOPD.

evidence.snippet: Respiratory insufficiency progressing to respiratory failure is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews confirms respiratory insufficiency as a major source of LOPD morbidity and mortality.

evidence.snippet: Approximately half will suffer respiratory involvement during the course of their illness
evidence.explanation: Frequency evidence - "approximately half" falls in the FREQUENT band (30-79%).

evidence.snippet: One-third of patients present with respiratory symptoms as their first manifestation of the illness
evidence.explanation: Supports the description's claim that respiratory symptoms are the presenting complaint in about a third of patients.

steps/12.description: Respiratory muscle weakness, principally of the diaphragm, progresses to ventilatory failure and is the leading cause of death in untreated LOPD. In roughly a third of patients respiratory symptoms are the presenting complaint, ahead of limb weakness.

evidence.snippet: Diaphragm weakness leads to nocturnal hypoventilation, which can result in sleep disruption.
evidence.explanation: Directly links diaphragm weakness to nocturnal hypoventilation in LOPD.

evidence.snippet: Patients suffering from respiratory compromise may present with symptoms of sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) before overt signs of respiratory failure.
evidence.explanation: Supports sleep-disordered breathing as an early, pre-failure respiratory manifestation.

steps/13.description: Diaphragm weakness is expressed earliest during sleep, so sleep-disordered breathing and nocturnal hypoventilation typically precede overt daytime respiratory failure and are accompanied by sleep disruption, excessive daytime sleepiness, and reduced health-related quality of life.

evidence.snippet: Some adults have developed arteriopathy, including dilatation of the ascending thoracic aorta.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews names ascending thoracic aortic dilatation as an adult (late-onset) manifestation of Pompe disease.

evidence.snippet: echocardiography (to include assessment for aortic dilatation in those with LOPD)
evidence.explanation: The surveillance recommendation is LOPD-specific, which is why this phenotype is curated on the late-onset entry rather than left to the umbrella entry.

steps/14.description: A minority of adults with LOPD develop an arteriopathy whose best-characterized expression is dilatation of the ascending thoracic aorta. It is distinct from the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy of infantile-onset disease - the LOPD myocardium is typically spared - and it is specific enough to LOPD that GeneReviews adds aortic assessment to the annual echocardiogram for this group. Its mechanism is now curated on this entry: it is the aortic expression of the dilative arteriopathy node, downstream of lysosomal glycogen storage in vascular smooth muscle. That causal step is recorded as PROVISIONAL rather than established - see the arteriopathy node and the Gaa-/- mouse link for the evidence that qualifies it.

evidence.snippet: Dilative arteriopathy was found in 19 patients (19/30), with vertebrobasilar dolichoectasia found in 17 patients and dilatation of the anterior circulation arteries found in 8 patients.
evidence.explanation: 17 of 30 imaged LOPD adults, which is 57 percent and maps to the FREQUENT band (30-79 percent).

evidence.snippet: The maximum diameter of the basilar artery was correlated with disease duration
evidence.explanation: Supports the PROGRESSIVE clinical course annotation on this phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Four out of six patients had brain vascular anomalies including dolichoectasia of the basilar artery and ectasia of internal carotids.
evidence.explanation: Independent replication in a separate European cohort, which is why this is curated as a recurrent phenotype rather than a single-cohort observation.

steps/15.description: Elongation and dilatation of the vertebrobasilar arteries is the single most common vascular abnormality in LOPD and is usually asymptomatic until it is looked for. Basilar artery diameter correlates with disease duration, so it behaves as a progressive manifestation rather than a static malformation.

evidence.snippet: In addition, aneurysms (7/30) and fenestrations (3/30) were discovered.
evidence.explanation: Documents intracranial aneurysm formation as part of the LOPD arteriopathy.

evidence.snippet: Another patient with juvenile onset disease had both thoracic and basilar artery aneurysms.
evidence.explanation: Shows the aortic and intracranial arms of the arteriopathy occurring in the same patient, supporting them as one systemic vascular process.

evidence.snippet: At 1 year follow-up, enzyme replacement therapy did not modify the size of cerebral vessels
evidence.explanation: Supports the statement that this manifestation did not respond to enzyme replacement therapy over the observed interval.

steps/16.description: Beyond the vertebrobasilar system, LOPD arteriopathy affects the anterior circulation, produces saccular and fusiform aneurysms, and coexists with arterial stenosis in a third of patients. Enzyme replacement therapy did not reduce vessel calibre over a year of follow-up, so this arm of the disease is not currently treatment-responsive.

evidence.snippet: Seven patients (7/30) had acute cerebral infarction or hemorrhage.
evidence.explanation: 7 of 30 imaged LOPD adults, which is 23 percent and maps to the OCCASIONAL band (5-29 percent).

evidence.snippet: Two patients had clinical signs related to the arteriopathy, including partial paralysis of the third cranial nerve and transient ischemic attacks.
evidence.explanation: Independent documentation of symptomatic cerebrovascular events attributable to the arteriopathy.

steps/17.description: Acute cerebral infarction or intracranial hemorrhage occurs in a minority of LOPD adults and may be the presenting event. It is the clinically consequential endpoint of the intracranial arteriopathy and the reason vascular imaging is proposed as routine workup in this group.

evidence.snippet: White matter hyperintensities were present in 13 patients (13/28).
evidence.explanation: 13 of 28 imaged patients, which is 46 percent and maps to the FREQUENT band (30-79 percent).

steps/18.description: T2/FLAIR white matter hyperintensity accompanies the large-artery disease in roughly half of imaged LOPD adults, with cerebellar and brainstem microbleeds in a smaller subset. Together these constitute the small-vessel arm of LOPD cerebrovascular involvement.

evidence.snippet: These patients also complained of gastrointestinal symptoms (chronic constipation and gastrointestinal reflux).
evidence.explanation: Documents reflux as a reported symptom in this LOPD cohort.

evidence.snippet: patients reported a marked improvement of intestinal symptoms
evidence.explanation: Supports the statement that the gastrointestinal symptoms, unlike the vascular findings, improved on enzyme replacement therapy.

steps/19.description: Reflux is reported by LOPD patients alongside constipation and is attributed to glycogen storage in gastrointestinal smooth muscle rather than to the limb myopathy. It improved markedly on enzyme replacement therapy in the one series that followed it, which distinguishes it from the vascular arm of smooth-muscle disease.

evidence.snippet: These patients also complained of gastrointestinal symptoms (chronic constipation and gastrointestinal reflux).
evidence.explanation: Documents chronic constipation as a reported symptom, supporting both the phenotype and its CHRONIC temporality annotation.

steps/20.description: Chronic constipation is reported by LOPD patients and is attributed to the same intestinal smooth-muscle storage lesion as reflux.

evidence.snippet: explaining reports of symptoms such as urinary incontinence and dysphagia
evidence.explanation: The autopsy study links bladder smooth-muscle involvement to reported urinary incontinence in LOPD.

steps/21.description: Urinary incontinence in LOPD is attributed to lysosomal glycogen storage in bladder smooth muscle demonstrated at autopsy, rather than to pelvic floor weakness secondary to the limb-girdle myopathy.

evidence.snippet: It also allows a low level of leaky wild-type splicing, leading to a childhood/adult phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Links the residual enzyme produced by leaky splicing to the attenuated childhood/adult disease course.

edges/1.description: Residual GAA activity slows, but does not prevent, lysosomal glycogen accumulation, producing a decades-long rather than months-long storage course.

evidence.snippet: Late-onset Pompe disease (LOPD), caused by reduced rather than absent GAA, presents with a milder form, any time from 1 year to adulthood.
evidence.explanation: Attributes the milder late-onset phenotype specifically to reduced rather than absent enzyme.

edges/2.description: Residual enzyme activity is sufficient to keep cardiomyocyte glycogen turnover below the threshold that produces infantile hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The quantitative threshold itself has not been measured in human myocardium, so the link is recorded with unknown intermediates.

evidence.snippet: Evidence of increased aortic stiffness in some patients and smooth muscle involvement in LOPD raises the possibility of aortic involvement.
evidence.explanation: States that smooth muscle is involved in LOPD, which is the step from the enzyme deficit to the smooth-muscle storage node.

edges/3.description: The same partial enzyme deficit is exhausted in smooth muscle as well as in skeletal muscle, opening the extra-muscular arm of the disease.

evidence.snippet: Our findings here demonstrate a progressive age-dependent autophagic buildup in addition to enlargement of glycogen-filled lysosomes in multiple muscle groups in the KO.
evidence.explanation: Shows autophagic buildup accompanying glycogen-filled lysosomes in multiple muscle groups.

edges/4.description: Glycogen-engorged lysosomes disturb autophagic flux in myofibers.

evidence.snippet: Additionally, we detected upregulation of autophagy genes and downregulation of the genes involved in ribosomal and mitochondrial function leading to defective oxidative phosphorylation.

edges/6.description: Cumulative storage and autophagic damage destroy contractile architecture in proximal lower-limb and paraspinal muscle.

evidence.snippet: We observed an increase in the proportion of slow and regenerative muscle fibres and macrophages in LOPD muscles.

evidence.snippet: Measurements derived from the quantitative method correlated well with Medical Research Council scores of muscle strength, with moderate correlations found for the 6-minute walk test, the 4-step stair climb test, and spirometry in the supine position.

edges/10.description: Loss of contractile tissue in limb-girdle and axial muscle produces the characteristic LOPD weakness pattern.

edges/11.description: Inspiratory muscle failure is expressed first during sleep, when accessory muscle recruitment falls and ventilation depends on the diaphragm.

evidence.snippet: In untreated LOPD, the most common cause of death is respiratory failure.

edges/12.description: Progressive diaphragm failure produces daytime hypercapnic respiratory failure, the leading cause of death in untreated LOPD.

evidence.snippet: Vascular abnormalities, such as aneurysms and arterial dolichoectasia, likely caused by glycogen accumulation in arterial walls, have been reported in non-classic Pompe patients.

edges/13.description: Glycogen-laden smooth muscle cells in the tunica media are the proposed structural cause of progressive arterial wall remodeling and dilatation.

The same sentence shows the vessels did not respond, which is why the arteriopathy arm is not curated with this argument.

edges/20.description: Dilative and stenotic arteriopathy predisposes to both infarction and hemorrhage, but the proportion of LOPD strokes attributable to the arteriopathy rather than to conventional risk factors has not been established.

edges/21.description: Small-vessel involvement accompanies the large-artery disease; white matter change is its parenchymal correlate.

evidence.snippet: To extend the findings of prior studies, we found that multiple types of splice site variants beyond the classic c.-32-13T > G variant are often associated with a milder phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Shows the late-onset phenotype tracks with splice-site (leaky) alleles generally, not only c.-32-13T>G.

evidence.snippet: Of the definite LOPD participants, 8 (89%) were Caucasian and were heterozygous for the common leaky (IVS1) splice site mutation in the GAA gene (c -32-13T>G), with a second mutation that was previously confirmed to be pathogenic.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the dominance of the leaky IVS1 allele among LOPD patients in a North American neuromuscular cohort.

evidence.snippet: Our study concluded that Italian patients exhibited a characteristic genetic profile similar to that of the broader European population, with the c.-32-13T>G variant being the most prevalent.
evidence.explanation: A second, independent European cohort confirms c.-32-13T>G as the most prevalent allele, so the leaky-allele finding is not specific to the North American series.

evidence.snippet: In the whole cohort of patients analyzed with reduced or borderline activity, genetic testing was done, and we found 39 patients with two causative mutations in GAA gene connected to PD, and 22 subjects with GVUS variants.
evidence.explanation: Bounds the genotype-first framing - in a screened cohort, a substantial minority carried variants of uncertain significance rather than a resolvable genotype, which is the practical limit on classifying a patient by GAA sequence.

genes/0.notes: The LOPD genotype is defined by retention of at least one allele that still produces some functional enzyme. c.-32-13T>G is by far the commonest such allele in populations of European ancestry, but it is not the only one: several other splice-site variants are similarly associated with the late-onset phenotype, whereas two non-splice-site (typically null) alleles produce infantile disease.

evidence.snippet: At 78 weeks, the estimated mean changes from baseline in the primary end points favored alglucosidase alfa (an increase of 28.1+/-13.1 m on the 6-minute walk test and an absolute increase of 3.4+/-1.2 percentage points in FVC; P=0.03 and P=0.006, respectively).

Benefit in LOPD is real but partial, and is limited by autophagic mistargeting of enzyme in skeletal muscle.

evidence.snippet: At 78 weeks, the estimated mean changes from baseline in the primary end points favored alglucosidase alfa (an increase of 28.1+/-13.1 m on the 6-minute walk test and an absolute increase of 3.4+/-1.2 percentage points in FVC; P=0.03 and P=0.006, respectively).

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Recombinant enzyme supplies the deficient lysosomal hydrolase and reduces the stored glycogen burden in muscle.

evidence.snippet: The mainstay of treatment for SDB and respiratory failure in LOPD is non-invasive ventilation (NIV), which aims to ensure adequate ventilation, particularly during sleep, and prevent acute hypercapnic failure.
evidence.explanation: Establishes non-invasive ventilation as standard management of respiratory failure in LOPD.
