edges/2.description: Impaired ureagenesis prevents hepatic ammonia disposal, producing the proximal-UCD biochemical profile.

evidence.snippet: N-Acetylglutamate synthase (NAGS) deficiency is an extremely rare autosomal recessive metabolic disorder affecting the urea cycle, leading to episodes of hyperammonemia which can cause significant morbidity and mortality.

evidence.snippet: Mutation analysis using in silico mutation prediction tools and molecular dynamics simulations predicted the identified variant, p.Gly23Val-MRAS, to be damaging to normal protein function and adversely affect effector interaction regions and the GTP-binding site.
evidence.explanation: In silico prediction and molecular dynamics simulation localizing the founding NS11 variant to the effector-interaction and GTP-binding surfaces of M-Ras. Computational arm of a mixed-source paper.

evidence.snippet: Gly23 and Thr68 are highly conserved residues, and the corresponding codons are known hotspots for RASopathy-associated mutations in other RAS proteins.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the NS11 variant spectrum is confined to conserved RASopathy hotspot codons rather than being distributed across the gene.

steps/1.description: NS11 is initiated by a germline heterozygous missense substitution in MRAS, almost always at one of a narrow set of codons — Gly23 (p.Gly23Val, p.Gly23Arg), Thr68 (p.Thr68Ile) or Gln71 (p.Gln71Arg) — that correspond to known RASopathy and oncogenic hotspots in other RAS-family GTPases. The substitutions lie in or adjacent to the P-loop, switch regions and GTP-binding site, and are predicted to perturb effector-interaction surfaces and nucleotide handling.

evidence.snippet: Subsequent ectopic expression experiments revealed a 40-fold increase in MRAS activation for p.Gly23Val-MRAS compared with WT-MRAS.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the gain of function at the level of M-Ras activation state.

evidence.snippet: Functional analyses documented high level of activation of MRAS mutants due to impaired GTPase activity, which was associated with constitutive plasma membrane targeting, prolonged localization in non-raft microdomains, enhanced binding to PPP1CB and SHOC2 protein, and variably increased MAPK and PI3K-AKT activation.
evidence.explanation: Supports both the impaired GTPase activity and the constitutive membrane localization of NS11 mutants.

steps/2.description: Impaired intrinsic GTP hydrolysis leaves mutant M-Ras persistently GTP-bound. Activation is quantitatively large: ectopic expression of p.Gly23Val-MRAS produced an approximately 40-fold increase in M-Ras activation relative to wild type. The GTP-loaded mutant is also constitutively targeted to the plasma membrane and dwells abnormally long in non-raft microdomains, so the active protein is retained where its effectors are engaged.

evidence.snippet: The MRAS GTPase, a close relative of RAS oncoproteins, interacts with SHOC2 and protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) to form a heterotrimeric holoenzyme that dephosphorylates this S259 RAF site.
evidence.explanation: Defines the holophosphatase and its substrate, the inhibitory RAF S259 site.

evidence.snippet: The SMP complex forms only when MRAS is in an active state and is dependent on SHOC2 functioning as a scaffolding protein in the complex by bringing PP1C and MRAS together.
evidence.explanation: The crystal structure shows the holophosphatase assembles only around active, GTP-bound M-Ras, which is why a constitutively active NS11 mutant drives complex formation.

evidence.snippet: MRAS forms a high-affinity SHOC2-MRAS-PP1C (SMP) complex, while canonical RAS isoforms (KRAS, HRAS, NRAS) form analogous but lower-affinity assemblies.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that M-Ras, not a canonical RAS isoform, is the high-affinity partner in this holophosphatase, because of structural features specific to M-Ras. Directness is INDIRECT: the affinity contrast is background that the paper's new SHOC2-KRAS-PP1C structure rationalizes, and the same paper cautions that affinity and cellular dependency come apart, so it is cited for the isoform specificity of the complex and not for the magnitude of any downstream effect.

steps/3.description: M-Ras, the leucine-rich-repeat scaffold SHOC2 and protein phosphatase 1 assemble into a heterotrimeric holoenzyme in which M-Ras and SHOC2 act as regulatory subunits conferring specificity for RAF, and M-Ras additionally acts as the membrane-targeting subunit. Noonan-causing substitutions in any of the three components — MRAS, SHOC2 or PPP1CB — promote assembly of this complex, which is the shared biochemical lesion linking NS11 to SHOC2-related and PPP1CB-related Noonan-spectrum disease.

evidence.snippet: Thus, Noonan syndrome in individuals with SHOC2, MRAS, or PPPC1B mutations is likely driven at the biochemical level by enhanced ternary complex formation and highlights the crucial role of this phosphatase holoenzyme in RAF S259 dephosphorylation, ERK pathway dynamics, and normal human development.
evidence.explanation: States the mechanistic model connecting MRAS mutation, holophosphatase assembly and RAF S259 dephosphorylation to Noonan syndrome.

steps/4.description: Dephosphorylation of the inhibitory S259 site on CRAF (S365 on BRAF) by the MRAS-SHOC2-PP1 holophosphatase is a rate-limiting step in RAF activation. With mutant M-Ras driving complex assembly, this brake is released more readily and RAF signalling into MEK-ERK is potentiated.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, our findings further emphasize the relevance of the MRAS-SHOC2-PPP1CB axis in the control of MAPK signaling, and the contribution of both MAPK and PI3K-AKT pathways in MRAS functional upregulation.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that both MAPK and PI3K-AKT arms are engaged by MRAS functional upregulation.

evidence.snippet: Additional biochemical assays demonstrated enhanced activation of both RAS/MAPK pathway signaling and downstream gene expression in cells expressing p.Gly23Val-MRAS.
evidence.explanation: Independent demonstration of RAS/MAPK hyperactivation by an NS11 variant.

evidence.snippet: NS and a number of other phenotypically overlapping developmental disorders termed “RASopathies” are caused by dysregulation, which is generally embodied by an increase in signaling, of this pathway early in development.
evidence.explanation: Grounds the claim that the developmental (craniofacial, growth, neurodevelopmental) Noonan features downstream of this node are caused by increased RAS/MAPK signalling during early development.

evidence.snippet: RASopathy is a group of disorders primarily affecting the nervous system, heart, skin and craniofacial development. These conditions result from pathogenic variants affecting genes encoding components of the RAS/MAPK signaling pathway, a phosphorylation cascade involved in regulating cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival
evidence.explanation: Names the organ systems whose development is disturbed by RAS/MAPK pathway dysregulation, covering the neurological, cardiac and craniofacial phenotypes this node feeds.

steps/5.description: The convergent cellular consequence of activating MRAS variants is upregulated signal flow through the RAF-MEK-ERK cascade, with variably increased PI3K-AKT signalling. This is the shared final common pathway of the RASopathies, and it accounts for the Noonan-spectrum craniofacial, growth and neurodevelopmental features that NS11 shares with the parent Noonan Syndrome entry.

evidence.snippet: p.Gly23Val-MRAS is both necessary and sufficient to elicit a cardiac hypertrophy phenotype in iPSC-CMs that includes increased cell size, changes in cardiac gene expression, and abnormal calcium handling
evidence.explanation: Isogenic-control experiments establish necessity and sufficiency of the NS11 variant for the cardiomyocyte phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Additionally, patient and disease modeled iPSC-CMs displayed impaired Ca2+ handling, including increased frequency of irregular Ca2+ transients and changes in Ca2+ handling kinetics.
evidence.explanation: Documents the calcium-handling component of the cellular phenotype.

steps/6.description: In patient-derived and CRISPR-engineered isogenic iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes, p.Gly23Val-MRAS is both necessary and sufficient to produce increased cell size, a cardiac hypertrophy gene-expression signature, and impaired calcium handling with an increased frequency of irregular calcium transients and altered kinetics. This is the cell-level substrate of the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy that defines NS11 clinically.

evidence.snippet: Prenatal signs of Noonan syndrome as well as findings in fetal pathology are not specific, including increased nuchal translucency, cystic hygroma, serosal effusions or hydrops (consequences of lymphatic drainage disorders), polyhydramnios
evidence.explanation: States that the nuchal translucency, serosal effusion and hydrops findings of Noonan syndrome are consequences of lymphatic drainage disorders, the causal claim this node carries.

evidence.snippet: In our case, the pathogenic MRAS variant explains the phenotype observed, in particular increased nuchal translucency, dysmorphic features, cardiomyopathy, ductus venosus agenesis and pulmonary lymphangiectasia.
evidence.explanation: Documents that the lymphatic manifestations in the antenatally diagnosed patient are attributed to the MRAS variant itself, anchoring this node in MRAS-related disease rather than the general Noonan spectrum.

steps/7.description: Lymphatic vessel development is disturbed in MRAS-related Noonan syndrome, as across the wider Noonan spectrum. In the single antenatally diagnosed NS11 patient, histology showed dilated pulmonary lymphatic vessels lacking a muscular medial layer, and the prenatal picture of increased nuchal translucency, serosal effusions and hydrops is attributed in Noonan syndrome to disorders of lymphatic drainage. This tissue-level lesion accounts for the fluid-accumulation phenotypes that dominated the reported fetal course.

evidence.snippet: This report reinforces the high frequency of HCM among individuals harboring MRAS variants, contrasting to the 20% overall prevalence of this cardiac anomaly in NS.
evidence.explanation: Contrasts the near-universal HCM of MRAS-related disease against the much lower background rate in Noonan syndrome generally.

evidence.snippet: The present case provides evidence that HCM does not represent an obligatory, early-onset and severe complication in subjects with MRAS variants.

steps/8.description: The organ-level lesion that distinguishes NS11 within the Noonan spectrum. Reported patients have shown hypertrophic cardiomyopathy far more consistently than Noonan syndrome overall, in which HCM affects roughly 20-30%; the MRAS cases are additionally weighted towards early onset, outflow tract obstruction, and poor prognosis, with deaths in the neonatal and infant periods. The severity is nonetheless not invariant — an adult with the recurrent p.Thr68Ile substitution had only mild, late-onset left ventricular hypertrophy — so obligate early severe HCM is not a safe inference from genotype.

evidence.snippet: These findings suggest that pathogenic MRAS variants confer a high risk of severe HCM (100% of cases).

evidence.snippet: This report provides additional evidence that a narrow spectrum of activating mutations in MRAS represents another rare cause of NS, and that MRAS has to be counted among the RASopathy genes predisposing to HCM.

evidence.snippet: The diagnosis of Noonan is established in a proband with suggestive findings and a heterozygous pathogenic variant in BRAF, KRAS, MAP2K1, MRAS, NRAS, PTPN11, RAF1, RASA2, RIT1, RRAS2, SOS1, or SOS2 or either a heterozygous variant or biallelic pathogenic variants in LZTR1 identified by molecular genetic testing.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists MRAS among the genes in which a heterozygous pathogenic variant establishes a molecular diagnosis of Noonan syndrome.

genes/0.notes: MRAS encodes M-Ras (RAS-related protein 3, R-Ras3), a RAS-family small GTPase that transmits signal to RAF through the SHOC2-PP1 holophosphatase. NS11 is caused by heterozygous germline missense variants at a narrow set of conserved hotspot codons. Reported pathogenic changes are c.68G>T (p.Gly23Val), c.67G>C (p.Gly23Arg), c.203C>T (p.Thr68Ile — the most frequently recurrent) and c.212A>G (p.Gln71Arg); all reported occurrences have been de novo.

evidence.snippet: It also identifies infective endocarditis as a previously unreported complication in MRAS-associated NS with outflow tract obstruction, highlighting the importance of careful cardiac surveillance in patients with RASopathies.
evidence.explanation: Motivates cardiac surveillance specifically in MRAS-associated Noonan syndrome.

treatments/0.description: Because hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is present in essentially every reported NS11 patient and can be obstructive from infancy or emerge late in adulthood, echocardiographic surveillance is the central management task. Cardiovascular anomalies in Noonan syndrome are otherwise treated as in the general population. A recognized complication of outflow tract obstruction in this group is infective endocarditis, which prompted a call for careful cardiac surveillance in RASopathy patients.

treatments/1.description: Myectomy has been used to relieve outflow tract obstruction in NS11, including in the index patient at age 8. Outcomes have not been uniformly good — a 2-month-old infant died after myectomy — so the balance of risk in early infancy is unsettled.

evidence.snippet: She received off-label treatment with the MEK-inhibitor trametinib which resulted in complete remission of the cardiac hypertrophy and a significant improvement of the pulmonary valve stenosis.
evidence.explanation: The only reported instance of MEK inhibition reversing severe early-onset RASopathy hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Directness is INDIRECT because the patient carried a RIT1 variant, not an MRAS one: the inference step is that both act through the same RAF-MEK-ERK arm that this treatment targets. It raises the rationale above pathway plausibility to a demonstrated cardiac response in a related RASopathy, and does not establish efficacy in NS11.

evidence.snippet: Recently, repurposing of medications inhibiting the RAS/MAPK on a compassionate use basis has emerged as a promising concept to improve the outcome of these patients.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the compassionate-use repurposing framework under which MEK inhibition is actually offered for RASopathy hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which is the route by which an NS11 patient would receive it today. Directness is INDIRECT and evidence source is OTHER: this is a review covering RASopathy-associated cardiomyopathy as a class, and it reports no MRAS patient.

treatments/3.description: Because NS11 acts through RAF-MEK-ERK hyperactivation, MEK inhibitors are the mechanistically aligned targeted therapy and have been proposed for MRAS-related disease. This is a rationale, not established care: no MRAS -specific interventional trial has been reported.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, emerging targeted therapies, such as MEK inhibitors, offer potential for treatment.
evidence.explanation: Identifies MEK inhibition as the emerging targeted approach for MRAS-related Noonan syndrome; evidence source is OTHER because this is a review/case-report proposal rather than a reported intervention.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: MEK inhibitors block the MEK-ERK arm downstream of the activated MRAS-SHOC2-PP1/RAF axis.

evidence.snippet: In Raf1L613V/+ mice, 6 weeks of treatment significantly improved left ventricular chamber dimension, posterior wall thickness, heart mass, and cardiomyocyte size, resulting in reversal of cardiac hypertrophy.
evidence.explanation: The substantive preclinical result: reversal of established hypertrophy in a Noonan knock-in mouse. Directness is INDIRECT because the model carries a RAF1 variant, not an MRAS one - the inference step is the shared RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT output that this entry's own node names.

evidence.snippet: In cardiac-targeted fly models, rigosertib reduced cardiac hypertrophy and outperformed trametinib.
evidence.explanation: Places this agent against the MEK inhibitor curated above in the same screen. Directness is INDIRECT: a Drosophila comparison does not establish relative efficacy in human MRAS-related disease.

treatments/4.description: Preclinical only, and listed here because it is the one reported agent whose target profile matches both arms this entry models. MEK inhibition addresses the MAPK arm alone, whereas NS11 variants raise MAPK and PI3K-AKT output together; rigosertib inhibits both. It reversed established cardiac hypertrophy in Raf1 knock-in mice and outperformed trametinib in a Drosophila RASopathy panel. No MRAS model or patient has been treated with it, so this is a target-profile rationale and not a therapy for NS11.

evidence.snippet: Rigosertib, a novel dual RAS/MAPK and phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/AKT pathway inhibitor, is currently in clinical trials for treatment of melanoma and recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the dual target profile, which is why this agent maps onto this node rather than onto the MAPK arm alone. Directness is INDIRECT: the sentence describes the drug, not its effect in any MRAS system.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Rigosertib inhibits the RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT arms together, which is the pathway pair this node names.

evidence.snippet: Functional analyses documented high level of activation of MRAS mutants due to impaired GTPase activity, which was associated with constitutive plasma membrane targeting, prolonged localization in non-raft microdomains, enhanced binding to PPP1CB and SHOC2 protein, and variably increased MAPK and PI3K-AKT activation.
evidence.explanation: States the canonical ordering directly: impaired GTPase activity is given as the cause, with enhanced SHOC2/PPP1CB binding among its consequences.

evidence.snippet: Subsequent ectopic expression experiments revealed a 40-fold increase in MRAS activation for p.Gly23Val-MRAS compared with WT-MRAS.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the gain in activation state that the canonical model treats as the primary lesion.

hypotheses/0.description: The established account of NS11 treats the hotspot substitutions as conventional RAS-family activating mutations: they impair intrinsic GTPase activity, so mutant M-Ras accumulates in the GTP-bound active state, and that persistently active protein drives holophosphatase assembly, RAF activation and downstream RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT output. On this model the nucleotide state is the primary lesion and complex formation is its consequence.

evidence.snippet: The switch toward active GTP-bound M-Ras conformation takes place through its allosteric stabilization by the holophosphatase.
evidence.explanation: The claim that separates this model from the canonical one: the conformational transition to the effector-competent state is attributed to complex binding, not to nucleotide loading alone.

evidence.snippet: However, the GppNHp-bound M-Ras Q71R and Q71L mutants display the active state II conformation in the SMP complexes, suggesting that these mutants drive M-Ras-GTP into the active conformation similar to the canonical Ras oncogenic Q61 mutants
evidence.explanation: Applies the model to p.Gln71Arg, a reported NS11 hotspot substitution: its effect is described as driving the switch regions into the active conformation within the complex, and is explicitly likened to the canonical RAS Q61 oncogenic mutants rather than being set against them.

hypotheses/1.description: A refinement rather than a rival of the canonical account. All-atom molecular dynamics work argues that M-Ras is an atypical RAS switch: even when GTP-loaded, wild-type M-Ras predominantly occupies the inactive state I switch conformation, so nucleotide loading is necessary but not sufficient to produce an effector-competent protein. The active state II conformation is instead stabilized allosterically once M-Ras is bound within the SHOC2-M-Ras-PP1 holophosphatase. On this reading an NS11 substitution acts at two points rather than one: it raises the GTP-bound population, as the canonical model says, and it additionally drives the switch regions into the active conformation and binds the holophosphatase more tightly. The distinction is not academic for therapy, because it places a second druggable step at complex assembly rather than at nucleotide handling.

evidence.snippet: Therefore, long-term follow-up of these individuals and further descriptions are required to fully understand the complete phenotypic spectrum of NS associated with MRAS germline variants, including if these individuals present an increased risk for cancer.
evidence.explanation: Explicitly names the cancer-risk question as unresolved for MRAS-related Noonan syndrome.

open_questions/0.rationale: p.Gln71Arg is a recurrent oncogenic substitution in RAS homologs across various cancers, and other RASopathies carry defined tumour predisposition. No NS11 patient has been reported with a malignancy, but the reported cohort is tiny and several patients died in infancy, so the question is unanswerable from current data rather than answered in the negative.

evidence.snippet: The present case provides evidence that HCM does not represent an obligatory, early-onset and severe complication in subjects with MRAS variants.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the intra-genotype discrepancy in cardiac severity that this gap concerns.

open_questions/1.rationale: p.Thr68Ile is the most frequently recurrent NS11 variant and has been reported both in a neonate who died of cardiac failure and in an adult with only mild, late-onset left ventricular hypertrophy. Identical genotype with opposite cardiac trajectories implies modifiers, mosaicism, or ascertainment bias towards severe paediatric cases, and the distinction matters directly for counselling and for whether early myectomy is offered.

evidence.snippet: These RAS inhibitors do not affect SMP formation because they do not bind MRAS.
evidence.explanation: States the gap directly: the RAS inhibitors that block the canonical complex leave the M-Ras-containing complex untouched, so they are not a route into the NS11 lesion.

open_questions/2.rationale: MRTX1133 and RMC-6236 block assembly of the canonical SHOC2-RAS-PP1C complex, but neither binds M-Ras, so neither would be expected to act on the SMP complex that NS11 variants drive. That is the specific gap: it is unremarkable that RAS-directed inhibitors miss most RASopathy proteins, but NS11's lesion sits in the one RAS-family protein these drugs leave out of a complex they otherwise engage. An engineered M-Ras mutant has been shown to accept MRTX1133 and to have its complex assembly blocked by it, which establishes that the site is in principle addressable, but no compound that engages wild-type or NS11-mutant M-Ras has been reported. The gap matters because it separates NS11 from the RASopathies for which downstream MEK inhibition is the practical route.

evidence.snippet: LZTR1-mutant male mice exhibit low birth weight, distinctive facial features, and cardiac hypertrophy.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the premise of the gap rather than the gap itself: germline knock-in modelling of a Noonan gene does reproduce the multi-system human phenotype in vivo. Directness is INDIRECT because the gene is LZTR1, not MRAS - the paper is cited to show the approach works and has not been applied here, not to make any claim about M-Ras.

evidence.snippet: In Raf1L613V/+ mice, 6 weeks of treatment significantly improved left ventricular chamber dimension, posterior wall thickness, heart mass, and cardiomyocyte size, resulting in reversal of cardiac hypertrophy.
evidence.explanation: Shows what a germline model buys: an interventional readout on established cardiac disease. Cited here to size the gap rather than to fill it - directness is INDIRECT because the mouse carries a RAF1 variant, so the equivalent experiment remains impossible for MRAS.

open_questions/3.rationale: Every model system curated on this entry is an iPSC-derived cardiomyocyte preparation. No germline MRAS knock-in mouse, zebrafish or other whole-organism model has been reported, which is why this entry carries no `animal_models` section. The absence is specific to MRAS rather than to the approach: knock-in mice have been generated for other Noonan genes and do reproduce low birth weight, facial dysmorphism and cardiac hypertrophy. It matters here more than it would for most RASopathies, because the NS11 features that a dish cannot report are exactly the ones that define the disease - outflow tract obstruction, growth failure, craniofacial dysmorphism, and the neurodevelopmental phenotype. The developmental branch of this entry's mechanism is currently extrapolated from the general RASopathy paradigm rather than demonstrated with MRAS-specific in vivo data. What such a model would be for is already demonstrated next door: in Raf1 knock-in mice, six weeks of rigosertib reversed established cardiac hypertrophy. That answers the reversal half of the question in a neighbouring Noonan gene and leaves the MRAS-specific half, and the prevention half, untestable for want of a model.

evidence.snippet: Because of the severity of the cardiac involvement, other clinical findings could not be addressed in detail.
evidence.explanation: Documents that non-cardiac findings in MRAS patients are under-characterized, which is why their mechanisms remain open.

open_questions/4.rationale: Each of these findings is documented in a single reported MRAS patient. Class-level RASopathy explanations exist — the broad or webbed neck is classically interpreted as the residuum of fetal nuchal lymphedema, and Noonan polyhydramnios is often attributed to impaired fetal swallowing — but none of these mechanisms has been examined in an MRAS patient, and the path from RAS/MAPK hyperactivation to chest-wall deformity or joint laxity is not characterized for any RASopathy gene. The reported cohort is too small and too cardiac-dominated for these features to be mechanistically resolved, so no causal edge is asserted for them.

evidence.snippet: This is the first report to our knowledge of a human phenotype resulting from a mutation in WNT10A, and it is the first demonstration of an ectodermal dysplasia caused by an altered WNT signaling pathway, expanding the list of WNT-related diseases.
evidence.explanation: Establishes WNT10A as the causative gene for OODD and links WNT signaling disruption to ectodermal dysplasia.

evidence.snippet: WNT10A is expressed in the skin and epidermis and it has shown to be critical for the development of ectodermal appendages.
evidence.explanation: Confirms WNT10A expression in skin/epidermis and its critical role in ectodermal appendage development.

evidence.snippet: WNT10A gene encodes a canonical wingless pathway signaling molecule involved in cell fate specification as well as morphogenetic patterning of the developing ectoderm, nervous system, skeleton, and tooth.
evidence.explanation: Confirms WNT10A role in canonical Wnt pathway and morphogenetic patterning of ectoderm and tooth.

steps/1.description: WNT10A encodes a secreted glycoprotein ligand of the canonical WNT signaling pathway. Loss-of-function mutations abolish WNT10A binding to Frizzled receptors, preventing activation of the beta-catenin destruction complex inhibition and downstream TCF/LEF-mediated transcription. This disrupts ectodermal appendage morphogenesis including teeth, hair follicles, nails, and sweat glands.

evidence.snippet: Odonto-onycho-dermal dysplasia (OODD) is a rare form of ectodermal dysplasia characterized by severe oligodontia, onychodysplasia, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, dry skin, hypotrichosis, and hyperhidrosis of the palms and soles.
evidence.explanation: Summarizes the spectrum of ectodermal appendage defects seen in OODD including teeth, nails, skin, and hair.

steps/2.description: Disrupted WNT/beta-catenin signaling during embryonic development leads to hypoplasia or aplasia of ectodermal appendages. Teeth are most severely affected (oligodontia/anodontia), followed by nails (dystrophy, thinning), hair (sparse, dry), and sweat glands (hypohidrosis or paradoxical hyperhidrosis of palms/soles).

evidence.snippet: Mild to severe oligodontia was observed in all patients bearing biallelic WNT10A mutations.
evidence.explanation: Biallelic WNT10A mutations directly support the dental branch of the pathograph.

steps/3.description: WNT10A deficiency disrupts tooth and oral ectodermal placode development, producing severe oligodontia, selective tooth agenesis, tooth-shape anomalies, and reduced tongue papillae.

evidence.snippet: severe oligodontia, onychodysplasia, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, dry skin, hypotrichosis, and hyperhidrosis of the palms and soles
evidence.explanation: This clinical summary supports nail and hair involvement as part of OODD.

steps/4.description: Disrupted ectodermal appendage morphogenesis affects hair shafts and nail units, producing dry or sparse hair and nail dystrophy.

evidence.snippet: severe oligodontia, onychodysplasia, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, dry skin, hypotrichosis, and hyperhidrosis of the palms and soles
evidence.explanation: This clinical summary supports the skin and sweating branch of OODD.

steps/5.description: WNT10A-related epidermal and sweat-apparatus defects produce palmoplantar keratoderma, broader hyperkeratosis or xerosis, and abnormal sweating of palms and soles.

evidence.snippet: Schöpf-Schulz-Passarge syndrome, which is so far considered a unique entity by the findings of numerous cysts along eyelid margins and the increased risk of benign and malignant skin tumors

evidence.explanation: Rescue experiment placing RAC1 activation downstream of LRRK1 in the resorption defect, supporting the direction of this node's mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Previous studies have revealed that knockout (KO) of Lrrk1 in mice causes severe osteopetrosis, and a human mutation of Lrrk1 leads to osteosclerotic metaphysial dysplasia.

evidence.snippet: His skeletal phenotype recapitulated that seen in the Lrrk1-deficient mouse. The shared skeletal hallmarks included severe sclerosis in the undermodelled metaphyses and epiphyseal margins of the tubular bones, costal ends, vertebral endplates and margins of the flat bones.

steps/10.description: LRRK1 is a leucine-rich repeat kinase that phosphorylates and activates the small GTPases RAC1 and CDC42 in the osteoclast within minutes of RANKL stimulation. Loss of LRRK1 kinase function leaves RAC1/CDC42 underphosphorylated and inactive and the osteoclast unable to resorb, and expressing a constitutively active RAC1 partially restores resorption. In humans this produces osteosclerotic metaphyseal dysplasia, in which the sclerosis is concentrated at the metaphyses and epiphyseal margins rather than being generalised.

evidence.snippet: we show that TCIRG1, encoding the osteoclast-specific 116-kD subunit of the vacuolar proton pump, is mutated in five of nine patients with a diagnosis of infantile malignant osteopetrosis
evidence.explanation: Identifies TCIRG1 as the proton pump subunit whose loss causes defective osteoclast acidification in human ARO.

evidence.snippet: they fail to resorb bone because they cannot acidify the extracellular resorption lacuna

evidence.snippet: mutations in TCIRG1, CLCN7, OSTM1, SNX10 and PLEKHM1 lead to osteoclast-rich ARO (in which osteoclasts are abundant but have severely impaired resorptive function)
evidence.explanation: Comprehensive review confirming that osteoclast-rich ARO results from impaired osteoclast function rather than impaired differentiation.

steps/11.description: The majority of osteopetrosis cases result from mutations in genes required for acidification of the osteoclast resorption lacuna. TCIRG1 encodes the a3 subunit of the vacuolar proton pump (V-ATPase), and its loss prevents acid secretion into the resorption lacuna. CLCN7 encodes a chloride-proton antiporter that provides the chloride conductance needed to maintain electroneutrality during proton pumping. OSTM1 stabilizes CLCN7. Without adequate acidification, hydroxyapatite dissolution fails and bone matrix cannot be degraded, leading to progressive accumulation of unresorbed primary spongiosa.

evidence.snippet: we report mutations in the gene encoding RANKL (receptor activator of nuclear factor-KB ligand) in six individuals with autosomal recessive osteopetrosis whose bone biopsy specimens lacked osteoclasts
evidence.explanation: First identification of RANKL mutations as a cause of osteoclast-poor osteopetrosis in humans.

evidence.snippet: exogenous RANKL induced formation of functional osteoclasts from their monocytes, suggesting that they could, theoretically, benefit from exogenous RANKL administration
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that the differentiation defect is rescuable by providing exogenous RANKL, confirming the microenvironment-based mechanism.

steps/12.description: A subset of ARO cases result from mutations in TNFSF11 (encoding RANKL) or TNFRSF11A (encoding RANK), which are essential for osteoclast differentiation from monocyte-macrophage precursors. These osteoclast-poor forms lack mature osteoclasts entirely. In TNFSF11 (RANKL) deficiency, the defect lies in the bone microenvironment (osteoblasts fail to produce RANKL), so HSCT does not correct the phenotype. In contrast, TNFRSF11A (RANK) mutations affect the hematopoietic osteoclast precursors themselves, so HSCT can theoretically provide functional RANK-expressing donor monocytes.

evidence.snippet: Pathogenic variants in PLEKHM1 and SNX10 can be classified among the latter as they impair vesicular transport within the osteoclast and therefore result in the absence of a ruffled border.
evidence.explanation: States the shared mechanism for both genes bound to this node: impaired osteoclast vesicular transport with absence of the ruffled border.

evidence.snippet: Some of the typical radiological hallmarks of osteopetrosis can be seen, and most cases present as a relatively mild form segregating in an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance.
evidence.explanation: Supports the milder recessive course this node's description attributes to the vesicular-transport forms.

evidence.snippet: We found that Plekhm1 colocalized with Rab7 to late endosomal/lysosomal vesicles in HEK293 and osteoclast-like cells, an effect that was dependent on the prenylation of Rab7.

steps/13.description: A third route to osteoclast-rich osteopetrosis, distinct from both the acidification defect and the osteoclast-poor differentiation defect. PLEKHM1 couples RAB7-positive late endosomal and lysosomal vesicles to the osteoclast plasma membrane, and SNX10 acts in the same vesicular trafficking step. When either is lost the osteoclast differentiates normally but fails to build a ruffled border, so the secretory machinery never reaches the bone-facing membrane and resorption fails despite intact proton-pumping capacity. This is the mechanistic route behind the relatively mild, intermediate course that most reported PLEKHM1 and SNX10 cases follow.

genes/4.notes: TNFSF11 encodes RANKL, the key osteoclastogenic cytokine. Biallelic mutations cause osteoclast-poor ARO, the numbered form OPTB2 (MONDO:0009816). Because the defect lies in the microenvironment rather than the osteoclast precursor, HSCT does not correct the phenotype.

evidence.snippet: mutations in TNFSF11 and TNFRSF11A lead to osteoclast-poor ARO
evidence.explanation: Review confirms TNFRSF11A (RANK) mutations as a cause of osteoclast-poor ARO.

evidence.snippet: Genetic testing identified 15 variants in 12 patients, including 8 variants in the CLCN7 gene (53%), 6 in the TCIRG1 gene (40%), and 1 in the TNFRSF11A gene (7%).
evidence.explanation: A 14-child cohort in which TNFRSF11A contributed one of the 15 detected variants, showing that it is a rare cause relative to CLCN7 and TCIRG1. The percentages are shares of detected variants, not of patients, so they are not recorded as case_fractions.

genes/5.notes: TNFRSF11A encodes RANK, the receptor for RANKL on osteoclast precursors. Biallelic mutations cause osteoclast-poor ARO, the numbered form OPTB7 (MONDO:0012859), and can present with an osteoclast-rich pattern depending on the specific mutation.

evidence.snippet: mutations in TCIRG1, CLCN7, OSTM1, SNX10 and PLEKHM1 lead to osteoclast-rich ARO
evidence.explanation: Review identifies SNX10 as one of the genes causing osteoclast-rich ARO.

evidence.snippet: Pathogenic variants in PLEKHM1 and SNX10 can be classified among the latter as they impair vesicular transport within the osteoclast and therefore result in the absence of a ruffled border.
evidence.explanation: Sources the vesicular-transport mechanism and the absent ruffled border for SNX10, which were previously asserted in this entry without a citation.

genes/6.notes: SNX10 encodes sorting nexin 10. Biallelic mutations cause ARO, the numbered form OPTB8 (MONDO:0014040), typically with a milder course. The lesion is in osteoclast vesicular transport, so the ruffled border fails to form.

evidence.snippet: loss-of-function mutations were found to underlie the osteopetrotic phenotype of the incisors absent rat as well as an intermediate type of human osteopetrosis
evidence.explanation: Primary report identifying biallelic PLEKHM1 loss of function in intermediate human osteopetrosis.

evidence.snippet: monocytes from a patient homozygous for the mutation differentiated into osteoclasts normally, but when cultured on dentine discs, the osteoclasts failed to form ruffled borders and showed little evidence of bone resorption
evidence.explanation: Places the PLEKHM1 defect after osteoclast differentiation, at ruffled-border formation, distinguishing it from the osteoclast-poor RANKL/RANK forms.

genes/7.notes: PLEKHM1 couples RAB7-positive late endosomal and lysosomal vesicles to the osteoclast ruffled border. Biallelic loss of function causes the intermediate recessive numbered form OPTB6 (MONDO:0012679). The gene was already named in this entry's cited review snippets but was not bound to a gene term until now.

evidence.snippet: One mutation, a heterozygous deletion mutation in exon 11 (c.3051_3052delCA), was identified in the patient but not in his relatives.
evidence.explanation: The single-proband heterozygous genotype behind the dominant PLEKHM1 form, and the limit of the evidence for it.

evidence.snippet: overexpression of a PLEKHM1 CA-deletion mutant resulted in a dramatic decrease in the interaction between PLEKHM1 and the small GTPase Rab7 compared to wild-type PLEKHM1
evidence.explanation: Functional support that the reported heterozygous variant disrupts the PLEKHM1-RAB7 interaction required for osteoclast vesicular transport.

genes/8.notes: A heterozygous PLEKHM1 exon-11 deletion was reported in one patient with a relatively malignant course and was absent from his tested relatives; this is the basis for the dominant numbered form OPTA3 (MONDO:0020848). Recorded separately from the biallelic record above, and flagged as single-proband evidence rather than an established dominant disease.

evidence.snippet: By whole exome sequencing in a boy with OSMD, we identified a homozygous 7 bp deletion (c.5938_5944delGAGTGGT) in the LRRK1 gene.
evidence.explanation: Primary report identifying biallelic LRRK1 loss of function in human OSMD.

evidence.snippet: Our data indicate that Lrrk1 regulates osteoclast function by directly modulating phosphorylation and activation of small GTPase RAC1/Cdc42 and that its function depends on ANK, ROC, WD40, and kinase domains.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the molecular step at which LRRK1 acts in the osteoclast, which is the mechanism node this gene is wired to.

genes/9.notes: LRRK1 is a leucine-rich repeat kinase that phosphorylates and activates the small GTPases RAC1 and CDC42 in osteoclasts. Biallelic loss of function causes osteosclerotic metaphyseal dysplasia (MONDO:0014080), in which the osteosclerosis is localised to the metaphyses and epiphyseal margins. LRRK1 does not account for all OSMD cases.

evidence.snippet: The only therapy shown to be capable of providing lasting benefit is allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HCT). We report the outcome of 10 patients with infantile malignant osteopetrosis treated with HCT
evidence.explanation: Reports outcomes of HSCT for infantile osteopetrosis, with 5 of 10 patients surviving.

evidence.snippet: We recommend early referral for consideration of HCT with a related or unrelated donor as neurosensory manifestations of osteopetrosis are generally not reversible
evidence.explanation: Emphasizes the importance of early transplantation before irreversible neurological damage occurs.

evidence.snippet: guidelines for the indication of haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (which can provide a cure for many types of ARO), are outlined
evidence.explanation: Review confirms HSCT as a curative treatment for many types of ARO.

evidence.snippet: These individuals did not show any obvious defects in immunological parameters and could not be cured by hematopoietic stem cell transplantation
evidence.explanation: Confirms that RANKL-deficient osteoclast-poor osteopetrosis does not respond to HSCT because the defect is in the microenvironment.

treatments/0.description: HSCT is the only curative treatment for osteoclast-rich forms of ARO. Donor-derived monocyte-macrophage precursors differentiate into functional osteoclasts that restore bone resorption. Best outcomes are achieved with early transplantation before irreversible complications develop. HSCT is not effective for osteoclast-poor forms (TNFSF11 mutations) or for ADO2.

evidence.snippet: We suggest that calcitriol should not be used in high doses and instead recommend symptom-based supportive therapy for disease complications because noninfantile osteopetrosis has no effective treatment
evidence.explanation: Consensus guidelines recommend supportive therapy for non-infantile osteopetrosis.

evidence.snippet: We recommend ongoing monitoring for changes in mineral metabolism and other complications, including cranial nerve impingement, anemia, leukopenia, and dental disease
evidence.explanation: Guidelines outline specific complications requiring ongoing monitoring.

treatments/1.description: For non-infantile forms where HSCT is not indicated, management is supportive. Includes monitoring for cranial nerve impingement, anemia, dental disease, and mineral metabolism abnormalities. Calcium and vitamin D supplementation may be needed for hypocalcemia.

evidence.snippet: Whole-exome sequencing and intensive data sharing identified a recurrent de novo PACS2 heterozygous missense variant in 14 unrelated individuals.
evidence.explanation: The recurrent de novo variant in the founding cohort.

steps/1.description: A heterozygous de novo missense variant, in nearly all reported individuals the recurrent c.625G>A p.(Glu209Lys) change. This node records the lesion only. Note the disorder is defined by one recurrent substitution rather than by a spectrum of loss-of-function alleles, which is why the downstream arms are all consequences of a single specific protein change rather than of absent protein.

evidence.snippet: Functional studies demonstrated that the PACS2 recurrent variant reduces the ability of the predicted autoregulatory domain to modulate the interaction between the PACS2 FBR and client proteins, which may disturb cellular function.
evidence.explanation: The functional measurement for this arm. Note the source's own hedge - "may disturb cellular function" - which is why no specific downstream cargo defect is asserted here.

steps/2.description: The variant reduces the ability of the predicted autoregulatory domain to modulate the interaction between the PACS2 cargo/furin-binding region and its client proteins. This is the trafficking-control arm, and it is separate from the proteostasis arm below because the two were established by different experiments.

evidence.snippet: we observed that the PACS-2 E209K protein exhibited a slower turnover rate relative to PACS-2 wild type (WT) upon cycloheximide treatment in 293T cells
evidence.explanation: The turnover measurement, made by cycloheximide chase in 293T cells.

steps/3.description: The E209K protein has a slower turnover rate and longer half-life than wild type. Curated separately from the autoregulatory arm because it is a stability change rather than an interaction-control change, and because it is what the increased 14-3-3-epsilon association was attributed to.

evidence.snippet: a regulatory protein in neurodevelopment known as 14-3-3ε was identified as having an increased association with PACS-2 E209K
evidence.explanation: The interaction measurement behind this node.

steps/4.description: The variant protein shows increased association with 14-3-3-epsilon, a regulatory protein in neurodevelopment. This is the specific altered interaction that the proteostasis change produces, and the one the apoptosis phenotype is attributed to.

evidence.snippet: we found that PACS-2 E209K increased susceptibility to staurosporine-induced apoptosis in HCT 116 cells
evidence.explanation: The apoptosis measurement, together with the cell line it was made in.

evidence.snippet: Overall, our findings suggest PACS-2 E209K alters PACS-2 proteostasis and favors complex formation with 14-3-3ε, leading to increased cell death in the presence of environmental stressors.
evidence.explanation: The authors' summary chain, and the phrase "in the presence of environmental stressors" is the conditionality this node preserves.

steps/5.description: Cells expressing E209K die more readily than wild-type-expressing cells when challenged with staurosporine. The conditional framing matters and is preserved here: this is increased susceptibility under an applied stressor, not constitutive cell death. The cell type in which it was measured is a serious limitation, recorded in the discussions.

evidence.snippet: Cerebellar abnormalities may be similar but PACS2 individuals exhibit a pattern of clear dysgenesis ranging from mild to severe.
evidence.explanation: Establishes dysgenesis as the characteristic pattern and its severity range, contrasted against the paralogous PACS1 disorder.

evidence.snippet: Brain MRIs evidenced anomalies of the posterior cerebellar fossa, foliar distortion of the cerebellum, vermis hypoplasia, white matter reduction, and lateral ventricles enlargement.
evidence.explanation: The imaging findings across the systematic review cohort.

steps/6.description: Foliar distortion of the cerebellum with vermis hypoplasia and posterior fossa anomalies. This is the imaging finding that most distinguishes DEE66 from other developmental and epileptic encephalopathies, and it is a malformation rather than a degenerative change.

evidence.snippet: Mixed focal and generalized epilepsy occurred in the neonatal period, controlled with difficulty in the first year, but many improved in early childhood.
evidence.explanation: Supports that a seizure-generating cortical state exists in the neonatal period. Typed PARTIAL because it evidences the seizures, not the excitability mechanism this node names.

steps/7.description: Cortical networks become seizure-prone in the neonatal period. This node is inferred from the clinical seizure phenotype: no electrophysiological characterisation of excitability has been published in any PACS2 model or in patient-derived neurons, which is a stated gap rather than an oversight.

evidence.snippet: Mixed focal and generalized epilepsy occurred in the neonatal period, controlled with difficulty in the first year, but many improved in early childhood.
evidence.explanation: Gives both the onset and the characteristic later improvement.

evidence.snippet: Compared to the defined PACS1 recurrent variant series, individuals with PACS2 variant have more consistently neonatal/early-infantile-onset epilepsy that can be challenging to control.
evidence.explanation: Contrasts the seizure course against the paralogous PACS1 disorder, which is what makes the neonatal onset a discriminating feature.

steps/8.description: Mixed focal and generalised seizures begin in the neonatal period and are difficult to control through the first year, but many patients improve in early childhood. The age-dependent improvement is curated as part of this node rather than as a separate outcome, because it is a property of the seizure disorder itself and distinguishes DEE66 from most developmental and epileptic encephalopathies.

evidence.snippet: Their phenotype was characterized by epilepsy, global developmental delay with or without autism, common cerebellar dysgenesis, and facial dysmorphism.
evidence.explanation: Names global developmental delay as a core feature of the syndrome.

steps/9.description: Delayed motor and speech milestones with intellectual disability of variable degree. Two upstream routes converge here - the cerebellar and cortical malformation arm, and the neonatal seizure burden - and no published analysis separates their contributions.

edges/1.description: The substitution sits in the predicted autoregulatory domain and degrades its function.

edges/2.description: The variant protein turns over more slowly than wild type.

edges/3.description: The stabilised variant protein forms more complex with 14-3-3-epsilon.

edges/4.description: The authors attribute the increased cell death to this complex formation.

edges/5.description: Proposed as the route to the cerebellar phenotype, but the link is untested in neural tissue - see the discussion on the heterologous cell system.

edges/6.description: A hyperexcitable neonatal cortex generates the presenting seizures.

edges/7.description: Early seizure burden plausibly compounds the developmental phenotype that the malformation arm also produces; the published data do not separate them.

evidence.snippet: PACS2 is an important PACS1 paralog and encodes a multifunctional sorting protein involved in nuclear gene expression and pathway traffic regulation.
evidence.explanation: Gives the protein's function and its relationship to PACS1.

evidence.snippet: Both proteins harbor cargo(furin)-binding regions (FBRs) that bind cargo proteins, sorting adaptors, and cellular kinase.
evidence.explanation: Describes the furin-binding region whose regulation the pathogenic variant impairs.

evidence.snippet: Glu209Lys and one case of the heterogenous missense variant PACS2 pGlu211Lys
evidence.explanation: Records the second recurrent allele and, importantly, that it rests on a single case - which is why the curated mechanism stays scoped to E209K.

evidence.snippet: is not found in population databases, such as the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD)
evidence.explanation: Population-database absence, one half of the variant-interpretation evidence.

evidence.snippet: According to ClinVar, it is pathogenic/likely pathogenic
evidence.explanation: The clinical classification, the other half.

genes/0.notes: PACS2 encodes a multifunctional sorting protein that traffics cargo between the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi, mitochondria, lysosomes and plasma membrane, working through an N-terminal furin-binding region that engages cargo together with adaptor proteins. Unlike most developmental and epileptic encephalopathy genes, the disorder is defined by one recurrent substitution rather than a spectrum of loss-of-function alleles, so the mechanism curated here is the consequence of a specific protein change and not of absent protein. Deliberate scope note: PACS2's role at mitochondria-associated ER membranes is well described in the general cell biology literature and is frequently invoked for this disorder, but no source verified for this entry measures a MAM-integrity defect for the E209K variant itself. The entry therefore curates what was measured - autoregulatory-domain impairment, slowed turnover, increased 14-3-3-epsilon association and increased stress-induced apoptosis - and does not assert a MAM defect. PACS1, the paralog, causes Schuurs-Hoeijmakers syndrome through its own recurrent variant, and the two disorders were explicitly compared when DEE66 was delineated. A second recurrent allele, p.(Glu211Lys), is reported in a single case and sits two residues from the main hotspot in the same regulatory region; the mechanism curated here is derived from E209K and this entry does not assume the two behave identically. The c.625G>A allele is absent from population databases and classified pathogenic or likely pathogenic in ClinVar, which is what makes a single heterozygous finding diagnostic in the right clinical context.

evidence.snippet: Compared to the defined PACS1 recurrent variant series, individuals with PACS2 variant have more consistently neonatal/early-infantile-onset epilepsy that can be challenging to control.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the difficulty of control that motivates multi-agent management.

evidence.snippet: were treated with valproate or levetiracetam (~50%), phenobarbital (~33%), and carbamazepine (~25%), and seizure frequency appeared to decrease with age
evidence.explanation: Gives the agents actually used and their approximate response rates, which is what the therapeutic_agent bindings above record. Note these are proportions treated with each agent rather than a controlled efficacy comparison.

treatments/0.description: Seizures require multiple medication trials in the first year and are difficult to control, but frequently become easier to control or remit with age. This entry does not rank individual agents, because the cited sources describe the course rather than comparing drugs head to head.

evidence.snippet: Mixed focal and generalized epilepsy occurred in the neonatal period, controlled with difficulty in the first year, but many improved in early childhood.
evidence.explanation: Typed PARTIAL deliberately: the source establishes that seizures are controlled with difficulty and later improve, but does not attribute the improvement to medication rather than to the natural course.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Symptomatic seizure suppression. The link is to the seizure node only - no antiseizure medication addresses the trafficking or proteostasis arms.

evidence.snippet: However, seizure recurrence occurred when the treatment was shifted to oral vitamin B6
evidence.explanation: Typed PARTIAL because it qualifies rather than supports the treatment: the response did not persist on oral pyridoxine, which is what distinguishes a pyridoxal-phosphate-specific effect from general vitamin B6 responsiveness and is also the reason the benefit cannot be called durable.

treatments/1.description: Intravenous pyridoxal phosphate produced an initial seizure response in reported cases, and seizures recurred when treatment was switched to oral vitamin B6. That pairing is the clinically actionable part: it suggests responsiveness specific to the active cofactor rather than to pyridoxine, and it is worth a trial early in a neonatal-onset encephalopathy where the alternative is prolonged multi-agent empiricism. The evidence is a small number of reported cases, not a trial.

evidence.snippet: initially responded to intravenous pyridoxal phosphate
evidence.explanation: The reported seizure response.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Symptomatic seizure response. No mechanism links pyridoxal phosphate to the PACS2 trafficking defect, so the link is to the seizure node only and this entry makes no claim that the response is disease-specific.

evidence.snippet: The identification of pathogenic genetic variants in DEEs remains crucial for deciphering this complex group and for accurately caring for affected individuals (clinical diagnosis, genetic counseling, impacting medical, precision therapy, clinical trials, etc.).
evidence.explanation: States genetic counselling as one of the direct consequences of establishing the molecular diagnosis in this disease group.

treatments/2.description: Offered given the near-universal de novo occurrence and autosomal dominant inheritance once established, with recurrence risk limited to gonadal mosaicism.

evidence.snippet: we found that PACS-2 E209K increased susceptibility to staurosporine-induced apoptosis in HCT 116 cells
evidence.explanation: Names both the effect and the cell line, which is precisely the mismatch: HCT116 is a colorectal carcinoma line, not neural tissue.

evidence.snippet: Overall, our findings suggest PACS-2 E209K alters PACS-2 proteostasis and favors complex formation with 14-3-3ε, leading to increased cell death in the presence of environmental stressors.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own conclusion is conditional on environmental stressors, which is a weaker claim than the constitutive developmental death the cerebellar phenotype would require.

evidence.snippet: Glu209Lys mutation alters the regulatory domain, reflected by difficulties in PACS2 binding cargo proteins, which negatively impacts neuronal migration, neurogenesis, interneural communication, cerebellum development, and dendritic arborization
evidence.explanation: Names the trafficking-centred alternative route to cerebellar dysgenesis, which is the competing account this mismatch cannot currently exclude.

open_questions/0.rationale: This is the sharpest limitation in the entry, and it is structural rather than incidental. Every mechanistic measurement supporting the apoptosis arm comes from transfected transformed cell lines, and the apoptosis readout additionally requires an applied stressor rather than reporting spontaneous death. The disease phenotype, meanwhile, is a cerebellar malformation and a neonatal cortical epilepsy - neither of which is a cell-autonomous stress-death phenotype, and neither of which has been reproduced in any published in vivo model. A mouse carrying the variant has been reported to exist but no peer-reviewed phenotypic characterisation is available, and patient-derived iPSC neurons are in progress without published data. So the causal edge from apoptotic susceptibility to cerebellar dysgenesis is typed as having unknown intermediates for a reason: it is the field's working hypothesis, not a demonstrated route. The alternative possibility, that the developmental malformation arises from disturbed cargo trafficking during cerebellar morphogenesis with apoptosis playing little part, is equally consistent with everything currently published, and the same systematic review names candidate intermediates for it - neuronal migration, neurogenesis, cerebellum development and dendritic arborization - none of which requires cell death.

evidence.snippet: Mixed focal and generalized epilepsy occurred in the neonatal period, controlled with difficulty in the first year, but many improved in early childhood.
evidence.explanation: The observation itself - difficult control followed by improvement - which is what has no mechanistic account.

evidence.snippet: Only 4 cases have been reported in adults to date.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies how thin the adult evidence is, which is why the possible later progressive phase is raised as a question rather than curated as a disease stage.

open_questions/1.rationale: Age-dependent improvement sets DEE66 apart from most developmental and epileptic encephalopathies, where drug resistance persists, and it is a clinically consequential difference: it changes what families are told and how aggressively early polytherapy is pursued. Yet nothing explains it. The cerebellar dysgenesis is a fixed malformation and cannot remit, so whatever improves is not the structural lesion. No electrophysiological work in any PACS2 system has characterised cortical excitability at any age, so there is no measurement of the thing that is supposed to be changing. The question is sharpened by the small adult literature, which describes progressive decline rather than continued improvement - only four adults have been reported, so this is a signal rather than an established biphasic course, but if real it would mean the early remission masks an ongoing process rather than reflecting a resolved one.

evidence.snippet: Functional studies demonstrated that the PACS2 recurrent variant reduces the ability of the predicted autoregulatory domain to modulate the interaction between the PACS2 FBR and client proteins, which may disturb cellular function.
evidence.explanation: The most specific published functional consequence of the variant. Its own hedge - "may disturb cellular function" - marks how far short of a defined organelle phenotype the evidence currently stops.

open_questions/2.rationale: PACS2 is well established in the general cell-biology literature as a regulator of ER-mitochondria contact sites, and reviews of this disorder frequently carry that role forward as the mechanism. The gap is that the step from "PACS2 does this" to "the E209K variant breaks this" was not evidenced in any source verified for this entry. This entry therefore curates only what was measured - autoregulatory-domain impairment, slowed turnover, increased 14-3-3-epsilon association, increased stress-induced apoptosis - and deliberately does not carry a MAM node, because doing so would import a plausible mechanism as though it were a finding. That matters beyond bookkeeping: a MAM-centred model predicts calcium-handling and mitochondrial-energetics phenotypes and suggests quite different therapeutic targets from a trafficking-centred or proteostasis-centred model, and the three are currently not distinguished by evidence.

evidence.snippet: We describe six persons from three families with three homozygous protein truncating variants in PUS7
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic protein-truncating PUS7 alleles as the initiating lesion in the founding cohort.

evidence.snippet: The absence of highly extreme phenotypes such as short stature or microcephaly in this family might reflect genotype–phenotype correlation, since this family presented with a PUS7 missense mutation that may be hypomorphic, while previously reported families carried nonsense or frameshift mutations that may cause loss of function.
evidence.explanation: Documents the allelic spectrum and the proposed hypomorph-versus-null genotype-phenotype gradient.

steps/1.description: The disorder is initiated by inheritance of two damaging PUS7 alleles. The reported allelic spectrum includes frameshift alleles, nonsense alleles, a deletion of the penultimate exon that escapes nonsense-mediated decay but removes the C-terminal catalytic region, and missense alleles. Missense alleles appear to behave as hypomorphs, producing a milder phenotype without microcephaly or short stature.

evidence.snippet: PUS7 encodes the RNA-independent pseudouridylate synthase 7.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the gene product whose activity is lost, and its RNA-independent (guide-RNA-free) mode of substrate recognition.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, the missense variant of the S. cerevisiae ortholog failed to complement the growth defect of S. cerevisiae pus7Δ trm8Δ mutants.
evidence.explanation: Yeast complementation shows that a patient missense allele is a complete loss-of-function at the level of enzyme activity, not merely a destabilising substitution.

steps/2.description: PUS7 is an RNA-independent (stand-alone) pseudouridine synthase of the TruD family that isomerises uridine to 5-ribosyluracil without a guide snoRNA. Loss of its activity removes pseudouridine from every class of PUS7 substrate at once: cytosolic tRNAs, a defined set of mRNAs, and tRNA-derived small fragments.

evidence.snippet: PUS7 loss leads to hypo-pseudouridylation of 7SK, which promotes dissociation of the positive transcription elongation factor b (P-TEFb) complex from 7SK. The release of P-TEFb from 7SK increases serine 2 phosphorylation (Ser2P) in the RNA Pol II C-terminal domain and enhances transcription elongation.
evidence.explanation: The full molecular chain from PUS7 loss to enhanced Pol II elongation, demonstrated in cell lines.

steps/3.description: Loss of PUS7 leaves 7SK snRNA hypo-pseudouridylated, which releases the positive transcription elongation factor b complex from 7SK, raises serine-2 phosphorylation of the RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain, and enhances transcription elongation. This is a transcription-level rather than a translation-level consequence of the same enzymatic deficit. It is included because it is mechanistically established for PUS7 loss, but its relevance to the neurodevelopmental phenotype is entirely untested: the work was done in colorectal cancer cells, and no patient tissue has been examined.

evidence.snippet: Patient-derived cells showed decreased pseudouridylation signals specifically for PUS7 substrates at position 13 of at least 10 different cytosolic tRNAs, but not at other positions.
evidence.explanation: States both the breadth (at least ten tRNAs) and the specificity (position 13 only) of the modification loss in patient cells.

evidence.snippet: All identified PUS7 variants resulted in aberrant pseudouridylation of at least 10 cytosolic tRNAs at position 13.
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation that the position-13 defect is common to the whole reported allelic series.

steps/4.description: Patient cells lose pseudouridine specifically at position 13 of at least ten different cytosolic tRNAs, with other pseudouridine positions in the same tRNAs preserved. The defect is therefore a clean, position-specific ablation of one modification rather than a general collapse of tRNA maturation.

evidence.snippet: Mechanistically, we identify PUS7 targets in GSCs through small RNA pseudouridine sequencing and show that pseudouridylation of PUS7-regulated transfer RNA is critical for codon-specific translational control of key regulators of GSCs.
evidence.explanation: The direct demonstration that PUS7-dependent tRNA pseudouridine controls translation in a codon-specific rather than a global manner.

steps/5.description: PUS7-dependent tRNA pseudouridylation biases translation toward or away from particular codons, so its loss changes which transcripts are efficiently decoded. This is the most satisfying available answer to the central puzzle of the disorder: how the loss of a broadly expressed housekeeping RNA writer produces a selective, largely neurological phenotype rather than uniform cellular failure. The mapping was performed in glioblastoma stem cells, and the equivalent codon-level analysis has never been done in neurons or neural progenitors.

evidence.snippet: We show that the disease-related variants lead to abolishment of PUS7 activity on both tRNA and mRNA substrates.
evidence.explanation: Establishes mRNA as a genuine second substrate class lost in patients, not only tRNA.

steps/6.description: PUS7 recognises a UNPsiAR-type sequence motif and pseudouridylates a defined set of mRNAs. Patient cells show reduced mRNA pseudouridylation, although the functional consequence of this arm has not been established as disease-relevant.

evidence.snippet: Mechanistically, the Ψ "writer" PUS7 modifies and activates a novel network of tRNA-derived small fragments (tRFs) targeting the translation initiation complex.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the tRF arm and its molecular target, the translation initiation complex.

steps/7.description: PUS7 pseudouridylates a network of tRNA-derived small fragments (tRFs). The modification is what activates them; unmodified tRFs cannot engage the translation initiation complex.

evidence.snippet: PUS7 inactivation in embryonic stem cells impairs tRF-mediated translation regulation, leading to increased protein biosynthesis and defective germ layer specification.
evidence.explanation: Directly names the loss of tRF-mediated translation regulation as the consequence of PUS7 inactivation.

evidence.snippet: Building on evidence that mTOG-Ψ targets polyadenylate-binding protein cytoplasmic 1 (PABPC1), we employed isotope exchange proteomics to reveal critical interactions between mTOG and functional RNA-recognition motif (RRM) domains of PABPC1.
evidence.explanation: Identifies PABPC1 as the direct molecular target of the pseudouridylated tRF, which is what makes this the mechanistically best-resolved arm.

evidence.snippet: Mechanistically, this hinders the recruitment of translational co-activator PABPC1-interacting protein 1 (PAIP1)3 and strongly represses the translation of transcripts sharing pyrimidine-enriched sequences (PES) at the 5' untranslated region (UTR), including 5' terminal oligopyrimidine tracts (TOP) that encode protein machinery components
evidence.explanation: Spells out the repressive step that is lost in PUS7 deficiency and names the class of transcripts derepressed, including those encoding the translational machinery itself.

steps/8.description: PUS7-modified tRFs act as brakes on the translation initiation complex. The best-resolved arm is the mini-tRF carrying a 5-prime terminal oligoguanine (mTOG): its pseudouridine engages the RNA-recognition-motif domains of PABPC1, which blocks recruitment of the translational co-activator PAIP1 and represses translation of transcripts carrying pyrimidine-enriched and 5-prime terminal oligopyrimidine sequences, many of which encode components of the protein-synthesis machinery itself. Removing the brake therefore releases initiation from its normal ceiling, and does so in a feed-forward way because the derepressed transcripts build more translational machinery.

evidence.snippet: Patient fibroblasts demonstrated upregulation of protein synthesis, including elevated MYC protein, but did not exhibit increased rates of cell proliferation.
evidence.explanation: The primary human-cell evidence for the translational phenotype, including the dissociation from proliferation.

evidence.snippet: These findings strengthen the correlation between neurodevelopmental disease, particularly autism spectrum disorders, and the rate of protein translation.
evidence.explanation: Links the translational phenotype to the neurodevelopmental outcome in the authors' own framing.

steps/9.description: The convergent cellular consequence of losing PUS7 across all three substrate classes is loss of translational homeostasis. Fibroblasts from PUS7-deficient patients show upregulated protein synthesis with elevated MYC protein, and notably this occurs without a corresponding increase in proliferation rate, which distinguishes the neurodevelopmental consequence from the proliferative consequence of upregulated translation in cancer.

evidence.snippet: Interestingly, the dysregulation of protein translation also resulted in mildly decreased levels of HPRT1 protein suggesting an association between dysregulated protein translation and the LNS-like phenotypic findings.
evidence.explanation: Reports the reduced HPRT1 protein level and the authors' proposed link to the Lesch-Nyhan-like features.

steps/10.description: A translation-level, sequence-independent reduction in hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase protein. This is a proposed explanation for the Lesch-Nyhan-like hyperuricaemia and self-injurious behaviour observed in one sibling pair, and it has not been replicated in other PUS7 cohorts.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, pus7 knockout in Drosophila melanogaster results in a number of behavioral defects, including increased activity, disorientation, and aggressiveness supporting that neurological defects are caused by PUS7 variants.
evidence.explanation: Animal loss-of-function evidence that the neurological and specifically aggressive phenotype follows from loss of the enzyme.

evidence.snippet: Crucially, PUS7 knockdown in the ILPFC selectively impaired fear extinction memory formation without altering baseline fear expression, establishing a causal link between Ψ-dependent RNA processing and activity-dependent synaptic structural remodeling in this microcircuit.
evidence.explanation: Region-specific mouse knockdown showing that PUS7 is required for activity-dependent synaptic remodelling, a plausible cellular substrate for the cognitive phenotype.

evidence.snippet: The findings indicated that RNA pseudouridylation, along with tRNA modification is important for proper neural development
evidence.explanation: Independent restatement that the pseudouridylation defect converges on neural development.

steps/11.description: The convergent neural consequence. Human evidence is the invariant cognitive and behavioural phenotype; experimental support comes from pus7 knockout in Drosophila, which reproduces increased activity, disorientation and aggressiveness, and from mouse infralimbic prefrontal cortex knockdown, which selectively impairs an activity-dependent synaptic plasticity behaviour.

evidence.snippet: Crucially, PUS7 knockdown in the ILPFC selectively impaired fear extinction memory formation without altering baseline fear expression, establishing a causal link between Ψ-dependent RNA processing and activity-dependent synaptic structural remodeling in this microcircuit.
evidence.explanation: Region-specific mouse knockdown establishing a causal, plasticity-specific requirement for PUS7.

steps/12.description: A distinct, more disease-proximal neuronal mechanism than the developmental one. In mouse infralimbic prefrontal cortex, learning drives pseudouridine deposition on exons of synaptic regulatory genes and upregulation of synaptogenic transcripts, and PUS7 is required for this. Knocking PUS7 down in that region selectively blocks extinction learning while leaving baseline behaviour intact, which shows the requirement is for plasticity rather than for maintenance. This provides a candidate substrate for the cognitive and behavioural phenotype that is separable from the growth phenotype. It is mouse knockdown in adult cortex, not a germline model of the human disorder, so it is a mechanistic analogy and not a demonstration.

evidence.snippet: Both patients also had features of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, including hyperuricemia and self-injurious behavior, but without pathogenic variants in HPRT1.
evidence.explanation: The clinical observation defining this node.

steps/13.description: Hyperuricaemia with self-injurious behaviour resembling Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, observed in PUS7-deficient siblings with a normal HPRT1 gene. This branch of the graph is reported in a single family and should not be treated as a core feature of the disorder.

evidence.snippet: PUS7 gene pathogenic variants cause a deficiency in an RNA-independent pseudouridine synthase, which results in a neurodevelopmental phenotype characterized by various degrees of psychomotor delay, acquired microcephaly, aggressive behavior, and intellectual disability.
evidence.explanation: Explicitly characterises the microcephaly as acquired rather than congenital.

steps/14.description: Head circumference is typically normal or near-normal at birth and falls progressively across childhood, which is why the microcephaly is described as progressive or acquired rather than congenital. Brain MRI architecture is normal in most reported patients.

evidence.snippet: Recently, papers reported that variants in PUS7 in 16 patients were involved in marked growth retardation with microcephaly, associated with intellectual disability and behavioral issues such as self-injurious and aggressive behavior.
evidence.explanation: Summarises growth retardation as a defining feature of the previously published cohort.

steps/15.description: Poor overall growth with short stature and low weight, described as marked growth retardation in the larger cohorts. Growth failure is a feature of the truncating-allele families and was absent in the one reported missense (hypomorphic) family.

evidence.snippet: These features are common but non-specific, with the exception of aggressiveness that manifests at a very early age.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the discriminating behavioural feature within the otherwise non-specific phenotype.

steps/16.description: Moderate to severe intellectual disability with delayed or absent speech, plus a behavioural signature dominated by aggression of unusually early onset, and in a minority autistic traits, self-injury, stereotypies and sleep disturbance. The 2026 review argues that the core features are non-specific but that the very early onset of aggressiveness is the discriminating clue.

evidence.snippet: We show that the disease-related variants lead to abolishment of PUS7 activity on both tRNA and mRNA substrates.
evidence.explanation: Directly links the patient alleles to abolished enzymatic activity.

edges/1.description: Damaging biallelic alleles remove or inactivate the TruD-family pseudouridine synthase encoded by PUS7.

evidence.snippet: Functional characterization of the two mutations confirmed that both result in decreased levels of Ψ13 in tRNAs.
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived lymphoblastoid cells show the specific loss of the PUS7-dependent tRNA modification.

edges/2.description: Loss of the enzyme removes the position-13 pseudouridine it normally installs in cytosolic tRNAs.

evidence.snippet: Pseudouridylation of mRNA was also decreased, but the functional significance of this observation was unclear.
evidence.explanation: Documents the mRNA arm of the substrate loss and, honestly, its uncertain functional weight.

edges/3.description: The same catalytic loss removes pseudouridine from PUS7-dependent mRNA substrates.

evidence.snippet: Mechanistically, the Ψ "writer" PUS7 modifies and activates a novel network of tRNA-derived small fragments (tRFs) targeting the translation initiation complex.
evidence.explanation: Establishes tRNA-derived fragments as a distinct PUS7 substrate class whose activation depends on the modification.

edges/4.description: PUS7 also pseudouridylates and thereby activates a network of tRNA-derived small fragments; loss of the enzyme leaves these fragments unmodified and inactive.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report that pseudouridine synthase 7 (PUS7) can mediate pseudouridylation of 7SK small nuclear RNA (snRNA), a regulator of RNA polymerase II (Pol II) promoter-proximal pausing.
evidence.explanation: Establishes 7SK snRNA as a fourth PUS7 substrate class, distinct from tRNA, mRNA and tRNA-derived fragments.

edges/5.description: PUS7 also pseudouridylates the 7SK small nuclear RNA, which restrains RNA polymerase II promoter-proximal pausing. Whether this arm contributes to the human disorder is untested, so the edge belongs to an emerging rather than the canonical mechanism model.

evidence.snippet: We and others have previously emphasized the predilection of Mendelian diseases caused by tRNA modification genes to CNS involvement and how this suggests the vulnerability of the brain to any perturbation of tRNA modification, presumably through its deleterious effect on protein synthesis
evidence.explanation: The authors state this link as an inference ("presumably"), so the edge is curated as INDIRECT with PARTIAL support rather than as a demonstrated mechanism.

edges/6.description: Loss of a conserved tRNA body modification perturbs the translational apparatus.
